The generator network uses transposed convolutional layers to up-sample the input feature vectors. A series of transposed convolutional layers are used with various channel counts, including 64, 128, 256, and 512. The blocks at each level indicate the input feature vector’s dimensions.

Finally, the structure of the samples produced by this model is similar to that of the input data.

MobilenetV3 based feature extraction

In this section, MobileNetV3 based feature extraction technique is applied to extract the significant characteristics from the preprocessed data. This architecture consists of several bottleneck components. One of the bottleneck components in this system is the residual framework. In a conventional bottleneck framework, feature extraction only has one path; however, in our technique, there are two paths for feature extraction. It’s called partial residual structure. This structure is employed to reduce the residual framework’s calculation expense.

In MobileNetV3, the advanced version of a sigmoid function called hard swish (hswish) is utilized. It reduces the network’s size, complexity, and training parameters. This activation function is illustrated in the following equation.

(7)
h − swish(x) = x.σ(x)

(8)
$$.\sigma(x) = \frac{{Re}LU6(x + 3)}{6}$$

The piece-wise linear complex analog function is represented here by a(x).

In this partial residual structure, the bottleneck block’s input feature map is separated into two equal portions and given as the input to path 1 and path 2, respectively. In path 1, the significant features from the input are extracted through the convolution layer (1*1 filter size), depthwise convolution layer (3*3 filter size), and again convolution layer with 1*1 filter size. The result of the residual learning segment is directly connected to another path through the shortcut connection. Likewise, in path 2, the attributes are extracted from the input through the convolution layer (1*1 filter size), depthwise convolution layer (5*5 filter size), and convolution layer with 1*1 filter size. Finally, the output of these two paths is concatenated via the transition layer. This transition layer includes batch a normalization layer (BN), 1*1 pointwise convolutional kernel, and hswish activation functions for the fusion of the feature maps. We included dilated convolution in the 3*3 and PS convolutions of the first and last Mobile modules. Dilated convolution enlarged the receptive field and enhanced the information extraction. To decrease the loss of information during the fusion process, the cross-layer connection is introduced among the modules.

Improved LeNet-5 based Classification

For classification, the Lenet-5 network receives the feature maps obtained from the MobileNetV3 network. LeNet is a robust and simple-to-use algorithm. Additionally, it increases the chance of real-time execution and reduces structural complexity. In total, the LeNet-5 has eight layers. They are an input layer, two convolution layers, two fully linked layers, two subsampling layers, and an output layer. The subsampling layer of this network serves as the pooling system.

The extracted features from the MobileNetV3 are sent to leNetS’s input layer for attack classification. A dropout layer is put among the fully connected layer and the convolution layer with a dropout rate of 0.8 to prevent overfitting. The subsampling layer’s kernel size is set to 2×2, while the kernel size of the convolutional layer is assigned to 5x5. To minimize parameter training, the total number of neurons in the connection layer is reduced from 120 to 84. The significant features are selected in the subsampling layer, and the input feature matrix is subsequently reduced in two dimensions based on the 2x2 pool size while keeping the fundamental characteristics of the data. The functionality of the pooling layer is expressed in equation (7),

(9)
anl = pool(anl − 1)

Here, pool(.) stands for the maximum pooling operation, the output iof the preceding layer is typically written as an , the nth sample is denoted by n, and the production of the lth layer is generally represented as an Thisframework’s last layer is the fully connected layer. There are two thoroughly combined layers in traditional Lenet-5. However, this study uses only one fully linked layer to simplify the network’s computations and reduce the parameter’s numbers. To normalize the input of each layer, we additionally inserted BN after each convolution layer and after the fully connected layer. It accomplishes the objective of rapid training by ensuring that the input data distribution in every layer is steady.

The ReLU activation function is utilized in this network to connect every neuron. The neuron’s output is transmitted to the output layer from the fully connected layer, which can integrate local information with the capacity to distinguish between classes. The fully connected layer, therefore, plays an essential role in traditional classifiers. The output of the fully connected lth layer is described in the following equation.

The fully connected lth layer’s output is shown in equation (8). In that, b’ is the offset term, and the convolutional kernel is denoted by wt.

(10)
anl = f(wl⋅anl − 1+bl)

Here, w1 represents the convolutional kernel and offset term denoted by b’

The softmax layer is the last output layer. The output class with the most significant probability is chosen by this layer. The equation that follows illustrates this function.

(11)

Here, The probability of the nth instance for vtn classes is Ovn (n=1,2,3 N; v=1,2,3 V). if represents the estimated outcome probabilities of the nth instance in v classes, the global (E) and local (En) error formula of the nth sample is given in the following equations

(12)
$$E_{n} = \frac{1}{2}\underset{v = 1}{\overset{V}{\sum^{}}}\left\| {t_{n}^{v} - o_{n}^{v}} \right\|_{2}^{2}$$

(13)
$$E = {\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{N}E_{n}}$$

The output is then generated by the softmax layer using the classes’ maximum probabilities.

Mitigation phase

When the suggested framework identifies a DDoS assault, the mitigation module is activated. This module aims to employ defenses to lessen the harm brought on by an assault. The remote SDN controller turns on the congestion control algorithm block to defend against Cyberattacks. The activated OF switches must drop a specific intervention connection and transfer the network services to the proper network hosts under the direction of the remote SDN controller. When investigating traffic requests from particular source hosts as DDoS attacks, OF switches, proceed per the instructions of the SDN controller. In this manner, the network assets are transferred to authorized customers to continue the regular network activity.

Experiments and Results

The effectiveness of the DDoS intrusion detection mechanism in the SDN simulation framework is examined in this section. The simulation experiments are conducted using TensorFlow’s Keras framework and the Python language with 24 GB of memory. The processor used was an Intel 15-6300HQ4 core, and the operating system was Windows 10. Additionally, an NVIDIA GTX 960 graphics card accelerates the GPU. A topology with 14 OF switches and 28 hosts has been built using Mininet. The choice of a controller is crucial for simulating an SDN network. For the experiment, we used the PDX controller. To confirm that the network’s connected hosts can be activated, ICMP ping packets are sent back and forth among nodes.

For investigation analysis, Eighty percent of the experimental data set is used for training, while twenty percent is used for testing. The default learning rate was set to 0.001 throughout the training phase. The activation function was set to ReLU, the number of epochs was set to 100, and the optimizer was set to adaptive learning rate optimization algorithm (Adam)for training deep learning networks.

Dataset Description

InSDN dataset

A team from University College Dublin created the InSDN, a brand-new dataset, in September 2020. Using a logical method, this dataset was produced. These include DoS, DDoS, Brute

Force Assaults, Probe, U2R, Web-Attack, and BotNET. It also covers more contemporary, less uncommon types of attacks. Additionally, primary application services like SSH, FTP, Email, DNS, HTTP, and HTTPS are included in the InSDN dataset’s regular traffic. The dataset simulates actual attack scenarios with 83 statistical variables and contains 343,939 benign and malicious traffic, similar threat data in the real computer network.

CICIDS2017 dataset

A recent open-source dataset for intrusion detection called CICIDS-2017 was created by the Canadian Institute of Cybersecurity. The date, destination, source IP addresses, assaults, protocols, and destination ports are used as the labels of the dataset. The original network traffic features are present in this dataset, and it was gathered over five days and contains 2,830,743 entries and 80 internet traffic characteristics. The dataset includes a CSV file containing regular intrusion traffic and eight traffic monitoring sessions. There are several distinct types of assaults in this dataset, including DDoS, DoS, SSH, brute force, FTP, botnet, infiltration, Heartbleed, and web attacks.

Evaluation Metrics

The most common performance metrics, such as F-score, recall, precision, and accuracy, are used to assess the model’s performance. These metrics are calculate dusing equations (14)–(17).

(14)
$$Accuracy~ = \frac{tr_{p} + tr_{n}}{~number\ of\ samples~}$$

(15)
$$~~Precision~ = \frac{tr_{p}}{tr_{p} + fl_{p}}$$

(16)
$${Re}~call~ = \frac{tr_{p}}{tr_{p} + fl_{n}}$$

(17)
$$~F1~ - ~score~ = 2 \times \frac{~precision~ \times ~recall~}{~precision~ + ~recall~}$$

Here True Negative (trn) and True Positive (trp) denote values that were accurately predicted, while False Negative (fln) and False Positive (flp) denote occurrences that were incorrectly classified.

Result and Discussion

Performance Analysis on InSDN Dataset

In this part, the effectiveness of the suggested technique on the InSDN dataset is discussed. The performance of the recommended strategy for multiclass classification on the InSDN dataset is shown in Table 1 and Fig. 2. It can be seen from the graph and table that the proposed approach’s prediction performance is best for the normal, DDoS, DoS, and probe categories. However, in U2R and Web-attack classes, the proposed technique’s performance is slightly lower than in other classes. Because the similarity of these attacks is a high degree to regular traffic, given that the attacker legally gained access to the target system. As a result, complexity can be imposed by the learning classifier when defending the appropriate decision bounds.

Accuracy is the primary factor used to determine the IDS’s intelligence. IDS intelligence for classifying traffic into the attack and regular classes is indicated by a maximum accuracy value. Due to the imbalanced data based on the various web attack patterns, most existing techniques poorly detected the web attacks in the InSDN dataset. Therefore, in this paper, to overcome the imbalance problem, the CGAN approach oversampled the unbalanced samples in the training dataset. As a result, the suggested technique achieves very high detection accuracy for all classes of web attacks.

Performance Analysis of Mitigation

Figure 6 displays the amount of bandwidth used by the network during live DDoS attacks. Moreover, it demonstrates how the network performance would change throughout specific simulation segments while DDoS attacks were active. They also show significant performance when implementing the proposed framework’s DDoS detection and mitigation. Once DDoS attacks start to be generated, we can see that network traffic grows dramatically. When we execute the suggested architecture, network traffic drastically lowers, and most DDoS attacks are identified and neutralized. It implies that the defensive strategy worked in the network, and the resources are returned to the authorized users in this manner.

Conclusion

To accurately identify network attacks in an SDN network, this article developed a deep learning-based method. In the SDN network dataset, attacks are detected, and attack classes are categorized using MobileNetV3 and LeNet-5. Our investigation of the proposed methoD's performance against other approaches revealed that it successfully identified the various network attack types in the InSDN and CICIDS2017 datasets, achieving accuracy rates of 99.56% and 99.72%, respectively. The suggested approach outperformed the other comparable methods in both datasets, enabling its use against various DDoS attacks on the SDN environment. The proposed strategy can aid in identifying and mitigating DDoS attacks while preserving a network’s regular operation.

Our upcoming study will analyze new attack types, like phishing attacks, for test evaluation. To understand how this IDS can respond to the attack in real time, we also intend to implement our suggested model in a real SDN network.

Comprehensive Autonomous Vehicle Optimal Routing With Dynamic Heuristics

V. Ragav21

Vellore Institute of Technology, Chennai Campus, India

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-24

Abstract

Auto manufacturers and research groups are working on autonomous driving for a long period and achieved significant progress. Autonomous vehicles (AV) are expected to transform road traffic reduction from current conditions, avoiding accidents and congestion. The proposed model to improve AV user experience uses a hybrid AV Network of multiple connected autonomous vehicles which communicate with each other in an environment shared by human-driven vehicles. The proposed Optimal AV Network (OAVN) solution provides better coordination and optimization of autonomous vehicles, improved Transportation efficiency, improved passenger comfort and safety, a real-time dynamic adaption of traffic & road conditions along with improved in-cabin assistance with inputs from various sensors. The true optimal solution for this problem is to devise an automated guidance system for vehicles in an AV network, to reach destinations in the best possible routes along with passenger comfort and safety. A custom-informed search model is proposed along with other heuristic goals for better user experience. The results are analyzed and compared to evaluate the effectiveness of the solution and identify gaps and future enhancements.

Keywords: Autonomous vehicles Networks, dynamic routing, variable heuristics, AV Safety.

Introduction

The concept of autonomous driving has been in talks for more than seven decades. In spite of several attempts by engineers to give shape to this idea, failed to succeed. From the first attempt by Ernst Dickmanns in 80’s called VaMP((Kroger, 2016), tested in a controlled environment & DARPA Grand Challenge(Thrun et al., 2007), there are umpteen attempts made till present Waymo & Autopilot.

To completely bring the benefits of AV technology, all vehicles need to be connected both to one another and to roadside systems (traffic light systems, traffic monitoring, emergency or maintenance services). These connections in the network need to be in real-time with low latency and high reliability leveraging the benefits of modern networks like SG services.

Typically AV connects to the network for V2V (Vehicle to Vehicle) and vehicle-to-network (V2N) communication through a dedicated network to exchange information AV networks can be rated in S stages, Assisted Operations, Partial autonomous, conditional, High, and fully autonomous stages.

As AV network size increases the operational expenses to manage them, predictive maintenance, and optimal routing needs increase. The proposed model collates data from various sensors, applies Machine Learning(ML) models, and optimizes through hybrid path routing algorithms for better navigation and traffic avoidance.

Objectives and Assumptions

When the AV networks mature with increased adaptability, the need for intra-vehicle communication and optimizing their routes to meet the goals and constraints are necessary. For this, a Coordinated Autonomous Vehicle Decision Making with Network Heuristics optimization approach is proposed, which learns & adapts to the environment.

  1. Goal: To propose an AV network model to enable optimal traversal of AV from source to the destination with user-controlled heuristics, meeting defined optimality conditions.
  2. Optimality Conditions: Minimum distance (minimum energy consumption), Minimum time to destination, Maximum Comfort & Safety
  3. iii. Assumptions of proposed Solution: The model assumes that all Autonomous vehicles are connected and controlled by the same network. Autonomous vehicles are in a mixed environment with human-driven vehicles

All the basic AV maneuvering features are matured and available such as object detection, obstacle avoidance, network communication, etc, while the solution focuses on macro optimal navigation.

AV Network Environment

Autonomous vehicles need increasingly sophisticated systems, with high-performance computers and a large number of advanced driver assistance system sensors, such as HR cameras, LIDAR (Light Detection and Ranging), and noise sensors.

These eco-systems generate large amounts of data, which demands high-speed data nodes, links, switches, and assemblies. The inside of the AV is like an information highway with data streams flowing in different directions managed for better comfort and safety. Automotive OEM manufacturers follow the network connectivity standards. The network support depends on the need like infotainment to ADAS (Driver Assistance) with bandwidth needed to 1 to 25 GBPS range.

V2X, (vehicle-to-everything) interfacing technology permits vehicles to directly communicate with each other, and roadside infra / users to deliver road safety, traffic management, smart mobility & sustainability of environment. Both sensor & radio-based interfaces are needed for V2X (Choi et al., 2017).

Vehicle to Network (V2N) aims to send information among vehicles through high-bandwidth/reliability & low-latency network ecosystem. V2N systems integrate vehicles with data centers consonantly for stable information exchange. V2N network also connects vehicles with other vehicles in the network. Though popular apps can provide traffic updates and navigation, they have limitations. Vehicles share more detailed information about their position, status, speed, direction, intersection movement assist (IMA), and Left turn assist (LTA) to improve safety. V2N can also prompt pedestrian devices (V2P) to avoid possible accidents.

  1. The AV cloud infra stores HD maps, multimedia streams from vehicles and live traffic data as V2N updates. This also provides computing infrastructure to execute Machine language and routing algorithms proposed.

Proposed Optimization Model

Model Component and Interfaces

The AV optimal routing model is based on sensing (perception), understanding localized scenarios, dynamic path planning & guided navigation control. Among these Path planning is the complex step to find a collision-free path in a given constrained real-time environment (Mac et al., 2016). It is a non-deterministic polynomial-time hard problem to solve (Chen & Quan, 2008). Different sensors, and interfaces used are detailed in Fig. 2, along with device details, purpose, and algorithms used for different tasks. The AV sensors are categorized based on their location such as in-cabin, outside AV, and inside AV-machinery loaded sensors. The inside vehicle sensors used are microphones, HD cameras, smoke detectors, IR (for user cabin temperature control), etc. Outside sensors used are Lidar, Ultrasonic sensors, cameras, etc. Inside AV sensors include microphones (for wear and tear detection using anomaly detection) and sensors for engine health monitoring.

AV Sensors, functions, and ML algorithms

All the sensor data and video streams are collated by Sensor fusion methods and scene/environment visualization is deduced. The single vehicle sensor streams and fusion data is transmitted to AV cloud storage with vehicle identification. Similar information is collected from multiple vehicles in the Optimal AV Network ( OAVN) proposed as a comprehensive solution.

Different machine learning (ML) models proposed as in Table 1, are executed in cloud computing infrastructure along with minor pre-processing done at edge nodes. The system/user/passenger preferences on comfort parameters are also fed to the Network.

The ML outputs are fed as heuristic parameter updates along with user preferences as a co- efficient of dynamic A* algorithm for optimal route search. The dynamic A* algorithm gets updated node data continuously from environment and direct the component vehicles in optimal route to avoid collision and traffic in a better route for comfort and safety.

4.3 The Dynamic A* Network route optimization:

To select an optimal route from the source to destination, various search algorithms such as uniform cost search (UCS)[6], greedy search (best first search), A* search were compared and analyzed. Among the algorithms, A* performed better(Cui & Shi, 2010), compared to others on similar environments. The proposed dynamic A* search model works to meet the varying constraints and responses from the environment(Seo et al.,2009). The changes are represented by the heuristic function at each node(Fe rg uson et al., 2005). The ML model outputs define the changes to heuristic values and their coefficients, which are optimized by the dynamic A*. An optimal search solution using the A* Search is chosen, with variable heuristics (Distance, Time, Comfort, Safety) parameters. This model combines the results from computer vision through camera frames which detects obstacles, road conditions, and in-cabin safety aspects through ML Model learning is proposed.

Dynamic A* approach:

Let f(n)= the estimated cost of the solution

hi(n) = heuristic value with respect to time taken to reach the destination.

h2(n) = heuristic value with respect to comfort (road condition/traffic)

h3(n) = heuristic value for safety (constant & not changed for any condition)

(1)
$$\frac{~Thus,~\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{n}) = \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{n}) + \mathbf{h}_{1}(\mathbf{n}) + \mathbf{h}_{2}(\mathbf{n}) + \mathbf{h}_{3}(\mathbf{n})}{}$$

This provides optimal cost function for the normal heuristics conditions assumed.

This approach modifies the equation (1) with variable coefficients which are a result of Combining current heuristics cost, with inputs from the computer vision & in-cabin predicted model outputs, a new cost value is found.

(2)
f1(n) = w1g(n) + w2h1(n) + w3h2(n) + w4h3(n)

where, w1, w2 and w3 are the coefficients that determine the weight of each heuristic.

For example, based on the sensor output, which identifies quality of the road and the past experience of other vehicles traveled on same path earlier, the model analyses the comfort of travel and alters the coefficients of the heuristics (weights) appropriately.

The value of the heuristic function of each node is calculated by the ML models dynamically and fed to the search algorithm which returns the optimal route. The dynamic A* algorithm pseudocode is described below:

Dyn_A_star (start, goal, w1, w2)

create open set and closed set

add start node to open set with g(start) = 0

and f(start)= w1*h1(start) +w2*h2(start)

+w3 *h3(start)

while open set is not empty do

current_node = node in open set with

lowest f value

remove current_node from open set;

add current_node to closed set

if current_node is goal then,

return path from start to goal

if successor is in closed set then,

continue

tentative _g_ score = g(current_node) +

cost(current_node, successor)

if successor is not in open set or

tentative _g_ score < g(successor) then

set g(successor) = tentative _g_ score

set h1(successor) = heuristic_cost_

based_on_time(successor)

set h2(successor) = heuristic_cost_based

on_comfort(successor)

set h3(successor) = heuristic_cost_based_

on_safety(successor)

set f(successor) = g(successor)

+ w1*h1(successor)+ w2*h2(successor)

+w3 * h3(successor)

if successor is not in open set then,

add successor to open set

update heuristics based on current state of

the search

end while

return failure end function

Machine Learning AV Models

As detailed above, ML outcomes determine real- time heuristic values of above dynamic A* model. Assisted ML Algorithms used for various tasks like Computer vision (Object Detection), In- Cabin Assistance (ML), Comfort (smoother roads and lesser traffic), and preventive maintenance (with on machinery noises) are made mature with, repeated training and validation of data collected from different sensors The fusion modules collates different sensor outputs to understand the dynamically changing on-road scenarios.

For example, an outside AV HD camera (FUR Blackfly - BFS-U3-50S5C) is used for Object detection &, Obstacle avoidance A machine learning model such as a convolutional neural network (CNN) or a support vector machine (SVM) (Ponti I & Vern, 1998) can be trained to analyze video/image streams, detect single/ multiple objects and identify patterns that may indicate an obstacle with below model parameters.

A typical SSD300 object detector with Resnet-50 convoluted neural network (CNN) backbone is used for vehicle object detection from a color-compensated image stream/frames (Srivastava et al., 2021). Results analysis

In the above sections the proposed several widely used path planning algorithms and their variants, categorized based on the static and dynamic characteristics they can handle and their adaptability. These result comparisons are listed in table-3 below. The Optimality & Adaptability score is calculated from the scenarios, the model deduces and acts correctly, with the total scenarios validated.

From the above analysis, we find that the accuracy and relevance of the proposed dynamic heuristic A* algorithm perform better with improved adaptability to real-time scenarios and environmental conditions.

6.0 Conclusion and Enhancements

In the forthcoming era, AVs will become a vital part of the modern transport ecosystem(Chowdhury & Dey, 2016) and it is expected to transform the transportation industry in the coming years. Major research on AV prevailing is on individual vehicle navigational control through reinforcement learning and adapting to environment dynamics(Wen et al., 2020). Other areas of research on the optimization of AV networks through parameterized routing in dynamic road scenarios (Zhu & Aksun-Guvenc, 2020) and several quasi-learning approaches like grey wolf optimizer (Elsisi, 2022). Perception & representation of apt models, of real-life scenarios remains the highest challenge for reliable and smoother auto driving with safety measures. This article aims at a more comprehensive hybrid prototype, with dynamic heuristics to find AV network route optimization solution. The proposed model stores the environmental data from the OAVN to the cloud and controls the dynamic heuristics with user-controlled coefficients and found to perform better with real-time conditions.

Fake Review Detection in Movie Recommendation System Using Hybrid Method

P. Eshwara, Gokul Krishna, and S. Sathya Priya

Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

E-mail: 19113077@student.hinudstanuniv.ac.in; 19113073@student.hindustanuniv.ac.in; * sathyapriya80@gmail.com

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-25

Abstract

The paper proposes a hybrid method for detecting fake reviews in movie recommendation systems to eliminate the negative effects of artificial reviews on user choices. The proposed system uses a combination of network and profile features of the user to identify accounts posting fake reviews to promote or demote a particular movie. The network features include location and network usage while the profile features include account activity and creation date. The IP address of the fake accounts is then blocked to prevent them from further posting fake reviews. Real reviews from genuine accounts are used for movie recommendations, providing users with accurate and reliable recommendations based on their preferences. The objective is to enhance user trust in the recommendation system and to provide users with more reliable and authentic reviews. The study shows that the proposed hybrid method outperforms existing methods for fake review detection in terms of precision, recall, and accuracy. The results indicate that the proposed method significantly improves the credibility and reliability of recommendation systems by removing misleading and fake reviews.

Keywords: Hybrid model, Machine Learning, Network, Profile, Review

Introduction

Currently, how the media is consumed is heavily dependent on the people’s and critics’ reviews and tastes. But this can be easily tweaked and abused by the people who want to make the movie a hit or a flop by spamming fake reviews. Movies that are released and which are added in OTT platforms are subjected to reviews and ratings by the users and audience who consume them. Users taste in movies are subjective and can vary among a different set of people. The domain is majorly based on network security. Filtering out fake users and blocking their IP addresses is the prominent system and this system is appended to Movie recommendation system.

Fake reviews can be found everywhere and these fake reviews tend to mess with the algorithm of movie recommendation models and produce false suggestions to the users. There are multiple techniques in which the reviews can be filtered, but users keep on posting fake reviews for upcoming movies which reduces the efficiency of the movie recommendation models drastically. This system aims to target the users who post fake reviews and block them using I.P Blocking techniques and use these filtered reviews from the real accounts to suggest movies that will give a better and unbiased result based on the user’s taste in the movies. The users who post reviews are analyzed based on their Network and Profile features in the dataset and using Hybrid Machine Learning model, those are identified as fake and authentic accounts. The reviews from these authentic accounts are taken into consideration for the Movie Recommendation model which recommends movies for the user based on their taste and reviews.

This system helps in reducing the viewership of good movies due to bad campaigning and reviews spread by negative people. This also helps in identifying and clearing the context and genre of the movie because fake reviews can deviate the audience from the actual content of that particular movie. The previous systems provide fake reviews detection only using NLP by analyzing reviews posted by the users and not the actual users. Implementing Fake reviews can be posted by the same user from multiple accounts. Implementing an existing fake review detection system is not optimal. In many systems where fake users are identified, users cannot be controlled if the same thing is repeated with an alternative account. These issues are addressed in the proposed system.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. A summary of some of the literature referenced is provided in Section 2. In Section 3, the suggested system and modules are shown and discussed. The results and performance evaluation are presented in Section IV. In Part V, the conclusions are drawn and potential improvements are discussed.

Literature Survey

A system that uses sources, users, and articles as the input to a Multiview co-attention network model (Qureshi et al., 2021) to verify the credibility of the news. Provide three innovative representation components to depict consumers’ Personal prejudices, news sources, political bias, and thematic opinions in the news. The Multiview co-attention network model outperforms several top-class models, comprehending various false article identification algorithms, according to experimental results.

A system that uses the graph autoencoder to take advantage of the high level of memory and learning ability of Graph Convolution Network to identify features that accurately represent the fundamental characteristics of users who add reviews in movie recommendation systems

and movie rating dataset (Sun et al., 2022). The thorough experiment demonstrates that our method, PCA- Denoising Autoencoder Graph Convolution Network, is capable of achieving much higher accuracy compared to other different models for movie recommendation.

To do a binary classification of tweets, (Parisa Bazmi et al., 2023) suggested a dataset combining the connectivity patterns of news publishments with the user profile features. This feature set is employed in a machine-learning model. Creating a COVID-19 dataset for Twitter that’s used to detect fake news. Unique features are present in this dataset. It is a dataset of communities that, in addition to their context, also include linkages between retweeters and posters.

The system employs Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, and Random Forest to produce a standardized model for spotting bogus reviews. The work (Abdulqader, et al., 2022), which regards phony reviews as a type of deception, offers unified terminology to explain deception components and a clear mapping between deception theories and the chosen verbal and non-verbal indicators for fake review detection.

A fresh fake news dataset-building process has been developed (Kang et al., 2022). The dataset creates a heterogeneous graph structure to represent news, user features, and their interaction. In order to solve the Korean false news problem, the usage of a graph learning framework that efficiently makes use of users and data from the news and their interactions was suggested.

The features (extracted from user metadata and public data) have been analyzed by (Giuseppe D'aniello, et al., 2020) to see whether and to what degree predicting the dependability of social media users; A deep learning model for classification of users as reliable and unreliable to be appended to the user profile was designed, implemented, and experimentally evaluated on a publically accessible dataset.

These methods focus on the reviews posted by the users and not the actual users. The fake accounts are improving to produce authentic movie reviews which makes these methods irrelevant (Premkumar and Sathya Priya, 2020). Fake user identification is not optimized enough in the previous methods. The previous systems have just given solutions to identify fake reviews using NLP, or failed to identify or prevent the fake users from taking advantage. Consequently, the project’s goal is to raise the caliber of reviews, which will raise the caliber of the media that people consume. This will benefit the media by lowering the corruption of false users in key details and data.

Proposed System

From Fig. 1, the dataset contains 3 different partitions which are linked together using their common ID's: User Profile dataset, Review Dataset, and Movies Dataset. The User Information Dataset is pre-processed to remove the noisy data and given to the Fake User Analysis model. This model uses Naïve Bayes Classifier to analyze the dataset on two different aspects: The Network aspects and the Profile aspects. The Network aspects will have the features like Number of nodes, IP address, Number of edges, and Number of communities. The User aspects include the features like verified, Account Recovery Details, Payment Details, and Account activity in other websites.

By analyzing these features, the model can identify fake users from actual users. The models containing these features are combined using Stacking Classifier Hybrid ML model. This Stacking Classifier uses Logistic Regression as its Meta Classifier The reviews from the actual users are identified by the tagged id in the review dataset. The fake users identified are traced back to their IP and their IP address is blocked. The reviews of movies with actual users are loaded in the Movie Recommendation model. This dataset is converted into a rating matrix that contains the ratings only from the real users. This matrix goes through cleaning and transformation to put through the Principal Component Analysis algorithm. This algorithm is put through Denoising Autoencoder to extract the hidden features of the data and it is appended with Graph Convolution Network. Through this model, the users have suggested movies based on their tastes and reviews.

Algorithm:

Input: User Information and Ratings Dataset

Output: Recommended movies for the users.

Process: Hybrid ML model.

For in

  • IF: User is fake, I.P address of the user is blocked.
  • ELSE: User is real, the ratings of the real users are separated and formed a rating matrix (R).

Process: PCA-DAECGN(R)

Returns: Predicted value of the movie. The greater the value, the higher the user likes the movie. END

Process: Movies are recommended to each user based on the Predicted value for the respective movies.

The PCA-DAECGN algorithm is used for the movie recommendation system. The rating matrix and its transpose are formed from the reviews dataset which is given as input to PCA model. The output from the PCA model is given to the Denoising Auto encoders to extract the hidden features. The features are processed by GCN which gives the predicted score for each user corresponding to the movies.

Results and Discussion

Performance Metrics


$$\begin{matrix} \begin{matrix} & {~Accuracy~ = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + FP + TN + FN}} \\ & {~Precision~ = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}} \\ \end{matrix} \\ {Recall~ = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}} \\ \end{matrix}$$


$$~F1\ measure~ = \frac{2 \ast ~Precision~ \ast ~Recall~}{~Precision~ + ~Recall~}$$

The Network Feature Analysis and User Profile Feature Analysis are processed with n_model and u_model using Gaussian Naive Bayes Classifier and produce an accuracy score of 75% and 76% respectively. The features are then combined and evaluated using the naive Bayes model (better performing individual model). This gives an accuracy score of 86%. Then the combined features and models are given to the Stacking Classifier Hybrid ML model with Logistic Regression as the meta-classifier. Use of prediction probabilities and use of features from the primary models are set as True. Using Stacking Classifier Hybrid model, the accuracy score is 98%, which is 12% better than the existing high-performing model.

With the use of Confusion Matrix (Fig. 3), the performance of this model is evaluated and projected using Recall Score, Precision Score, and Fl Score which are tabulated in Table 1. The performance evaluation display that the proposed system overcomes the drawbacks of the previous models effectively.

Table 1. Performance Evaluation
Metrics Precision Recall Fl-Score Support

Fake Users 1.00 0.999 0.998 722
Average 0.999 3000
Macro Avg. 0.999 0.997 0.9 3000
Weighted Avg. 0.999 0.998 0.997 3000

The filtered dataset received from this model is given to the Movie Recommendation Model which displays an improved accuracy than the previous models and dataset used. Thus, this proves great improvement in splitting the features by network and user profile analysis, and combining the models using hybrid model is much more effective than using a single machine learning model to evaluate all the features together.

Notations used:

TP=True Positive, TN=True Negative, FP=False Positive, FN=False Negative.

Conclusion

The rising prevalence of fake reviews in movie recommendation systems is a significant problem that affects users’ decision-making processes. The existing systems primarily rely on sentimental analysis techniques, which may not be effective in identifying sophisticated fraudulent reviews. Therefore, the paper proposes a hybrid method that uses machine learning algorithms to detect fake reviews based on linguistic features, such as grammatical errors, writing style, and keyword patterns, without relying on sentimental analysis. The proposed system utilizes network and user profile features to trace the fake accounts from which fraudulent reviews are posted. The system accurately identifies false reviews and removes them, providing users with reliable and trustworthy movie recommendations. The hybrid method outperforms the existing systems in terms of precision, recall, and accuracy. The development of this technique is an important step toward ensuring the integrity and reliability of movie recommendation systems. It is important to note that fake users may deploy new methods to overcome this proposed system in the future. However, new features can be added to overcome such attacks and make the system more effective and relevant to changes in the future. In conclusion, the proposed hybrid method has the potential to enhance the credibility and reliability of movie recommendation systems, and it can be applied to other domains where fake reviews are prevalent, thereby providing a more robust and effective method for identifying fraudulent reviews.

Leprosy Screening Through Image Processing Methods

Pratham Agrawal,22

Corresponding author Email ID: *biji.cl@vit.ac.in

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-26

Abstract

The paper attempts to investigate the possibility of developing leprosy screening methods through image analysis. The conventional diagnosis of leprosy is typically based on clinical evaluation and is highly subjective. Skin smears are used to screen patients for leprosy. The lab personnel used the smears to get morphological information viz bacilli shape and the clusters for grading the severity of the disease. The examination consumes time and demands skilled technicians especially when it is of a low bacterial load or even negative, as bacilli per field of view for the entire smear which consists of around 500 fields. Hence, the Image processing workflow is designed in detecting and counting the number of Mycobacterium leprae. The workflow involves two methods (i) Object detection through thresholding and (ii) Contour detection based on filtering. Finally, the Mycobacterium leprae are counted using the generated mask or contour to report the presence or absence of the bacilli and the level of severity of the disease.

Keywords: Leprosy Screening, Thresholding, Segmentation, Contouring

Introduction

Leprosy caused by Mycobacterium leprae (M. leprae) is a progressive bacterial infection but is curable (Domachowske, 2019). Although the prevalence of this disease has significantly gone down after the introduction of the WHO regimen of Multi-drug Therapy (MDT) (WHO Expert Committee on Leprosy, 1998), the incidence remains still a concern. Very recently, a high incidence is reported in various states in India, despite advances in all spheres of medical sciences. Statistics by NLEP show 76% of new leprosy cases in some parts of India which includes children between the ages of 1 to 18 years. Based on the reports from all states by NLEP, a total of 57,672 leprosy cases are on record as of 2021. The report says the child cases detected in 2021 were 1616 (NLEP Annual Report 2020-2021. Fig. 1. shows the prevalence of leprosy in India for the years 2020 and 2021.

Leprosy, primarily affects the skin and peripheral nerves, leading to disfigurement and disability if left untreated. Leprosy remains a public health challenge in many parts of the world, particularly in developing countries with limited access to healthcare services. Early detection of leprosy is critical for effective treatment and prevention of disability(Rao & Suneetha, 2018). However, conventional methods for leprosy diagnosis are often time-consuming and require specialized training, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment initiation. Image analysis methods have emerged as a promising tool for digital microbiology imaging, enabling rapid and objective evaluation of skin lesions (Pal et al., 2018; Ferrari et al., 2017). Leprosy being a curable disease, early detection could reduce the chance of disease transmission. As reported and demonstrated, AI technology can help health workers to use specialized applications for guidance (Steyve et al., 2022). Leprosy analysis using skin smear images and clinical data is a promising approach to improve leprosy diagnosis and patient management. Skin smear images can provide valuable visual information about the location, morphological characteristics(size, shape, color, arrangement, uniformity) of the bacilli, which can aid in the diagnosis and classification of leprosy.

Computer vision algorithms can analyze these images and can provide assistive information to pathologists (Cui & Zhang, 2021). Furthermore, such an approach can provide insights into disease progression, treatment response, and disease control, facilitating personalized patient management and public health interventions (Caie et al., 2021). Computational models allow the lab personnel to perform a more effective diagnosis within an optimum time. Extensive laboratory work has not yet resulted in any useful tools for the early diagnosis of clinically unapparent disease. Primary objective of this study is to develop leprosy screening methods to increase accessibility to major diagnostic centers. There exists a research gap to develop a cheaper, more accessible screening system that can be distributed at a relatively low cost in poorer regions of the globe.

Medical professionals use medical image analysis as a diagnostic tool to detect diseases. Additionally, it enhances early detection and diagnosis of illness, which helps offer high-quality healthcare. Lab personnel look for the number of M. leprae in skin smears. The test involves taking a sample of tissue fluid from a small skin incision and staining it. They look for acid-fast bacilli, which are seen as thin pink rods on a blue background. The pink rods are dispersed evenly or unevenly, it can be straight or curved, solid or fragmented, or granular. Solid bacilli may be present in newly diagnosed, neglected cases as well as in relapse cases and may indicate the existence of living organisms. This is characterized by morphological index Fragmented and granular forms can be seen in treated cases.

Automation of smear images is of great interest among frontline workers as it is time-consuming and labor-intensive. Several techniques have been introduced using image processing to achieve the addressed task. Convolution neural networks (CNN) make use of the advantage of learning the characteristics of image features automatically, providing sufficient samples of images to learn. (Panicker et al., 2018) used a CNN by learning the characteristics of bacilli for the detection of tuberculosis from smear images. After pre- processing the individual patched bacilli is trained using CNN and achieved a detection sensitivity of 97.13%. Geometric features and shape descriptors can provide accurate results in determining the regions with bacilli. Applications of this method include the separation of overlapping bacilli in microscopic digital TB images (Priya Srinivasan, 2015). Bacteria can be identified with shape and color features. K-means clustering is claimed to be an efficient algorithm for clustering similar items (Forero et al., 2004). However, these algorithms are limited by outliers in the images caused by debris and blue background. Bacterial count indicates the total number of leprae bacilli in a patient’s smear. This count is used to grade the presence of leprosy. A similar application is proposed using contour profiling, size, and texture features for white blood cell count in blood smear images (Ghosh et al., 2016). In this paper, the bacilli count is performed using contour detection and compared with the thresholding mechanism. The performance of these methods is computed based on purity calculation.

Methodology

The data for this study is collected from the Schieffelin Institute of Health — Research & Leprosy Centre, Karigiri, Vellore. 44 retrospective data from the Department of Laboratories were collected. All skin slides were screened and the bacteriological index was calculated under an oil immersion field. It is graded in Ridley’s logarithmic scale from 0 to 6+ (Jopling & McDougall, 2005). If no bacilli are found, the entire smear is negative else positive and graded. If leprosy, skin smears identified as positive can be classified into different categories based on their clinical features and the number of skin lesions present. 3+ category refers to “multibacillary” leprosy, which means there are many bacteria present in the skin smear. Under this category, there may be numerous, large, and symmetrical with some degree of numbness or loss of sensation. 4+ category also refers to multibacillary leprosy but with more severe symptoms. The skin smear may be more widespread and involve the face, limbs, and trunk. There may be thickened nerves, and the patient may have significant numbness or loss of sensation. 5+ category refers to a severe form of leprosy known as “borderline lepromatous” leprosy. The skin smear may be very numerous and widespread, with a significant degree of numbness or loss of sensation. The patient may have nodules on the skin and thickened nerves. 6+ category refers to the most severe form of leprosy known as “lepromatous” leprosy. The skin smear may be widespread, with nodules and plaques on the skin. There may be significant thickening of the nerves, leading to loss of sensation and muscle weakness. Other organs may also be affected, leading to systemic symptoms.

This labor-intensive task of manual inspection is time-consuming as the specialist has to analyze the entire smear slides (approximately 500 fields) under the microscope in order to achieve the correct diagnosis. The detection of object boundaries forms an important step in computer vision. The study focuses on understanding how boundary detection in smear images will be successful for bacterial counting. Bacteriological Index is a key factor considered in screening for leprosy. The estimated morphological index presumed to be a count of live (solid) bacilli is an important determining factor to identify the degree of infectiousness of a patient. The workflow consists of two methods (i) Thresholding and (ii) Contour Detection.

  1. Global Threshold Segmentation

    In the study, the global threshold segmentation as proposed by Niu, Zuodong et al was adapted (Niu & Li, 2019). Considering the input image as I, then I(r,c ) represents the gray value with column c and row r of I. The output image after global threshold processing is O is given by


    $$O(r,c) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} {255I(r,c) > ~thresh~} \\ {0I(r,c) \leq ~thrsh~} \\ \end{matrix} \right.$$

    The algorithm involves two steps Fig. 2.

    The smear images are initially preprocessed by applying standard normalization followed by the threshold computation using Otsu method

    Connected Component Analysis (CCA) is performed on the binary image to generate a new labeled image and the count of labels can be taken as a measure of bacterial count.

  2. (Contour Detection)

The input image is initially passed through Image sharpening Laplacian filter. The filtering is performed by convolving the image with a kernel that approximates the second derivative of the image. This will sharpen the region of interest such as edges and corners, while suppressing areas with slowly varying intensity. The Laplacian filter can be implemented using various kernel sizes, and the size of the kernel will affect the degree of smoothing and noise reduction in the resulting image. In the study, the filter size adapted is 3x3. After filtering a binary edge map is produced. During the next stage, the sharpened color image will be converted to a grayscale. In order to extract the bacterial region (pink), canny edge filters with methods relevant to the morphology of bacteria were used. The Canny algorithm uses a series of steps to detect edges, which are defined as the boundaries between regions of contrasting intensities in an image. These steps included are shown in Fig. 3.

  1. Gaussian smoothing: The image is first smoothed using a Gaussian filter to reduce noise and remove high-frequency information.
  2. Gradient computation: The gradient of the smoothed image is then computed in both the horizontal and vertical directions. This provides information about the rate of change of intensity in each direction.
  3. non-maximum suppression: Next, the algorithm identifies local maxima in the gradient image, which corresponds to the edges. However, not all of these maxima are true edges, as some may be caused by noise or other factors. The non-maximum suppression step removes any non-maximal values in the gradient image.
  4. Double thresholding: Canny edge detection is performed by setting the threshold based on gradients
  5. Edge tracking by hysteresis: Finally, the algorithm performs edge tracking by hysteresis, which involves connecting the strong edges into continuous contours and suppressing weak edges that are not connected to strong edges.

The result of Canny edge detection is an image that highlights the edges in an image while suppressing noise and other irrelevant information. This can be useful in a variety of applications, such as object recognition, image segmentation, and feature extraction. Following the canny edge detection, dilation of the image was applied which add pixels to the boundary of the image which makes it easy to detect bacterial colonies. The size and shape of the kernel can be adjusted to achieve different levels of dilation. Finally, we apply contouring to the transformed image which essentially adds a border to the bacterial colonies we are looking for so that counting becomes easy for our proposed model. The contour detector consists of a generic hierarchical region tree mode to retrieve all possible contours from the binary image and contour approximation method for storing the contour points.

Result and Discussion

All experimental analysis is implemented using Python language with the collected 44 pictures. As shown in Figs. 5* and 6. It can be seen from the figure that the contour processing results are better than the global threshold segmentation method, which can completely segment the foreground and background and distinguish the target objects in the figure, and could provide a reliable bacterial count.

The original digital images obtained from the microscope are shown on the left side, while the segmented images are presented on the right. Fig.5. (a), represents the original microscopic smear bacterial image. Fig. 5. (b), a graph is displayed that shows the relationship between the pixel values and their frequency of occurrence in the image. Specifically, the x-axis represents the pixel values, while the y-axis displays the corresponding frequency count. The graph peaks at the higher pixel value side of the x-axis, indicating that the image contains lighter blue than dark blue, with very little red. This is because lighter colors typically have higher pixel values than darker colors. Fig. 5 (c) showcases the binary segmented image after thresholding. Thresholding involves the conversion of an image from color or grayscale into a binary image, i.e., an image consisting of only black and white pixels. This conversion makes it easier to analyze the image, as it contains only two contrasting colors that are easy to distinguish. In Fig. 5. (d), we can see the RGB image after segmentation. Segmentation refers to the process of dividing an image into different segments based on their pixel values. By segmenting the image, we can isolate and process only the important segments of the image, rather than processing the entire image. In this particular case, red color is added to the image, with areas of high bacterial density appearing as red regions. Fig. 6. (a) shows the input image which is processed under various operations to get the count of the bacterial colony. Fig. 6. (b) shows the output image after sharpening. This is utilized to enhance the diagnosis accuracy of medical images. This is done just in case to avoid the possibility that the medical image is blurry or lacks clarity, as it can hinder the identification of subtle details or abnormalities in the image. Fig. 5. (c) displays the outcome of the contour detection process applied to the input image. This image is generated after the application of a series of image processing techniques, including sharpening, grayscale conversion, Canny edge detection, dilation, and contouring. The resulting image is then employed to determine the number of contours present, which corresponds to the count of bacterial colonies in the image. Fig. 6. and Fig. 7. indicates the box plot for the bacterial count obtained after thresholding and contour detection methods. For 3+ grading category, the bacterial count range is from 82-909. 4+ grading category the range extended from 115-16712. 5+grading category the range is from 17 43-2597 and 6+ category reported range from 6367-15966. It has observed a certain level of overlap in the bacterial count in different grading levels. Color inhomogeneity and low contrast resulted in outliers and overlapping of counts during the segmentation. The current works lack the standardization of automated bacterial counting. In the future, we will work and propose a robust selective segmentation model to overcome the shortcomings Performance evaluation of the proposed methods was carried out using Structural similarity index measure (SSIM) and Mean square error (MSE). SSIM is used to evaluate the structural similarity between the ground truth and predicted smear leprosy masks. The SSIM of a pair of images (a, b) is given by a multiplicative combination of the structure (s), contrast (c), and Y . luminance (1) factors, as given below where a,ḃ,ÿ Sa2,S2, sa, sb and SaSb represent, respectively, the local mean, the local variance, and the local covariance between a and b. Constants c1, c2 , and are small constants that aim to characterize the saturation effects of the visual system at low luminance and contrast regions and that assure numerical stability when the denominators are close to zero.

(1)
$$l(a,b) = \frac{2\overset{˙}{a}\overset{˙}{b} + c_{1}}{{\overset{˙}{a}}^{2} + {\overset{˙}{b}}^{2} + c_{2}}$$

(2)
$$c(a,b) = \frac{2s_{a}s_{b} + c_{2}}{S_{a}^{2} + S_{b}^{2} + c_{2}}$$

(3)
$$s(x,y) = \frac{S_{a,b + c_{3}}}{S_{a}S_{b} + c_{3}}$$

SSIM range from [0, 1]. The experimental analysis with the sample dataset showed a maximum SSIM as 0.89, while the minimum reported value 0.52.

Mean Square Error (MSE) is used to measure the difference between the ground truth and the segmented image, the smaller the value of MSE, the better the segmentation performance. The minimum reported MSE value is 2138. As the morphology of bacilli are varying widely, still extensive research is needed to clearly segment the region of interest.

Conclusion

Experimental evaluation demonstrates the significance of automatic bacterial counting which correlated grading done by pathologists as per the bacteriological index. The results are preliminary outcomes of the hypotheses that require further in-depth validation to derive a mapping of Bacteriological Index. Extensive validation is needed to make our system deployable for M. leprae recognition applications

Real-Time V2V Communication for Collision Detection in VANETs Using ESP Mesh Protocol: An IoT-Based Implementation for the Internet of Vehicles

Darshit Niravbhai Vadgama, Gariman Bhutani, and Jayavignesh Thyagarajan

a School of Electronics Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology, Chennai Campus, Chennai, India

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-27

Abstract

This paper presents the development and evaluation of an automotive wireless communication system using an ESP32 microcontroller board and the ESP-MESH protocol. The ESP-MESH protocol was chosen for its advantages over other wireless communication protocols, including low latency, high throughput, scalability, and power efficiency. The system includes an ultrasonic sensor for small-scale distance measurement between vehicles and GPS for real-time data analytics for congestion control and efficient route planning. To test the system’s functionality and performance, it was simulated using NS2, SUMO, and OSM with multiple nodes. The results indicate that the system provides reliable and efficient communication between vehicles, fulfilling the primary goals of VANET technology. This study demonstrates the potential of the ESP32 microcontroller board and the ESP-MESH protocol as a promising solution for enhancing road safety and transportation efficiency in VANET communications as IoV.

Keywords: Mesh, Collision Detection, Road safety, ESP-MESH Communication Protocol, IoV

Introduction

VANETs (Vehicular Ad hoc Networks) are modified Mobile Ad hoc Networks (MANETs) that are designed for application in vehicular environments. VANETs are characterized by their highly dynamic network topology and limited communication range, making them challenging to design and implement ( (Anwer & Guy, 2014; Hasrouny et al., 2017). Despite these challenges, VANETs can deliver numerous benefits to the transportation sector, including improved road safety, congestion control, and better vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication. In the past few years, a lot of effort has been put forth in the field of VANETs to develop the necessary communication protocols that can accommodate various automotive applications.

The term “Internet of Vehicles” (IoV) implies a network of interconnected vehicles that can interact wirelessly with one other (V2V) and with infrastructure (V2I) like traffic lights, road sensors, and GPS satellites. IoV enables vehicles to exchange information in real-time, providing drivers with real-time traffic updates, route suggestions, and other important information that can help them navigate safely and efficiently technology relies on various sensors and communication devices installed in vehicles, such as GPS, radar, cameras, and LiDAR sensors, to collect and transmit data to other vehicles and the central infrastructure. This data can include information about vehicle location, speed, fuel consumption, etc. The IoV can also enable V2V and V2I communication and thereby prevent accidents and also reduce traffic congestion. Overall, the IoV has the potential to revolutionize the way towards Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) making it safer, more efficient, and more sustainable (Ji et al., 2020).

CONTACT Darshit Niravbhai Vadgama. Email: darshitniravbhai.v2020@vitstudent.ac.in Email: gariman.bhutani2020@vitstudent.ac.in (Gariman Bhutani)

Email: jayavignesh.t@vit.ac.in (Jayavignesh Thyagarajan)

This paper focuses on the IoT implementation of use cases such as if a vehicle detects a potential collision with another vehicle, it can automatically send an alert to the driver of the vehicle to take evasive action and also disseminate warning messages to vehicles beyond one-hop range through ESP Mesh Protocol to avoid traffic congestion (also calculated through node (OBU) density in a location provided by GPS) and re-routing. This research has focused on various aspects of VANETs, including network architecture, communication protocols, and routing algorithms. This paper’s objective is to explain and present VANET implementation in hardware as well as software.

Architecture and Components of Vanets

VANET is made up of numerous resources such as an Access Point, Automobiles, roadside units, and so on as shown in Figure 1. Sensors in Onboard devices that aid in the transmission of information to cars are also employed in the Vehicular Ad hoc Network.

  • RSU: A Roadside Unit (computing equipment) that offers connection assistance to passing vehicles.
  • OBU:The On-Bo ard Unit -A vehicle-mounted communication device. It determines the vehicle’s latitude and longitude using GPS. And an Ultrasonic sensor to calculate the distance between other objects or vehicles for collision avoidance.
  • Vehicles: Nodes are the designations given to vehicles that allow them to communicate with other vehicles or roadside resources.

Proposed System

In this paper, IoT vehicular node is designed with ESP32 as the microcontroller and ESP-MESH as the communication protocol and these nodes together coordinate to form the VANET (Framework EID, 2023; Kumari et al., 2020).

Ultrasonic sensors and GPS are interfaced as peripherals in each node. The ultrasonic sensor is a low-cost and reliable option for small-scale VANET implementations for distance calculation between two vehicles. GPS is integrated into the node for accurate vehicle location tracking and to enable real-time data analytics. Location tracking can guide the provision of safety warnings to drivers, thereby improving overall road safety. It can also be used to improve data packet routing within the VANET network, enabling effective communication between vehicles and with roadside infrastructure. Figure 2 shows the schematic diagram for interfacing ESP32 module with the Ultrasonic sensor and GPS module. The code for both hardware and software is available at https://github.com/Darshit-Vadgama/ VANET. (Anwer & Guy, 2014; Framework EID, 2023; Yu et al., 2011; Ghori et al., 2018) provides support for the simulation code. Figure 3 shows the OBU assembly unit.

Steps for implementing VANET

Vehicles communicate with each other the chosen networking protocol.

  1. Implement the network topology: Decide on the network topology based on the requirements of your project. For example, you can implement a simple star topology where all vehicles communicate directly with a central node or a more complex mesh network where vehicles communicate directly with each other.
  2. Implement the communication protocol: Implement the communication protocol on the ESP32 modules. This involves defining the format of the messages that are exchanged between the vehicles and implementing the necessary logic for handling the messages.
  3. Implement the routing protocol: Implement the routing protocol on the ESP32 modules. This involves defining the rules for how data is routed from one vehicle to another.

  4. Test and validate the system: Test the system by simulating different scenarios and validate that the system is working as expected as shown in Figs. 4 and 5 below where we have tested our hardware with 3 nodes. It shows the communication happening simultaneously with the collision avoidance warning system running parallelly (as set to show a warning message if distance is less than 100 cm).

Communication Protocol Used

ESP-MESH (Framework EID, 2023) protocol is a suitable choice for VANET communication due to its advantages over other protocols. It has low latency, high throughput, scalability, and power efficiency. It allows multiple devices to interconnect within a single local area network (LAN) and is developed on top of the Wi-Fi

As seen in Fig. 6, it makes it unnecessary for nodes to link to a central node, enabling several devices to be dispersed and still be connected over a sizable physical region. ESP-WIFI-MESH packet header lists the source and destination nodes’ MAC addresses and application data is stored in the payload as shown in Figure 7.

ESP-WIFI-MESH can handle packet forwarding at the network layer using routing tables, making it suitable for bi-directional data stream demonstrated in Figure 8. ESP-MESH’s AP (Adaptive Pacing) TCP is a congestion-controlling TCP method for multi-hop IEEE 802.11. TCP-AP monitors RTTs to restrict transmission rate and avoid congestion-related loss shown in Fig. 9.

Strengths of ESP-MESH protocol:

  • Self-organizing and self-healing capabilities, allow users to create and manage networks on their own.
  • Low latency and high throughput, which are important for real-time communication between vehicles in VANETs.
  • Scalable, allowing it to support a large number of nodes in the network, making it suitable for large-scale VANETs.
  • Power-efficient, allowing devices in the network to operate for extended periods.

Limitations of ESP-MESH protocol:

  • Limited range, as it is built on top of the Wi-Fi protocol.
  • Limited transmission distance due to the use of low-power radios.
  • May be susceptible to interference from other devices using the same frequency band.
  • Relatively new and less widely used compared to other networking protocols.

Routing Protocols Used

Proactive and reactive routing techniques are both relevant in this context. A demand-based responsive routing technology is called AODV. Only when it is necessary, AODV establishes the path. It has a route request-response mechanism that enables it to ask for a route and then decide the best course of action based on the response. This article discusses the creation of the AODV reactive routing protocol as well as implementation strategies using different simulators, including SUMO, OSM, and NS2.

Simulation Methodology

For analyzing the behavior of AODV on VANET, three distinct Simulator tools were used: SUMO (Kaisser et al., 2012), OSM, and NS2 (Ns, 2016). Work is provided in a basic cross-road implementation to show the flow of work, and the same flow is utilized to construct multiple scenarios. A networked vehicle simulator called Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO) is specifically designed for planning and evaluating vehicle movement patterns (Khairnar & Pradhan, 2011). OSM (Open Street Map) (Nawej et al., 2021)loads a map of the heterogeneous road and vehicular environment. We piled into the Chennai Guindy Cloverleaf highway.

Here are the steps to generate the scenario in SUMO 0.16.0:

  1. Create your map nodes by generating an a.nod.xml file.
  2. Draw your own map’s edges using an a.edg. xml file.
  3. Create the map configuration file by generating an a.netc.cfg file.
  4. Generate a map file by creating an a.net. xml file.
  5. Define the flow in your map by creating an a.flow.xml file.
  6. Configure automatic vehicle movement by generating an a.rou.xml file.
  7. Set up the simulation by creating an a.sumo. tr and a.sumo.cfg file.
  8. Render the simulation.
  9. Manually create trace files, or use the Trace Exporter software for more convenience.

Affordable portable satellite navigation systems and the limited availability of map information globally spurred the founding and growth of OpenStreetMap. GPS-enabled smartphones running iOS or Android enable easy crowdsourcing of geographic data. OpenStreetMap is a crowdsourced, open content license platform that allows individuals worldwide to collect and update geographic data, making it valuable and frequently updated.

To simulate, we must first export the XML file from the OpenStreetMap API as seen in Figure 10. Then, we must open that file in Ns2 using the procedures outlined above. Now, we’ll use SUMO to simulate traffic and run the XML file in Ns2 as seen in Fig. 11.

Finally, as shown in Fig. 12, we can examine the AODV routing protocol in NS2 and store all the results in a trace file. As seen in the trace file as shown in Figure 13, node 0 periodically sends out a warning message, which node 22 receives and acknowledges as part of collision avoidance tracking.

Results and Inferences

Through our implementation of a VANET using ESP32 and ESP-MESH protocol, we were able to demonstrate its reliability in operating over a range of 15-20 meters. ESP-MESH’s self-routing capabilities ensured that any node removed from the network would be re-routed and connected through an alternate route. We found that AODV routing protocol was an efficient choice for VANET implementation. However, we also observed that the GPS module we used was not always dependable, particularly in overcast conditions. It is recommended to use a more reliable modular GPS for more accurate location data. Nevertheless, our ultrasonic sensor worked correctly, and we were able to receive warning messages whenever we encountered a potential collision situation. Our communication protocol allowed for consistent real-time location data transmission of other nodes to the RSU or any node within range. In addition, we found that Ns2, SUMO, and OSM were effective in simulating VANET on a larger scale using AODV routing protocol. Our software produced successful results for our system, which can also be utilized to test and validate small-scale VANET systems. In summary, the hardware and software components of our VANET system were able to work effectively to produce successful results.

Conclusion and Future Work

The experimental results showcase the feasibility of deploying multiple nodes using the proposed system. However, the system encountered packet loss and delay issues under certain circumstances when the number of nodes increased within a specific range, highlighting the need for a more advanced routing protocol (da Silva et al., 2022). In future work, efforts will be directed towards simplifying the setup into a compact module such as a custom-designed PCB, and integrating it with ADAS (Advanced Driver Assistance System). Furthermore, highly congested and less congested traffic simulations will be carried out, and network performance metrics will be evaluated to identify efficient dissemination and routing strategies. Alternative routing protocols that offer better reliability and efficiency will also be explored and implemented to increase the dependability of the communication system. Additionally, further attention will be given to enhancing the security aspect (Hasrouny et al., 2017) of VANET for practical applications.
