Cyber Security Holes of JSON Web Token

Dr. Remya Chandran

Asst. Professor, Department of Computer Science, University of Calicut, Kerala,

E-mail: nivedika@gmail.com

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-28

Abstract

JSON Web Token (JWT) is frequently used in information exchange, authentication, and authorization. The most typical application of JWT among these use cases is for authorization. Once logged in, a user can access the routes, services, and resources that are authorized with that token by including the jWi in any subsequent requests. When a user logs in, the server creates a JWT with details about that user, including their user ID and role. After then, the JWT is transmitted back to the client and stored. The server can then check the JWT’s authenticity before processing any ensuing requests that the client sends after that. As a result, there is no requirement for a session state on the server, enabling secure communication between the client and server. Even if JWT is a very popular method used for “single sign-on” nowadays, it faces many challenges. This paper discusses the different identified vulnerabilities of JWT.

Keywords: JWT, vulnerability, security, authentication

Introduction

A JSON object called a JSON web token (JWT) is used to transmit data securely between two parties over the internet. It can be used as an authentication method and for information exchange. Tokens are primarily made up of a header, payload, and signature. There are dots between these three sections. JWT specifies the format of the data we are passing from one side to the other and offers Serialized and Deserialized formats. Data is primarily transferred via the network with each request and response using the serialized approach. While reading and writing data to the web token uses the deserialized method (Mahindrakar & Pujeri, 2020; Ahmed & Mahmood, 2020). The header, payload, and signature of a base64url-encoded JSON Web are indicated as shown in Figure 1 separated by dots:

Now consider an example of a token provided below:

eyJ hbGciOiJ lUzUxMils InR5cC161kpXVCJ 9. eyJuYW11Ijoibm12ZWRpa2EiLCJ1c2VyX25hbW Ui0iJuaXZIZGIrYS5kb2UiLCJpc19hZG1pbil6 ZmFsc2V9.h4TrOHFXEjBTOoie3Lx RBNWaDOhj7gBVmKS3X0mYkn5GE86C93 SfXACpVs1FnCOOdhLf5P19X72bgWllyZS1YWQ

The header includes information about the token, including its type and the signature algorithm (Shah & Mehtre, 2015). The header for this instance is shown in Figure 2 before encoding:

Information or claims about the user that will be checked by the application are included in the payload. In order to create the signature, the header, dot, and payload must first be base64url encoded. Then, depending on the symmetric or asymmetric encryption algorithm given in the header, the entire object must be signed using a secret key or a private key (Ethelbert et al., 2017). Since HS512 is a symmetric algorithm and was included in the header, It would work like this to encrypt and sign:

Fig 2. Sample Token

{ {
“alg”: “HS512”, “name”: “nivedika”,
“typ”: “JWT” “user_name”: “nivedika.doe”,
} “is_admin”: false
} }

HMACSHA512( base64UrlEncode(header) + “.” + base64Url Encode (payload), secret_key)

The base64url-encoded header and payload are then followed by the following signature:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzUxMilsInR5cC161kpXVCJ9. eyJuYW11Ijoibm12ZWRpa2EiLCJ1c2VyX25 hbWUi0iJuaXZIZGIrYS5kb2UiLCJpc1 9h ZG1 pbil6ZmFsc2V9.h4TrOHFXEjBTOoie3 LxRBNWaDOhj7gBVmKS3XOmYkn5 GE86C93SfXACpVs1FnCOOdh Lf5 PI9X 72 bgWUyZS1 YWQ

JWT Security Flaws

Letting the None

The JWT standard accepts a wide range of algorithms to produce a signature, including: None, RSA, HMAC, Elliptic Curve, etc. The None algorithm stipulates that there is no algorithm used to sign the signature verification by removing the signature token and setting an existing algorithm to None. If the usage of None algorithm is permitted, it’s possible to avoid the signing algorithm for a token is often some variation of RSA or HMAC, as defined in the token’s header. The algorithm type in the JWT header may, however, be defined as “none” for debugging purposes. Without a signature, we are unable to verify the authenticity of the token when the algorithm is set to “none.” Because there is no signature, the application does not check for one when the algorithm type is “none.” Therefore, by setting the algorithm field to “none,” while still convincing the application to accept a token, an attacker could alter crucial data in a payload. Having the application maintains a list of the permitted algorithms and discard any tokens that are not signed with one of the specified algorithms is one technique to prevent such an attack (Rawat et al., 2020).

“alg”:"HS512", “name”: “nivedika”,

“typ”: “JWT” “user name”: “nivedika.doe”,

“is_admin”: false

}.SIGNATURE

The token will seem as follows after being encoded and signed:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzUxMilsInR5cC161kpXVCJ9. eyJuYW11Ijoibm12ZWRpa2EiLCJ1c2VyX25hb WUi0iJuaXZIZGIrYS5kb2UiLCJpc19hZ G1 pbil6ZmFsc2V9.h4TrOHFXEjBTOoie3 LxRBNWaDOhj7gBVmKS3X0mYkn5GE86C 93SfXACpVs1FnCOOdhLf5P19X72bg WUyZS1 YWQ

If None is a permitted value for the algorithm, an attacker can quickly replace a legitimate algorithm with it, delete the signature, and replace the algorithm as shown in Figure 3:

Fig 3. Modified Token using None Algorithm

{ {
“alg”: “None”, “name”: “nivedika”,
“typ”: “JWT” “user_name”: “nivedika.doe”,
} “is_admin”: True
} }

The application will accept the modified token even though it is no longer signed. Because of this, it’s crucial to reject tokens with the alg header case differences: none / nOnE/ NONE /None /any other.

Confusing algorithms

JWT is capable of supporting symmetric and asymmetric encryption methods. You must employ a pair of public and private keys, or a secret key, depending on the encryption method. Asymmetric encryption allows an application to publicly reveal its public key while maintaining the privacy of its private key. As a result, anyone can verify this token using the application’s public key and sign tokens using its private key. The vulnerability known as “algorithm confusion” appears when an application neglects to verify that the algorithm of the token it has received matches the algorithm it has been told to expect (Kannan & Umasankar, 2018; Rawat et al., 2020; Darmawan et al., 2022).

The technique to check the signature in several JWT libraries:

  • verify(T, S) – if Symmetric algorithm is used Where T=Token and S=Secret Key
  • verify(T, PK) – if Asymmetric algorithm is used

Where T=Token and PK=Public Key

Unfortunately in some libraries, this method does not independently verify that the received token is signed using the appropriate technique for the application. For example, the second parameter will be treated by this technique as a shared secret key when HMAC is used(Symmetric algorithm) and as a public key in the case of RSA (Asymmetric algorithm). An attacker can create harmful tokens if the programme has access to the public key. The verify() method will use symmetric rather than asymmetric encryption and treat the public key as an HMAC shared secret when an attacker provides HMAC instead of RSA encryption because the application expects RSA encryption.

Using insignificant secrets

Only the secret being used can guarantee the security of a cryptographic signature utilizing symmetric encryption A weak secret used by an application makes it simple for an attacker to perform brute force to match the original signature. The attacker can construct legitimate signatures for fake tokens once the secret is known. Symmetric encryption must always be used with strong secrets to prevent this problem.

Failing to verify the signature

Several JWT libraries offer two ways to decode the token—one for decoding it and the other for verifying it:

  • decode(): Does not check the signature; It decodes the token .
  • verify( ): Verifies the signature and decodes the token.

These techniques might occasionally be mixed up by developers. In such instances, the program will accept any token and the signature won’t ever be validated (in a valid format). Additionally, developers may forget to re-enable signature verification after disabling it for testing. Such errors may cause privilege escalation or arbitrary account access. Let’s take the following valid token as an example, which is never truly verified:

{ {

“alg”: “HS384”, “name”: “nivedika”,

“typ”: “JWT” “user_name”: “nivedika.doe”,

} “is admin”: false

}

To achieve elevated privileges, the following token with any random signature can be submitted by an attacker:

{ {

“alg”: “HS384”, “name”: “nivedika”,

“typ”: “JWT” “user_name”: “nivedika.doe”,

} “is admin”: true

}

Kid parameter injections

The Key Id parameter kid may be present in the JWT header. It is frequently used to get the key from a disc or database. Using the key provided via the kid argument, the application validates the signature. If the parameter can be injected, attacks like RCE, SQLi, and LFI as well as signature bypass may be possible. Let’s begin using the following valid token to demonstrate this in action:

{ {

“alg”: “HS512”, “name”: “nivedika”,

“typ”: “JWT”, “user_name”: “nivedika.doe”,

“kid”: “key2” “is admin”: false

}. }

The following alteration shown in Fig. 4 could result in remote code execution if the kid parameter is susceptible to command injection:

Signature bypass: kid parameter injection + directory traversal

If software uses the kid parameter to get the key from the filesystem, it may be vulnerable to directory traversal. The program can then be forced to use a file as a key for verification that the attacker can estimate the value of. This can be accomplished using any static file that is part of the program. If an attacker is aware of the importance of the file as a key, they can build a malicious token and sign it with the identified key. Consider the below code, to force the application to utilize an empty key, an attacker could try to establish /dev/null as the key source:

“alg”: “HS512”, “name”: “nivedika”,

“typ”: “JWT”, “user_name”: “nivedika.doe”,

“kid”: “../../../../../../dev/null” “is_admin”: true

} }

In the event of a successful directory traversal to /dev/null, the attacker will have the opportunity to sign a malicious token with an empty string.

kid parameter injection + SQL injection = signature bypass

If a database key is obtained from an application via the kid parameter, SQL injection may be possible. If a hacker is successful, they can manipulate the value that a SQL query returns to the kid parameter and use it to sign harmful tokens. Assuming that the application obtains its JWT key via the kid argument. Let’s take a sample SQL query:

SELECT key FROM keys WHERE key.‘key2’

An attacker might then manipulate the key value by inserting a UNION - SELECT command into the kid parameter:

{ {

“alg”: “HS512”, “name”: “nivedika”,

“typ”: “JWT”, “user name”: “nivedika.doe”,

“kid”: “yyyy’ UNION SELECT ‘ bbb”"is_admin": true

} }

Fig. 4. Modified Token with kid parameter

{ {
“alg”: “HS5 12”, “name”: “nivedika”,
“typ”: “JWT”, “user_name”: “nivedika.doe”,
“kid”: “key21/usr/bin/uname” “is_admin”: false
1. }

If SQL attack is successful, the program will perform the below query to obtain the signature key:

SELECT key FROM keys WHERE key.‘yyyy’ UNION SELECT ‘bbb’

This query’s kid parameter returns bbb, allowing the attacker to sign an evil token with merely bbb. Before utilizing the kid option, applications should always sanitize its value to prevent these and other injection threats.

Replay attack

JWT tokens can be used in replay attacks if the methods for expiry and revoking contain flaws. In this situation, it is important to pay attention to “exp” (a token’s expiration date) and “jti” (a token’s unique identifier) claims and attempt to use a JWT token that has expired or been revoked.

Substitution attacks

There are attacks where one recipient tries to use a JWT that was meant for another recipient that it was not intended for. This is true in the following situations:

  • An application fails to validate (or incorrectly validate) that the issuer possesses the cryptographic keys required for the cryptographic operations of the JWT. (the iss claim)
  • When compared to a valid subject and/or issuer/subject pair at the application, the subject value or sub-claim does not validate (or does not validate adequately).
  • Sometimes the identical issuer may produce JWTs that are intended for use by several reliant parties or applications, the and claim isn’t applied to detect whether the JWT is being used by an intended party or by an unintended party by an attacker.

Changing a JKU header parameter

JWK Set URL is referred to as JKU. The URL of a group of keys used to validate the token can be specified in this optional header field. An attacker might host their key file and ask that the application use it to validate tokens if this field is allowed and not properly managed.

Changing a JWK header parameter

The key that is used to verify the token might be directly inserted into the token by attackers via the JWK (JSON Web Key) header field.

URL manipulation for X5U and X5C

Using the x5u and x5c header elements, attackers can provide the public key certificate that was used to validate the token. While X5C allows the token to contain the certificate values, x5u defines the information in the URI form.

Conclusion

JWT is an open internet standard that allows claims to be exchanged securely between parties as a JSON payload, with optional JSON Web Signature (JWS) and JSON Web Encryption (JWE). Due to their widespread implementation in commercial applications and their usage of digital signatures for verification, JWTs have become omnipresent in their use. If implemented correctly and when necessary, JWTs have become a powerful session and token-based authentication standard, which is arguably justified. By properly following a number of procedures like: (1) Never let verification be driven solely by the JWT header, (2) Know the structure of the algorithms, (3) Make sure to select a robust, suitable key size, and ( 4) Use well-known JWT libraries that have been proven to be secure, can effectively reduce algorithm vulnerabilities. They frequently aren’t deployed properly, though, and as a result, continue to be a favorite entrance point for bad actors.

Limitations And Future Work

Despite having several security issues, experts believe the JSON Web Token to be sufficiently secure. A developer can easily hurt himself by using JWT or a library that implements it improperly. The main flaws of JWT are Letting the none option in the header, confusing algorithms, kid parameter flaws, substitution attacks, replay attacks, and other header parameter flaws. As a future work JWT tokens are created using both encryption and signed, which is more secure.

Blockchain for Philanthropy

Shamith D. Rao,23

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-29

Abstract

Blockchain technology has gained popularity due to its decentralized nature and strong security properties. While blockchains are widely known for their use in decentralized cryptocurrencies, they can also be used in other innovative applications such as smart contracts, asset ownership records, cross-border payment solutions, and exchange finance. Blockchain technology’s unique public verifiability and the ability to be controlled by a trusted third party have made it increasingly attractive to the online charity community. However, charitable organizations often face issues related to fund misuse, inadequate audits, and scandals, leading to a decline in public trust. This paper proposes a solution that promotes transparency in charity operations using public blockchains, such as Ethereum. The proposed system ensures the secure transfer of funds between various actors in charity operations, promoting trust and security. Additionally, the system allows for the wider availability of goods and services to beneficiaries through smart contracts, escrow, and tokenization, providing an efficient and reliable mechanism for service providers, charities, and beneficiaries to operate. By utilizing a public ledger, the system enables the public to verify the transfer of funds between different actors in charity operations, promoting transparency and increasing public trust in charitable organizations. The proposed system aims to motivate effective philanthropy by building trust in charities, ultimately encouraging more significant philanthropic efforts. Adoption of blockchain technology by service providers, charities, and beneficiaries will further promote trust and security in the system. In summary, the proposed system enables secure and transparent charity operations that build public trust and promote effective philanthropy.

Keywords: Smart Contracts, Blockchain, Escrow, Validation, Tokenization

Introduction

People like to donate for various reasons, including godly principles, good intentions, excess money, etc. As indicated in Yasmin et al., (2014), 38% of philanthropic organizations reported misplaced accounts and inaccurate calculations. Most of these were religion-based foundations, the others were small-scale associations. A report by the UK Charities Aid Foundation (Charities Aid Foundation, n.d.) recognizes that for charitable uses, blockchains can take transparency and trust to the next level at the same time, decreasing the middlemen cost by almost 97% and giving-charitable organizations extended freedom for raising support. We investigate this by presenting a conventional blockchain-based philanthropic model that utilizes an online web-based platform where donors can pick which good cause projects to help, donating in the form of digital tokens or cryptocurrencies. These tokens can be used directly or converted to fiat currency by the receiver. This paper examines a system that is transparent, safe and provides a platform for the liquidation of goods via tokenization.

Current System

The current system (Fig. 1) is followed/ abides by most of the local philanthropic systems but at the same time is also believed to be of scam type (McDonnell, 2017). The main reason for that is the lack of transparency in the process that these organizations follow. Figure 1 below shows us a gross overview of what the process looks like in the real world. The donor donates the desired money to the middleman who in turn gives the “majority” of the amount to the concerned NGOs who supposedly “donate all” of this to the affected/ beneficiaries. The issue here is that it gets extremely difficult for the donor to track where his/her fund exactly went and what part of it was kept as commission. Let us say that the middleman keeps 1% as commission and forwards the amount to the NGO. No one knows how the NGO splits up the amount and where each part is gone/used. This may also be true with donors. One may claim to donate more than they did for the sake of showcasing the same in their portfolio. This method is used by multiple MNCs just to boost their image with the general public. There is no system for someone the non-participating party to verify the claims/ transactions. This results in very vague claims of delivering donations to the beneficiaries.

Following general governance, one of the largest reasons for complaints against charities is financial misconduct. This includes suspected embezzlement of funds and financial fraud (McDonnell, 2017). Furthermore, 48% of complaints against charities come from the public domain. This means there is a lack of trust between the public and the charities. Additionally, according to the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners (ACFE) 2018 National Report, non-profits accounted for up to 9%. The non-profits also faced a median loss of $75,000. Such financial loss can hinder the functioning of charities and nonprofits significantly ( “Report to the Nations,” 2018). According to Fidelity Charitable Report, (2016), 77% of the next generation of donors are only somewhat optimistic that their donations can have a positive impact on the social problems important to them. This arises the need for a transparent payment workflow powered by blockchain technology which can not only take the factor of trust to a whole new level but also essentially eliminate the role of the middleman saving us their commissions. Transparent payment workflow can reduce the number of scandals associated with charities and can help improve public trust in charities.

Related Work

Lee et al., (2018)proposes a system for charity donations using blockchain that preserves the privacy of the donor and provides transparency to the system. This study does not provide a way for the user to directly transfer funds to the beneficiary. This framework does not take into account associated stores and services that the beneficiaries may purchase. Naiknavare et al., (2022)proposes a system for charity using blockchain where they define 4 participating actors Donor, Beneficiary, Cooperative shops, and Charity Organizations. Their system uses blockchain to bring transparency to the flow of money between organizations. The study, however, does not guarantee the generation of genuine cooperative shops or if the services provided by the shops reach the beneficiaries. They also do not show any method to tokenize services provided by these shops which can be traded directly over the blockchain. Almaghrabi & Alhogail, (2022) propose a system that promotes the traceability of funds using blockchain. They have also introduced a system to notify the user when their funds reach the beneficiaries. This system brings does not provide adequate flexibility for the rearranging of funds by the charity. This study also does not consider the services provided by the contracted store.

Proposed System

The above-mentioned problems motivate us to propose a system infrastructure based on the Ethereum blockchain. This system needs to facilitate the users who are donors, beneficiaries, charity organizations, and the cooperative store where they would spend these tokens, to have a transparent view of the blockchain. That means they should be able to have complete access to all the transaction details i.e., sender, receive; time of the transaction, location (future implementation), amount, goods exchanged, etc. Since the nodes mining the blockchain would extend the longest-valid blockchain it gets impossible for the blockchain to be altered, making it immutable storage for transactions history. This enables each user to crosscheck the transacting amount and avoid fraudulent transactions with ease (Avdoshin & Pesotskaya, 2021). The system consists of users that play a major role which is classified as the donor/beneficiary, NGO, and Government entity. These users will be account holders in the blockchain network and each of them can uniquely identify in the network through their 160-bit account address. They can access their accounts and perform and sign transactions using their 256-bit private key. So, the different types of users are as follows:

System Design

The proposed system architecture (Fig. 2) consists of 3 parts. The first is the platform interface where the users can interact with the system, it contains actions like registering where the user can add an account in the system, post messages where the charity organization can post new information about the respective beneficiaries i.e. Name, issue, location, the amount needed, time left, etc. the browse post option lets the donor browse through the list of beneficiaries that the charity uploaded, then the Donate action allows the donor to donate the desired amount to either the beneficiary directly or to the charity organizations.

Now the second/middle layer of the architecture is the smart contracts. This contains the scripts for what actions need to trigger in response to other actions. For example, when the donor transfers coins to the beneficiary account, it executes appropriate actions making sure that the coins reach the desired public key address of the beneficiary. The transfer of funds can also be controlled by an escrow account. In this system, the charity will act as an escrow during the transfer of tones from the beneficiary account to the associated store. This will ensure that the services and goods offered by the associated store are in good condition and only after the assurance of the charity and the beneficiary will the transfer of tones take place. Another example could be when the user wishes to register themselves on the system using the platform interface, the smart contract then executes scripts to add the user to the database in the blockchain. The smart contracts will give control to the charity accounts to verify beneficiaries and associated stores. Only after the consent of a charity can a beneficiary or an associated store account can be created. As these rules are enforced by the smart contract no attacker can pose as either a beneficiary or an associated store. This provides an effective way of authorization and authentication of both the beneficiary and the associated store ensuring the proper use of donated funds. Then comes the Blockchain itself, it is the backbone of the system. All the transactions that happened in the past and those that will happen would be stored in this immutable linked list type of storage. Along with that, it provides the platform with actions like generating blocks and verifying transactions that any users and smart contracts can use to verify the genuineness of the transaction. It also acts as a local database on the platform to enable the user to quickly access already existing blocks with the list of transactions. The blockchain can also be used as a tokenization mechanism for the associated store products. This means physical goods can be tokenized and represented as crypto tokens. These tokens are used as a digitized representation of real word assets. Tokenization also has the added benefit of increasing the liquidity of physical goods. This tokenization will also improve the accessibility of goods to beneficiaries as it provides easy access to their needs. Tokenization of infrastructure using a similar scheme as Tian et al., (2020)can be used to achieve this result. Tian et al., (2020)provides an efficient way to do tokenization using blockchain and smart contracts.

User Workflow

The user workflow is shown below.

  • Doner: After the donor logs in, they are redirected to a screen [Figure 3] where a list of verified beneficiary details would be present. They would be able to select a particular beneficiary or the charity to which they want to donate to. After doing so the system would check the balance, if the balance is insufficient, he/she would be redirected to the deposit fiat currency page which is linked to a payment gateway where they can deposit some coins to their wallet. If the donor has sufficient balance and initiates a transaction, the smart contracts would trigger the transaction and update both the beneficiaries’ and the donor’s account balance.

  • Charity: The primary responsibility of the charity is to verify a beneficiary’s application for the genuineness of their situation. Only when the Charity feels the need is genuine and would need donations/ help, would it accept their application. After doing so the beneficiary details can be visible to the donors. The charity acts as an escrow account in the transaction between the beneficiary and the associated store, when the exchange is happening through a token.
  • Beneficiary: The beneficiary needs to submit their application that gets verified by the charity. Only on verification of their application will they be listed as a post in the database and will be visible to the donor. The beneficiary can also withdraw their coins in exchange for some fiat currency or can choose to use these coins with the associated stores that would provide goods/ services in exchange for those coins.
  • Associated Stores: These stores are responsible for providing resources to the beneficiaries in exchange for coins. The resources may be goods or services that the beneficiary needs. It is not necessary for the store to only accept coins in exchange for goods but also fiat currency if the beneficiary is ready to pay the same.

Blockchain Structure

The Blockchain structure (Fig. 4) would be very similar to that of the existing ones but with 2 key additions, the data for the verified list of beneficiaries (each beneficiary application first needs to get verified by the charity organization only after which it would be added to the blockchain, this action is being secured via the use of smart contracts), verified list of contracted stores and the data for users.

The block header stores the hash of the previous block, in a way pointing toward it. This is used to maintain a linked list-type structure moreover it essentially helps in maintaining the immutability of the blockchain, since the hash pointer is the hash of the previous chain, any change in the previous blocks would change the hash pointer in the current block hence identifying false/ fraudulent blocks. The timestamp maintains the exact time at which the block was mined. A nonce is a random number that is to be calculated by the miner to match the pattern of hash being followed in the blockchain. For example, if the pattern is that the hash of the block should start with 5 zeros, a nonce should be found such that hashing the complete block along with the nonce results in a block hash that starts with 5 zeros. This essentially determines the mining difficulty. Ethereum has two different kinds of nonces: account (transaction) nonces and Proof-of-Work (block) nonces. The Proof-of-Work nonce, which is utilized as a random number for mining, is included in each block. However, the nonce used in the transaction is an account nonce that symbolizes a transaction order that an account generates. Account nonce is used to prevent replay attacks, which is a network attack where legitimate blocks are incorrectly delayed or repeated. For example, a particular transaction sending tokens for a user account to a beneficiary account can be repeated continuously to void the user account. Account nonce essentially acts as a counter of transactions for accounts. The Merkle roots are the hash of all the hashes of the transactions. This helps in efficiently verifying the data in the nodes. If one node is changed, its hash changes, resulting in a change in Merkle root hash and intern changing block hash, hence signaling a faulty block. In our block, there are three Merkle roots used for verified beneficiaries, users, and transactions by the donor or the beneficiary. This was done to follow “separation of concerns”. One need not need to search a combined tree for data that could also be the last transaction. If the concerned data exists in three different trees, it is possible to search for it with 3 times more efficiency.

Results

The proposed design provides a transparent charity system that considers the flexibility required by charities to manage funds and allows donors to donate funds directly to a beneficiary that is verified by the charity. The proposed system also accounts for the verification of associated stores and the proper transfer of goods and services by having the charity as an escrow. The proposed solution also allows for the tokenization of services provided by the associated stores which will increase the liquidity and accessibility to the goods and services provided by the stores.

Conclusion

Using the above design, the blockchain system can be developed and implemented using Ganache which replicates a real-time Ethereum blockchain, which can later be scaled onto the real blockchain network. Such an implementation is low cost, especially when compared to the commissions taken by the middlemen in the traditional charity cycle. Due to its transparency, consistency of transactions, and faster confirmations, this can soon become a seal of trust amongst charity organizations. Several organizations want to take it a step further and develop brand-new coins to foster the development of new global ecosystems for contributors and nonprofits (Avdoshin & Pesotskaya, 2021). The system results in increased convenience to the charity too, since they can directly make use of the tokens in local stores that accept such forms of payment, and also the effort for maintaining the system from their side is almost negligible after initial setup. This system also adds accountability and security (Avdoshin & Pesotskaya, 2019)from the contracted stores as the transfer of tokens can be controlled by the charity that acts as escrow. This system also aids in increasing the accessibility of beneficiaries and charities to existing contracted stores. Due to the tokenization of the services of contracted stores, beneficiaries get added ease of transaction owing to a singular digital representation of the goods and services provided by the contracted store. Since all the transactions are taking place over a public blockchain, this system can help regain public trust in the charity system.

Predictive Analysis Using Big Data in the Treatment of Pulmonary Diseases

K. N. Jyothilakshmi24

Corresponding author E-mail Id: jyothyhere@gmail.com

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-30

Abstract

Big data analytics in healthcare refers to the use of large and complex datasets to improve patient care and outcomes, and to transform the way healthcare is delivered. With the increasing volume, velocity, and variety of data generated by healthcare systems and devices, big data has become a critical tool for healthcare organizations seeking to gain insights, make informed decisions, and drive innovation. Big data analytics in pulmonary medicine refers to the use of advanced data analysis techniques to process, analyze and make insights from large amounts of pulmonary health data. This includes medical records, imaging results, sensor data, and other relevant data sources. The goal of big data analytics in pulmonary medicine is to improve the understanding of lung diseases and develop more effective treatments, earlier diagnoses, and personalized medicine. By leveraging the power of big data, healthcare professionals can gain new insights into the underlying causes of lung diseases, track the progression of conditions, and identify potential risk factors. Big data analytics in pulmonary medicine holds immense potential to revolutionize the way lung diseases are managed, and ultimately improve patient outcomes.

Keywords: Bigdata analytics, Pulmonary diseases, Predictive analysis

Introduction

Big Data analysis is the process of looking through, purifying, manipulating, and modeling enormous and complicated datasets in order to find significant insights, patterns, and linkages. Big data analysis seeks to extract information and knowledge from data in order to make informed decisions and improve various processes and systems.

Pulmonary diseases are conditions that affect the respiratory system and can cause breathing problems. Some common pulmonary diseases include:

  • Asthma: A persistent respiratory illness marked by inflammation and airway constriction that makes breathing difficult.
  • Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): A collection of lung conditions that worsen over time and restrict airways, such as chronic bronchitis and emphysema, making breathing difficult
  • Lung Cancer: A cancer that begins in the lungs and spreads to other parts of the body, interfering with breathing and overall health.
  • Pneumonia: A lung infection characterized by inflammation and fluid buildup, making breathing difficult.
  • Tuberculosis (TB): This bacterial infection mainly affects the lungs but can also extend to other organs.

These diseases can be debilitating and even fatal, so early detection and treatment are critical for improving patient outcomes. Healthcare professionals are better able to detect and treat pulmonary disorders, which leads to better patient outcomes and quality of life. This is made possible by greater data availability and technology breakthroughs like big data, machine learning, and deep learning algorithms.

Big data analysis typically entails the application of advanced statistical and computational methods, as well as powerful data processing tools, to process and analyze massive amounts of data that are beyond the capabilities of traditional data processing applications (Raita et al., 2021). This includes data from a variety of sources, including social media, transaction records, log files, and sensors, among others.

Big data analysis results can be applied to a variety of applications and domains, including business intelligence, healthcare, finance, marketing, and public policy. With the ever-increasing volume, velocity, and variety of data generated today, big data analysis has become an indispensable tool for businesses seeking to gain a competitive advantage and foster innovation.

Big Data in Healthcare

The use of large and complex datasets to improve patient care and outcomes, as well as to transform the way healthcare is delivered, is referred to as big data in healthcare. Big data has become a critical tool for healthcare organizations seeking to gain insights, make informed decisions, and drive innovation as the volume, velocity, and variety of data generated by healthcare systems and devices has increased.

Big data in healthcare can be used for a variety of purposes, including:

  1. Predictive analytics: Big data can be mined for patterns and relationships that can be used to forecast future outcomes such as disease progression, patient behavior, and resource utilization.
  2. Clinical decision support: Big data can be used to help healthcare providers make clinical decisions by providing real-time information and insights, such as patient data, clinical guidelines, and evidence-based practices.
  3. Population health management: To inform public health policy and improve patient outcomes, big data can be used to identify and track population health trends such as disease outbreaks, health disparities, and patient risk factors.
  4. Personalized medicine: Big data can be used to create personalized treatment plans based on a person’s unique genetic, demographic, and clinical data, resulting in better patient outcomes and more efficient use of healthcare resources.

Big data has the potential to alter healthcare delivery and enhance patient outcomes, and its usage by healthcare institutions throughout the world is growing rapidly (Paoletti et al., 2009). To enable its effective use in healthcare, it introduces additional difficulties, including data privacy and security, data quality and accuracy, and data governance, which must be addressed.

However, the use of big data in healthcare introduces new difficulties, such as data privacy and security, data quality and precision, and data governance, which must be addressed to ensure its effective use in healthcare. Despite these obstacles, big data analytics in healthcare have the potential to modify how healthcare is delivered and improve patient outcomes, and its application is expanding swiftly in healthcare organizations around the world.

Several big data algorithms are utilized to treat pulmonary disorders, including the following:

  1. Machine learning algorithms: These algorithms analyze patterns and trends in patient data to predict future outcomes, diagnose diseases, and prescribe treatments. Deep learning algorithms: These algorithms analyze medical pictures, such as CT scans, using artificial neural networks to detect and classify lung disorders.
  2. Natural Language Processing Algorithms: These algorithms process and analyze patient medical records and notes, enabling more efficient and effective communication between healthcare practitioners.
  3. Predictive analytics algorithms: These algorithms utilize patient data to identify patients at high risk for lung disease and aim preventative

The choice of algorithm depends on the treatment’s specific needs and objectives, as well as the type and quantity of available data. Some algorithms may be more effective in certain circumstances, whereas others may be more suited to specific data types.

2.1 Predictive analytics algorithms in the treatment of diseases

Predictive Analytics uses Big Data to find significant patterns that can be used to forecast future occurrences and evaluate the merits of potential solutions. Any unknown data from the past, present, or future can be analyzed using predictive analytics. By identifying people who are at a high risk of developing lung problems, algorithms for predictive analytics play a key role in the treatment of pulmonary diseases. With the help of this information, preventative interventions can be targeted at specific people, reducing the spread of the illness (Ma & Wu, 2020).

Several forms of predictive analytics algorithms can be used to treat pulmonary disorders, such as:

  1. Risk prediction models: These algorithms determine an individual’s risk of acquiring a certain lung disease using patient data. This data can be utilized to build individualized preventative measures. Big data can be used to predict the progression of pulmonary diseases such as COPD or asthma. By analyzing patient data such as symptoms, treatment history, and environmental factors, predictive models can be created to forecast the future course of the disease. This can help doctors make better decisions about treatment plans and potentially prevent exacerbations.
  2. Decision tree algorithms: These algorithms use decision tree models to predict the results of various treatment options based on patient data. This can assist medical professionals in selecting the most effective treatment for each individual.
  3. Bayesian networks: These algorithms examine patient data and forecast disease outcomes using probabilistic methods. This information can be utilized to personalize treatment programs to the specific requirements of each patient.
  4. Identification of patients at risk: Big data can be used to identify patients with a high risk of developing pulmonary diseases. By analyzing huge databases of patient records and finding trends, predictive algorithms can spot individuals who are at risk for lung diseases, such as those who have a history of smoking or exposure to pollutants. This can enable physicians to intervene and provide preventive care at an early stage.
  5. Personalized treatment plans: Big data can be used to create individualized treatment plans for pulmonary disease patients. By analyzing patient data such as genetic information, medical history, and lifestyle factors, predictive algorithms can assist physicians in developing individualized treatment plans. This can result in more effective treatment and improved patient outcomes.
  6. Real-time monitoring: Big data can be used to monitor patients in real time, allowing doctors to detect changes in their condition and intervene before a serious exacerbation occurs. This can be done by using wearable devices or sensors that collect patient data, which can then be analyzed by predictive algorithms to provide early warnings of potential health problems.

In general, predictive analytics algorithms have the potential to enhance the precision and efficacy of lung disease diagnosis and treatments, leading to improved patient outcomes. The application of predictive analysis algorithms in big data can greatly aid in the treatment of pulmonary diseases by providing personalized care, early detection of health risks, and real-time monitoring of patients.

Numerous research studies have used big data analytics to identify new risk factors and disease mechanisms for various lung diseases. A study published in the journal Nature Communications used big data analytics to identify a new sub-type of lung cancer and developed a personalized treatment plan for patients based on their unique genetic profile. Study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) demonstrated that machine-learning algorithms can accurately diagnose chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) from electronic medical records. Study published in the New England Journal of Medicine used big data analytics to identify a novel drug target for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a deadly lung disease for which there is currently no cure.

While there has been significant progress in the use of big data analytics in pulmonary medicine, there are still some research gaps that need to be addressed to fully realize this potential.

  1. Lack of data standardization: One of the major challenges in using big data analytics in pulmonary medicine is the lack of standardization in data collection and management. Different institutions may use different data formats, making it difficult to compare and integrate data from multiple sources. Standardization efforts are needed to ensure that data can be easily shared and analyzed across different institutions.
  2. Limited diversity in patient populations: Many studies using big data analytics in pulmonary medicine have focused on specific patient populations, such as those with access to healthcare or those who are enrolled in clinical trials. This can lead to biases in the data and limit the generalizability of the findings to other populations.
  3. Ethical considerations: The use of big data analytics raises ethical concerns around data privacy and informed consent. Researchers need to ensure that patient data is collected and used ethically and that patients are fully informed about how their data will be used.
  4. Limited understanding of disease heterogeneity: While big data analytics has the potential to identify new disease subtypes and biomarkers, there is still a limited understanding of the heterogeneity of lung diseases. More research is needed to better understand the underlying mechanisms of these diseases and to identify new targets for treatment.
  5. Limited validation of findings: Many studies using big data analytics in pulmonary medicine are based on retrospective analysis of existing data. There is a need for more prospective studies to validate the findings from these retrospective studies and to ensure that the results can be translated into clinical practice.

Challenges in Predictions Using Big Data

Recognizing that Big Data availability does not automatically address every issue is crucial (Bacon, 2013). A notable illustration is the wealth of earthquake data, yet the lack of a trustworthy model that can correctly predict earthquakes (Silver, 2012). Use of theories, testing, and predictive models are some current issues (Silver, 2012; Poynter, 2014). The following difficulties with Big Data forecasting, in addition to these, have been noted and need careful consideration.

  1. One of the biggest challenges is the lack of employees with the requisite expertise to address the forecasting issue with big data.
  2. Big Data shows a growing noise-to-signal ratio, which means that noise is distorting the signal. Signal extraction becomes increasingly challenging when dealing with huge data sets.
  3. To manage the increased data intake properly, computing capabilities and the fundamental design of statistical software must be improved. To manage Big Data projections, even supercomputers might be needed (Needham, 2012).
  4. Big Data makes it more difficult to differentiate between random and statistically significant outcomes due to the enormous number of data that must be processed and anticipated (Efron, 2010).
  5. Big Data must be moved between sites in order for data mining algorithms to function, which might result in greater network connection costs. Data mining algorithms are frequently unable to work with data that is not put into their main memory. It is necessary to redesign the analytics architecture to support both real-time and historical data (Jadhav, 2013).

Conclusion

Big data analytics has the potential to revolutionize pulmonary medicine by enabling researchers and healthcare professionals to gain a deeper understanding of lung diseases and develop more effective treatments, earlier diagnoses, and personalized medicine. By using the power of vast volumes of data, healthcare practitioners can acquire new insights, make more educated decisions, and provide superior patient care. However, technical competence and medical knowledge are required for the effective use of big data analytics in pulmonary medicine. As the quantity of pulmonary health data continues to increase, it is expected that big data analytics will play a greater role in enhancing pulmonary medicine. Further research is needed to fully realize the potential of big data analytics in pulmonary medicine and to ensure that these tools are used ethically and responsibly. Overall, the integration of big data analytics into pulmonary medicine has the potential to greatly benefit patients and improve public health.

An Improved and Secured Elliptic Curve Cryptography Using Matrix Bitwise Complement for Data Security in Cloud

R. Mary Sheeba, and Dr. R. Parameswari

Department of Computer Science, School of Computing Sciences, Vels Institute of Science, Technology and Advanced Studies, Chennai, India

E-mail: maryrsheeba@gmail.com

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-31

Abstract

Data privacy and security in the cloud have been important topics in the current era. In many medical organizations, a large number of patient records are maintained as Electronic Health Records in the cloud. The biggest challenge in the medical field is to secure the patient’s confidential healthcare data. A robust and innovative data security approach is required to safeguard the details in the cloud environment. In this paper, an improved and secured elliptic curve cryptography (ISEC) with a novel mapping approach has been proposed in order to secure the data and increase the efficiency of the overall encryption process. In this technique, a string ASCII table is referred to, where each plain text character from the string is converted to the corresponding ASCII value. The ASCII value is added to the corresponding alphabet number and product with string occurrence position. The closest prime number (CPN) is generated based on a string ASCII-based table. This methodology neglects the repetition in string ASCII table. This approach allocates unique values for plain text and generates a prime number, which is further utilized for the encoding and decoding process using elliptic curve cryptography.

Keywords: elliptic curve, ASCII value, cryptography, bitwise complement

Introduction

Cloud computing is one of the most important concepts to store data efficiently. In the current era, small and large-scale industries, healthcare sectors, educational organizations, business administrators, individual users, etc., benefit from cloud resources. The main advantage of using the cloud sector is its unique features. The user can utilize the resource according to their need and it is also cost-effective for cloud users.

Cryptography is an important method integrated with encryption and decryption concepts. It provides security under various aspects, which involve vital tasks, such as generating the public and private keys, managing the keys throughout the session, and encoding/decoding the content. In the concept of cryptography, public key encryption, which contains public as well as private keys play a major role in encrypting and decrypting the data. When data are transmitted in the cloud environment, they should safely reach the destination with proper authentication, confidentiality, and integrity. Many existing encryption methodologies are vulnerable to protecting the data when they are in transmission (Hema & Kesavan, 2019). The innovation of cloud computing has given more facilities and services to huge healthcare-based providers. This boosts the providers to transfer all medical-related services to the healthcare cloud. This healthcare cloud is part of a cloud environment where medical reports, patient diagnosis details, information back-up, and monitoring information have been stored, transferred, maintained, and referred securely and confidentially. Though this cloud technology has many advantages, still many users are reluctant to prefer this facility due to data breaches and mishandling of data. To avoid such insecurities in maintaining healthcare records a robust type of encryption method is required.

The existing or conventional methodologies produce encryption of the data but with larger keys and also require more complex computations. Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) is a conventional public key cryptography method where it works based on large prime factorization in order to produce the best security for the customer data. It also uses both common and secret keys for authenticated data sharing but this method takes more time to execute due to its large and complex process. In recent years, to avoid such discrepancies elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) has been used and recommended by many researchers. When compared to the conventional method it produces the finest solution and better security for the healthcare data stored in the cloud.

Literature Review

In this section, advanced methodologies in elliptic curve cryptography have been discussed briefly Singh & Singh, (2015)introduced a mapping technique to encode the text using elliptic curve cryptography. The plain text is partitioned into various groups depending on ASCII value. The larger integer base was assigned for each group and it is fed as the starting point of the ECC (Kainalakaiinan & Tamilselvaii, 2015). In this paper, the author proposed a new set of methodologies to secure big data cloud repositories using the ECC algorithm. The huge dataset is split into continuous data parts based on IP resembled and maintained with alphanumerical names (Dhamodharan & Thaddeus, 2022). In Ref. Dhamodharan & Thaddeus, (2022), the author proposes a novel mapping methodology is proposed to make the speedup process more efficient. This work was compared with ElGamal ECC encryption and decryption time (Tallapally & Manjula, 2020). The author proposed a new idea to enhance the security level with a multilevel security scheme. Such multi-protection gives more security when compared to single-layer protection. The ECC key is given as an input for AES and using a Hessian algorithm, the input key is passed to TDES and finally, the output cipher is generated (Khan & Qazi, 2019). This paper has implemented the concept of ECC due to its easy computational and small key size. The author shows that ECC is more efficient in protecting the data in the cloud environment.

Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)

An elliptic curve is defined by the set of points using the equation Y2=x3+sx+t, where s and t are the elements of the field “K” to give away the point infinity and also the condition 4s3+27t2 # 0 should not equal to zero. The real numbers (R), rational numbers (Q), and complex numbers (c) are examples of fields where the elliptic curve can be defined. The elliptic curve is so special when there is a need for cryptography and key exchange concepts. It requires a shorter encryption key which takes very little memory and CPU resources. This elliptic curve is a public key cryptography in which 256 bits of EC provide the same protection as 3072 bits of RSA (Dhamodharan & Thaddeus, 2019). It is always a difficult task to transfer the text content to EC points.

ECC Over Finite Field

The elliptic curve with the finite field is used in cryptography with the help of coordinate points generated for the curve. The finite field in ECC is represented by y2=x3+sx+t mod P (Sandhia & Raja, 2022). Here “P” is the largest prime number in a finite field. For instance, if the set of all integers is 5 then “P” is also “5.” Therefore, the values of “x” and “y” will be the values in the set. Similarly, the value of “s” and “t” should not exceed the value of “P”

ISEC-Based Cryptosystem Technique to Secure Data Transfer in Cloud

In this section, the concept of the proposed work Improved and Secured Elliptic Curve (ISEC) has been discussed with its steps and methodology.

Phases of ISEC Mapping Technique

The proposed work involves various process steps such as generating a Closest Prime Number, Random generation Point, computing a Secret (Sk) Key, Private (Prk), and Public (Puk) key generation for encoding and decoding. The execution of these phases is integrated for the secure communication of data by Elliptic Curve Cryptography in the cloud.

CPN Generation

The Closest Prime Number is generated for the implementation of the process by referring to the new proposed ASCII, alphabet, and Character based table. Initially, the input is received from the user as a collection of strings (Das & Giri, 2018). Each bit of the word from the collection of strings is uniquely identified and the ASCII value is assigned to it. This ASCII table is known to all sets of users which makes the intruders easily identify the inputs. To avoid such issues, the ASCII value is multiplied by the position of character occurrence in the string and added along with the alphabet value. By including the character occurrence position value avoid the repetition in the string ASCII table. This final value is taken as input to generate the Closest Prime Number. The spaces in the string are referred to, by using special symbols and it is assigned routinely. The ASCII value of the special characters is evaluated along with the order of the symbols.

Key Generation Process

The Elliptic curve cryptography is a public key cryptosystem that needs both public and private keys to make a transaction more secure. Here the private keys are generated from randomly chosen elliptic curve points. Similarly, generator point (G) has also opted randomly from the generated EC points. The public key is produced from the combination of the generator point (G) and private key (Prk). To evaluate the receiver’s secret key convert the sender key into binary format and apply XOR & bitwise complement. After the bit complement process, the values are converted to decimal. Here, the secret keys are sent to the receiver along with the encrypted message. So, more concern should be shown about the secret key during the transaction. In order to avoid any unnecessary distraction from the intruders it is better to hide the original secret value. By this, the secret value is secured during the transaction.
  3. During the decryption process, the decimal value which is obtained from the XOR & bitwise complement is applied. Here the original value is not used in decryption which in turn produces better security for the data.

  5. Finally, the encoded message can be decoded by dividing Enc2 with srk +Enc1. This produces plain text as the output.

Conclusion

The term security is always connected with the cryptosystem. In this work, the Elliptic curve cryptosystem has been used with the conversion of each character into an ASCII string-based alphabetic sequence number, and the CPN is generated to get the points on ECC. The generator point “G” is randomly generated from the Elliptic curve points. The public and private keys are generated and the secret key is sent to the receiver with some modifications in order to preserve the key value from intruders.

Real-Time Over-The-Air-Programming (OTAP) for Wireless Sensor Network: Implementation and Analysis Using SENSEnuts IoT Platform

Chakravarthi Harshitha, Tallavalasa Venkatesh, and Jayavignesh Thyagarajan

School of Electronics Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology Chennai, India

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-32

Abstract

Numerous smart remote monitoring applications pertaining to the environment (specific to panchaboothas namely monitoring air {quality, gas concentration, pollution, etc}, fire, water, land, sky), habitat, military, surveillance, intrusion/border detection, health, etc.) focus on Internet of Things (IoT) based Wireless Sensor Network (WSN) solutions. The IoT sensor nodes are constrained in terms of resources namely computing, storage and battery and are programmed to perform tasks such as sensing, processing and wirelessly transmitting the monitored event as packets over low data rate networks and switch to sleep state when inactive to preserve battery power. In such remote monitoring locations that are restricted or limited in physical access, these constrained IoT devices are deployed in random or installed in regular manner. To support large-scale deployment of monitoring for such applications, it becomes highly essential to remotely control these IoT sensor nodes. OTAP provides remote connectivity to remotely monitor the devices and reprogram the devices when required. This enables to remotely flash the sensor nodes simultaneously and also displays the real-time gathered sensor data results for different applications. In this paper, we have implemented & tested OTAP using SENSEnuts Embedded IoT platform to remotely program the IEEE 802.15.4 compliant sensor mote and analyzed for different use cases. Also, challenges involved of flashing the firmware (compiled binary) over the air via the PAN coordinator are highlighted.

Keywords: SENSEnuts, Protocol, IoT node, OTAP, WSN

Introduction

Over The Air Programming (OTAP) has been widely adopted in mobile smartphone handsets to transmit firmware updates through wireless technology(WiFi/4Getc),In a pandemic-driven world, OTA Phasa huge impact and importance in IoT based WSN that demands more of remote monitoring and control. IoT based WSN consists of several sensor nodes, each node comprising of sensor(s) interfaced with a micro-controller and radio transceiver capture and wirelessly transmit information about the region of interest and perform actuation or control action appropriately. OTAP enables to dynamic flash of the program code over the air on the remotely deployed Internet.

of Things (IoT) networks. This gives the flexibility to enable re-programming over the air, to add new features to the existing code, fix the bugs or resolve the security vulnerabilities.

This work focuses on the remote monitoring of greenhouses. A greenhouse is a closed structure that provides optimal conditions for plant growth by controlling the indoor and outdoor environments. The walls of the greenhouse are made with transparent materials such as glass or plastic. To achieve optimal plant growth, several key parameters must be considered, including soil moisture, humidity, atmospheric and soil temperature, sunlight availability, and the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air. This work specifically focuses on two parameters: temperature and humidity, which affect plant growth. Using the SENSEnuts IoT platform, we test sensor nodes at different locations inside the greenhouse under varying conditions. We also propose over-the-air programming in greenhouse monitoring to remotely reprogram the SENSEnuts nodes as needed. The paper is structured as follows: WSN architecture, Literature Survey, Proposed System, Methodology, Results obtained under various test conditions, and Conclusion.

Literature Survey

In previous works (Sangeeth et al., 2016; Ramesh et al., 2013), the OTAP approach has been implemented in a remote-triggered laboratory, enabling real-time video streaming of results without requiring physical connections between the nodes and the system. According to an evaluation, SO% of students rated the performance as excellent, and 41% rated it as very good. The next phase of development involves integrating compression algorithms into the OTAP method.

According to Lata et al., (2020), SENSEnuts wireless sensor nodes were utilized in conjunction with a wireless sensor network to monitor the temperature and humidity within a miniature greenhouse laboratory model. The system was subjected to various testing scenarios and was found to have low power consumption, low cost, and a user-friendly approach for real-time monitoring of climatic conditions within a greenhouse.

In a comprehensive overview of OTAP, including discussions of the latest OAP protocols utilized in WSN applications and the test-bed implementations ( (Qandour et al., 2012; Ramesh et al., 2013; Steyn & Hancke, 2011; Hellbruck et al., 2011; Doddavenkatappa et al., 2011), presented in these works (Quadri et al., 2014). Over-the-air programming is a crucial process for resolving bugs, updating codes, and managing changes in application requirements.

The project (Frisch et al., 2017) aims to create a reliable and robust system for ESP8266 microcontrollers by developing and releasing encrypted firmware updates. Additionally, efforts are underway to expand and improve the functionality and security of the system, with the latest developments focusing on enhancing security features.

An article (Kilaru et al., 2022)discusses the utilization of wireless sensor networks (WSN) and weather forecasting to automate agriculture. It explains how the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud integration can automate irrigation and enhance security in farming. Moreover, the system can be adapted to create a sensor-cloud-based environment control system to cultivate vegetables and flowers in greenhouse farming during the off-season. The authors of the paper suggest that their system can be a valuable tool for improving the efficiency and productivity of farming.

IoT Based WSN Architecture

WSN involve deploying a large number of sensor nodes throughout a specific area, which can range from hundreds to thousands of nodes. WSN involves deploying a large number of sensor nodes throughout a specific area, which can range from hundreds to thousands of nodes. The sensor node typically comprises units such as sensor(s), processing unit, and communication unit as shown in Fig. 1. The gateway node (sink) acts as PAN coordinator to coordinate and collect data from the sensor nodes. The WSN employs the Zigbee protocol compliant with IEEE 802.15.4 specifications

Proposed System and Methodology

The proposed WSN system comprises several SENSEnuts IoT nodes developed by Eigen Technologies and deployed in the region of interest. Each SENSEnuts node is modular hardware platform stacked with Temperature and Light sensors and interfaced with JN5168 32 bit IEEE 802.15.4 compliant radio microcontroller that operates in the 2.4 GHz ISM frequency band. The sensor(s) in each node are tasked to transmit the data as packets under few test conditions such as single-hop (direct transmission) and multi-hop (via intermediate relay nodes to reach gateway) as shown in Fig. 2. The sensor nodes can also be re-flashed (reprogrammed) to change the data collection frequency etc using OTAP.

The TL (Temperature, Light) interfaced sensor node is deployed to monitor a particular zonewise area. Sensor nodes have been strategically placed at varying distances, and in order to test the OTAP for SENSEnuts motes. The gateway node is flashed and programmed with the PAN coordinator code to collect data from the deployed sensor nodes at specified time intervals. The gateway module is utilized for programming all sensor nodes, as well as interfacing with the PC and network. The TL sensor can collect data from the TMP102 temperature sensor, which has a range sensitivity of —250 °C to 800 °C and a resolution of 12 bits.

The SENSEnuts gateway node, depicted in Fig. 3 of the Greenhouse Monitoring System that utilizes Over The Air Programming (OTAP), comprises a radio IEEE 802.15.4 module and a USB gateway module. The node is battery-powered and equipped with two 1.5V AA batteries, housed within the protective plastic case to shield it from environmental conditions.

The compiled binary i.e the new program code (firmware) to be flashed onto the sensor devices is transmitted as several packets of fixed size of 64 bytes wirelessly over the air by the PAN coordinator (gateway node) until the complete binary file is received (i.e. all packets are successfully transferred and received by the sensor node error free i.e. individual packets are acknowledged and checksum validated). As the Over the Air (OTA) Layer is enabled in each sensor node (i.e coordinator devices), where the node is tasked to check if the flash memory is free, flush the memory, and once the compiled program code (binary file) is received completely it is stored in flash memory and command is sent to reboot with the new firmware (i.e program code). The methodology is two-step process:

  • Step 1: The compiled new program binary file (OTA code) is split as packets of 64 bytes each and transmitted via wire (USB) to program serially the PAN coordinator (Gateway node) initially. Each packet transmitted is acknowledged and checksum verified and once the complete binary file is transferred, the new firmware gets flashed in PAN coordinator.
  • Step 2: The PAN coordinator now starts searching the network and scans for the sensor devices (coordinator) connected in the network and starts programming the sensor nodes one by one by transmitting the compiled binary file as packets of 64bytes

Implementation

OTAP enables the programming of nodes by transmitting as data packets over the wireless network, allowing each node to program itself with the received data packets, without requiring a constant connection to PC. The received data packets put together are stored in the mote’s EEPROM. When a command is tasked to the PAN coordinator to modify or change a particular code, the starting address page is traced and cached to processor memory from the flash memory. The coordinator node is rebooted then automatically with the newly flashed program code.

For every data transfer, 64 bytes of data are sent and received from the PAN co-ordinator, providing an acknowledgment to the PC indicating whether the data was received or not as shown in Fig. 5.

OTA Total Packets

Based on the application, the total binary file size will increase for transmission. Along with that, the number of packets to be transferred also increases, as shown in Fig. 6.

Total Packets Transferred in Wireless Network for Each Application Code shows the different App code binary file sizes and number of packets transferring to pan coordinator via OTA.

OTA Flashing Time

If we need to wirelessly flash these nodes which are deployed at a larger separation distance, The flashing time has the potential to increase further due to the need for packet retries, which are necessary to compensate for packets lost as a result of poor channel quality. This phenomenon is depicted in Fig. 7 (OTA Flashing Network Setup Time for Different Network Sizes), where theoretical calculations outline the comprehensive time required to flash nodes within the network. For instance, consider a scenario with a total of 10 nodes. In this case, the cumulative packets transferred within the network amount to 5580 for the broadcast app code. The total time taken to flash these 10 nodes is approximately 11.16 seconds, assuming a fixed data transfer rate of 25KB. As the number of nodes increased, the time required to complete the flashing process increases linearly. This linear increase in flashing time with larger network sizes imposes limitations on scalability. Consequently, there arises a necessity to optimize the flashing time in order to accommodate the expansion of the network.

Conclusion

In this paper we implemented Over The Air Programming (OTAP) based WSN test bed implementation using SENSEnuts embedded IOT platform in LINUX to reprogram sensor motes wirelessly. The paper highlights the main challenges presented when we scale the size of the deployed WSN, the setup and reprogramming time will increase linearly. Due to the limitations of IEEE802.15.4 standard such as limited bandwidth (256Kbps), power and storage constraints, the flashing of binary files (firmware) wirelessly takes time and due to varying channel conditions, the complexity increases. The future work includes optimization of the flashing time and implementation of the remotely reprogramming in Greenhouse Monitoring Application.
