Manipulation of 3D Objects in Handheld Augmented Reality for Campus Virtual Visit

Motipalli Tharun, Romella Naveen, Muthukumaran Malarvel32

Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-41

Abstract

This framework demonstrates how to control augmented reality objects (AR). By the use of AR technology, it is the interaction of virtual goods with the actual world. It tries to make manipulating digital information for users seamless and simple. Gestures, input devices, computer vision, and visuals are used in the manipulation. Using virtual objects of the buildings and rooms, we will develop a virtual campus visit within this framework. This framework aids observers in comprehending a building’s elements and architecture. This suggested model explains how buildings and architecture are organized and can be useful as a virtual tour for the spectator. In this paper, we are using object tracking and Marker-Based Tracking in this framework. This paper aims to give a framework that can be used for a virtual tour of the campus by creating a better user experience.

Keywords: Augmented Reality, Computer Vision, Object Manipulation, Object tracking

Introduction

Handheld augmented reality (AR) has grown in popularity over the past several years across many industries, including education and travel (Yu et al., 2019). With the growing use of smartphones and tablets, handheld augmented reality offers an engaging and immersive way to experience both the physical and digital worlds at once. Virtual campus visits, (Voutos et al., 2022; Zhigang et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2021; Sundarramurthi et al., 2022; Kondlo et al., 2020)which let potential students or visitors experience a university campus more interestingly and educationally, are one possible use of handheld AR. The manipulation of 3D objects in handheld AR for virtual campus tours is still difficult, though. In this study, we offer a unique method for manipulating 3D objects in handheld AR for virtual campus tours (Jacobe et al., 202)as a response to this problem. Our method takes advantage of portable devices’ capabilities and augmented reality (AR) technologies to build a simple and user-friendly interface for engaging with virtual items on a college campus. We think that our strategy could improve the visitor experience and encourage university campus participation.

It has been demonstrated that augmented reality in education improves learning results and student engagement (Zhou & Tai, 2022). AR can help students envision and comprehend abstract ideas more concretely by offering an interactive and immersive experience. Additionally, a number of school-related activities, including campus tours, orientation sessions, and student recruitment events have made use of augmented reality (Jacobe et al., 2021).

The difficulty of naturally and intuitively engaging with 3D items in these settings is one obstacle to the implementation of augmented reality. Traditional AR interfaces frequently rely on touch gestures or other challenging to learn and master input techniques (Schmetz et al., 2019). However, recent developments in computer vision and machine learning have made it possible for new methods of manipulating 3D objects in augmented reality, including voice commands, gaze tracking, and hand tracking (Sundarramurthi et al., 2022). It describes a novel method for manipulating 3D objects in handheld augmented reality for virtual campus tours (Voutos et al., 2022; Zhigang et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2021; Sundarramurthi et al., 2022; Kondlo et al., 2020). Our method combines hand tracking and an intuitive way to interact with virtual items. Through a user study, we assess our strategy in addition to contrasting it with conventional touch-based interaction techniques (Schmetz et al., 2019). We think that our strategy can greatly improve user experience and raise interest in virtual campus tours.

Here in these above papers, the authors have worked on different technologies and methodologies. In this paper, we will be using Marker-Based Tracking for virtual campus experience.

The remainder of this essay is organized as follows. A summary of some of the literature to which we have made references is provided in Section 2. In Section 3, the suggested system and modules are shown and discussed. We present the Results and Discussion in Section 4. In Part 5, we come to some conclusions and future work and go over some potential next steps.

Literature Survey

Jacobe et al., (2021) propose a mobile application that utilizes augmented reality (AR) to enhance the tourism experience at the Wari Willka Museum in Peru. The authors begin by discussing the limitations of traditional museum experiences as well as the potential benefits of AR-based systems in providing visitors with a more engaging and interactive experience. They then describe the development of their mobile application, which allows visitors to access AR content such as virtual tours, 3D models, and multimedia presentations using their smartphones. Zhou & Tai, (2022) proposes a solution for enhancing museum visits through the use of smart augmented reality technology. The authors propose a smart augmented reality self-guiding application that uses a smartphone or tablet to display 3D models and animations, as well as provide audio and text descriptions of exhibits. The augmented reality technology enables visitors to interact with the exhibits and learn about them in a fun and engaging way.

Bakhmut et al., (2021)in their study, in order to enable virtual campus tours created an AR- based web application. The authors overlaid 3D models of campus structures and landmarks on real-world images taken with a smartphone camera. They did this by using image recognition and tracking technology. Each location’s historical and cultural value was also covered in the application’s supplemental material. Yu et al., (2019)in their study focused on developing techniques for natural and intuitive manipulation of 3D virtual objects in AR environments, specifically on handheld devices. The main goal of the study is to design a system that takes into account the effects of gravity in AR and provides a smooth, seamless user experience for object manipulation. The study likely employs computer vision techniques for tracking and interpreting the user’s hand movements and gestures, as well as machine learning algorithms for predicting the user’s intention and determining the desired manipulation.

Li et al., (2021)investigate the use of machine learning techniques for manipulating objects in augmented reality in their paper titled “Object Manipulation in AR Using Machine Learning Techniques” (AR). Traditional AR interfaces for object manipulation, such as touch or gesture- based methods, the authors argue, can be limited in functionality and intuitive use. To address this issue, the authors propose training the AR system with machine learning algorithms to recognize user intentions based on their movements and actions in the AR environment.

Wieland et al., (2021)in their study, describe the comparison of three collaborative 3D object manipulation techniques for handheld augmented reality: separation, composition, and hybrid is the focus of the paper. According to the study’s findings, the hybrid technique was the most efficient in terms of task completion time and error rate, while the composition technique was the most effective in terms of number of interactions

Yang et al., (2021)in their study propose a deep neural network-based method for augmented reality object manipulation in real- time. The proposed method entails training a deep neural network to predict the virtual object’s transformation parameters based on hand movements captured by the AR device. The authors go into great detail about the network architecture and training process, including how they used a large-scale dataset and data augmentation techniques to improve the network’s accuracy. Fang & Hong, (2021) is an analysis of existing research in the field of augmented reality (AR) and its applications for interactive assembly tasks. The survey focuses on the use of bare-hand gestures for controlling virtual objects and the consideration of occlusions in AR systems. The survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art in the field, including the various hand tracking and gesture recognition techniques used in AR interaction, the methods used to handle occlusions and the results of user studies and evaluations of AR assembly systems.

The Study by Fazliaty Edora Fadzli et al. on the topic (Nor'a et al., 2020)is an analysis of existing research in the field of handheld augmented reality (AR) and its applications for 3D manipulation using fingertips interaction. The survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art in the field, including the various techniques used for tracking and recognizing fingertips, the methods used to implement 3D manipulation using fingertips, and the results of user studies and evaluations of these systems.

The study by Schmetz et al., (2019) is focused on exploring and evaluating different methods for marking and annotating production parts using touch-based AR technology. The main goal of the study is to determine which touch-based AR marking techniques are most effective, efficient, and usable for industrial applications. The study likely involves a comprehensive literature review of existing research on touch-based AR marking, including both academic and industrial sources.

Proposed System

Design of the Model

First, we plan on gathering some 3D objects and the next step would be creating the 3D models in blender. Blender is a powerful and flexible 3D modeling tool that can make the process easier. In this framework, we’ll go through using Blender to create 3D models for augmented reality (AR) apps.

Before starting, it’s important to understand the requirements of the AR application you are working on. This includes factors such as the target device, the resolution and scale of the 3D models, and the specific features and animations needed for the AR experience. Once you have a clear understanding of these requirements, you can start creating the 3D models in Blender.

In the aforementioned Fig. 1 the 3D models are constructed. Here are the models for the staff room, conference room, and block building are shown in Figs. 1 (a—c), respectively. UV mapping and adding textures will be applied next. While UV mapping is used to specify how the textures are applied to the models’ surfaces, textures aid to give 3D models depth and realism. A variety of UV mapping and texturing techniques are available in Blender, including the capacity to paint directly onto 3D objects and produce unique textures.

After the 3D models are created and textured, the final step is to export them in a format that can be used in the AR application. Blender offers a range of export options, including popular 3D file formats such as .fbx and .obj. It’s important to ensure that the exported models are optimized for the target device and that any necessary animations or interactions are preserved in the export process.

Overview of System Architecture

Three layers make up the system architecture, which is how the framework operates. the output layer, the database layer, transition layer, and the recognition layer. These stages are crucial to the operation of the application. Vuforia and Unity are the tools we’re employing in this framework to create the application.

The suggested method for manipulating 3D objects in handheld augmented reality for virtual campus tours makes use of a modular system architecture to enable flexible and scalable implementation. An object database for 3D objects, a marker detection and tracking module, and a user interface module make up the architecture’s three core parts. The marker detection and tracking module use computer vision techniques to identify and follow physical markers in the user’s environment, giving the AR system precise position and orientation data.

A 3D object database, which houses the virtual representations of the campus buildings, landmarks, and other items, serves as the system’s brain. Also, the user’s location and orientation are determined via a marker-based tracking system, which is then utilized to overlay the necessary virtual items onto the actual surroundings The technology also has a visual guiding and feedback layer that the user may access while on the virtual visit. The suggested architecture offers a flexible and scalable framework for incorporating augmented reality (AR) in campus virtual visits by segmenting the various system components into independent layers.

There are many levels in the proposed architecture diagram shown in Fig. 2, including the output layer, the database layer, and the recognition layer.

Recognition Layer: The system’s recognition layer, which uses system input and output, is a crucial part of the whole system. The GPS and camera on a mobile phone act as system input sensors, and the screen displays the overlay visuals. The user’s present position in respect to nearby points of interest is ascertained by the GPS while the AR markers are scanned by the camera. The program shows details about a location of interest while the user is walking by and is within proximity to it.

Database Layer: Data management, which includes data input, storage, and processing, is handled by this layer. Live data from the sensor layer is processed in this layer. Databases are used to hold details about numerous structures and tourist attractions at this tier. This paper’s processing unit is the Vuforia AR server, which is housed in the Cloud.

Transition Layer: In our application, this layer manages the change from one scene to another. Using 2D and virtual buttons, scenes are transitioned from one to the next. Because canvas is used to create 2D buttons. In an AR scene, virtual buttons are used.

Output: The output portion is obtained from the database once image processing is finished or when points of interest have been located. The result will be a screen presentation of the superimposed data on the user’s mobile device.

The campus map is employed in this framework, and the buildings and labs can be seen in augmented reality. In this framework, 2D Buttons are utilized in a Scene made up of a main camera, a direction light, and a canvas for showing the map.

A campus map and a few UI buttons for the framework. There are buttons for opening and exiting the app as well as buttons for showing various items. Two distinct segments make up the transition between scenes. Virtual buttons are used to exit the augmented reality environment and return to the map scene. UI buttons cannot be used in an AR scenario. Scene modifications and functionality may be provided through C# scripts. Functionalities may be defined using scripts, and other features can be added using a variety of assets. The items could be given additional textures to increase visibility.

System Implementation

The application was created with an agile process. Images of different structures and laboratories are chosen and added to an online database. The AR mobile application was created with the help of Unity and the Vuforia SDK. This project’s scope was limited to Android-enabled mobile devices and was created with the Android SDK.

The Vivo V20 mobile phone was selected for testing due to its impressive specifications. It boasts a high-resolution display of 2400x1080, which provides a clear and vivid visual experience. The V20’s main camera has a 64MP sensor with a 26mm focal length and an aperture of f/1.9, allowing it to take clear, detailed pictures in a range of lighting situations. Additionally, the V20 is powered by a Snapdragon 720G processor and 8 GB of RAM, ensuring that the AR app can run smoothly and without any processing bottlenecks. Overall, the Vivo V20 is a reliable and powerful device that is well-suited for AR applications.

Results and Discussion

We used a mixed-methods approach in this study to assess the usefulness of portable augmented reality for virtual campus tours. The survey involved a set of questions to analyze the user understanding of the application. They are

H1. what do you think about the detailing and view of the virtual campus experience?

H2. what do you think about the user experience on interaction with virtual objects?

H3. what do you think about the interaction of the buildings, rooms and the manipulation of them like scaling and rotation?

We recruited SO volunteers from the public for the full-scale study, which included people between the age of 21 to 35. Participants were chosen based on their interest in virtual campus tours and their knowledge of portable augmented reality technologies. We employed a portable augmented reality application named “Virtual Campus Tour” designed expressly for this study for study. Using a combination of 3D models and real-time video, the program was created to present users with an immersive and interactive virtual tour of a university campus.

We gathered both quantitative and qualitative data for the pilot research. A survey was distributed to participants before and after the virtual campus tour to obtain quantitative data. The survey included Likert-scale and open-ended questions intended to evaluate the user experience and efficacy of the portable augmented reality technology. Interviews with participants were performed immediately following the virtual campus tour to acquire qualitative data. For the full-scale study, we collected quantitative data through the same survey used in the pilot study, as well as through a series of usability tests. Usability tests were conducted with a subset of participants and consisted of a series of tasks designed to assess the ease of use and functionality of the handheld augmented reality application.

Images of the survey responses recorded for Questions H1, H2, H3 and graph of their distribution are observed in Figs. 3(a—c). A significant degree of user satisfaction was evident in the results, with 90% of participants saying that the model enhanced their virtual visit experience. 85% of participants found the marker-based tracking system to be user-friendly and accurate in determining their position and orientation, which speaks volumes about how well-liked it was. 80% of participants said that using touch-based interaction techniques was intuitive and simple, which contributed to its popularity. Overall, the poll results show the value and promise of our suggested approach for integrating portable AR to improve the virtual campus visit experience.

Conclusion

This study’s goal was to create an Augmented Reality-based virtual tour guide (AR). This would make campus tours available without a guide. Throughout campus, AR markers have been placed at points of interest. Anybody with a capable mobile phone who has downloaded the necessary software may simply scan the markers with their phone. camera to discover the campus’s unique spots.

To give customers a smooth and interesting virtual visit experience, the model integrates a marker-based tracking system, a 3D object database, and intuitive interaction approaches. The success and potential of the suggested model were shown by the online survey results, with users indicating high levels of satisfaction with the system’s usability, accuracy, and utility. Further research in this field may entail extending the model to include more sophisticated interaction methods, including gesture recognition or haptic feedback, as well as connecting the system with other campus resources, like course schedules or campus maps. Overall, the suggested paradigm shows promise for utilizing portable AR to improve the virtual campus visit experience. While only compatible with Android smartphones, the program will eventually support iOS devices as well. Future additions could include the inclusion of tools like text-to-speech and navigation

Locality Recommendation System Using Exploratory Data Analysis and Affinity Propagation

Abhishek Varma, Leela Krishna and Muthukumaran Malarver33

Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-42

Abstract

In recent decades, the recommendation system is widely used in the field of location findings, online retail shops, real estate, healthcare, etc., The available methods are providing satisfactory performance. however still, the research is being proposed. Therefore, in this paper, we proposed a new model for location recommendation. Generally, a location recommendation system provides a suggestion to the users to find appropriate locations based on preferences. The user might like to settle in a specific neighborhood depending on elements like distance to a road, a mall, and other features. For example, if we take google maps as an example, it just provides a map view of locations and directions, but it cannot show a specific area or region where all the user’s preferences are met. To fill that gap, we have developed a model which recommends locations by taking personalized user and Context-Aware Recommendations like climate and weather conditions using geolocation plotting. This paper presents a detailed methodology for the development of the proposed system including the way of approach, usage of Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), and implementation of affinity propagation algorithm.

Keywords: Recommendation system, Exploratory Data Analysis, Affinity Propagation, Geolocation plotting, context-aware recommendations

1 Introduction

Location recommendation systems (Pan et al., 2022)provide suggestions to users about the most suitable locations for various purposes. These systems use various algorithms and techniques such as data mining, deep learning (Dellal-Hedjazi & Alimazighi, 2020), machine learning (Fanca et al., 2020), and geographic information systems (GIS) (Xiaofang et al., 2007) to recommend locations based on user preferences and historical data. Finding the right location using a recommendation system is a challenging task. Location recommendation systems can be used in various domains such as travel, food, entertainment, and many more. They can also be integrated into other applications such as maps, search engines, and e-commerce platforms to provide more relevant results.

The purpose of our developed model is to provide a more personalized and personalized and efficient experience to users which saves them time and effort in finding the right locality. The current recommendation systems for locality are often based on ratings and reviews, which may not be reliable and personalized. Additionally, these systems do not consider contextual factors that may affect user preferences such as weather and climate conditions. Therefore, there is a need for a more sophisticated approach that utilizes data analysis and machine learning techniques to provide accurate and personalized recommendations.

This proposed model aims to provide users with a more personalized location by utilizing the Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) technique (Lee & Lee, 2022)and Affinity Propagation algorithm (Tang et al., 2022). The system will take into consideration various factors such as user preferences, weather, and climate conditions to provide accurate and relevant recommendations. The use of EDA will help in gaining insights into the data and identifying patterns and relationships between different factors. Affinity Propagation, on the other hand, will help in clustering similar data points and providing the final recommendations based on the most suitable cluster.

The method and strategy utilized to generate suggestions are what sets the proposed system apart from the existing model. Current location recommendation models frequently rely on straightforward techniques like content-based filtering or K-means clustering (Saini et al., 2022). These approaches might only work for certain people, but they are not always customized to the requirements and preferences of the person. The suggested system makes use of sophisticated data analysis methods to give users a more detailed and personalized location recommendation experience.

2 Literature Survey

Geo-locational data is a rapidly growing field of study that has revolutionized the way we understand the world around us. With the proliferation of Global Positioning System (GPS)- enabled devices and the ubiquity of location- based services, we are generating vast amounts of geo-locational data every day. However, analyzing and making sense of this data presents a unique set of challenges. The development of effective recommendation systems has become increasingly important for businesses seeking to enhance customer satisfaction and loyalty. The following literature provides a detailed discussion of various recommendation systems proposed earlier.

Sumithra et al., (2022)proposed a methodology for finding accommodations and lodging using K-Means Clustering that would categorize accommodation for travelers according to individual choices for facilities, affordability, and proximity to the location to find the best choice.

Kishan et al., (2022 )proposed a recommendation model to identify the most suitable lodging for an individual in a destination of a precise location by categorizing lodging for the people according to their choices of facilities and spending plans. It entails applying Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering to segment population and spatial information, which would be decided to apply on the geo-locational data obtained from REST API in classifying temporary accommodation for the people in full compliance with their priority areas.

Pandya et al., (2016)involved in the development of a novel hybrid approach that combines clustering and association rule mining to overcome data sparsity and cold start problems in recommendation systems. Their approach clusters the rating matrix based on user similarity and applies the clustering Algorithm on Boolean data generated from the clustered data to efficiently generate rules.

Xu et al., (2022)were involved in exploring the recent research on mini-batch AP clustering algorithm by focusing on the main approaches used, the advantages and disadvantages of the method, and the applications in various domains.

Ma et al., (2020)implemented a POI behavioral change model based on the LBSN methodology. various kinds of information were integrated: customer check-in data, attribute data, spatial impact of POIs, and proximity of Objects. The Foursquare databases were used to carry out the study. The study showed that the factorization method achieves greater accuracy than other contemporary approaches.

Li et al., (2020) have proposed a two-stage clustering technique called DDAP in order to enhance the effectiveness and functionality of affinity propagation clustering and density curves. The suggested approach chooses a limited number of possible exemplars using the two variables of each cluster center in order to minimize the dimension of the similarity measure, and then it performs message-passing on the partial similarity matrix.

Bandi et al., (2020)presented a brand-new method for dynamically categorizing textual Big Data that draws inspiration from Enhanced Learning and Segmentation approaches. This method can prepare the data for machine learning with few manual tasks and deliver great insights.

Park et al., (2020)created a technique to group the RRHs using a customized form of the affinity propagation clustering algorithm in order to enhance the combined distribution of radio remote heads in densely packed tiny cellular systems.

Panwar et al., (2021)suggested a methodology using machine learning to develop a recommendation engine utilizing big data within the framework of an e-commerce platform and also to provides valuable insights into the subject of data exploration. The research contribution begins by outlining the methods and techniques employed directly in sentiment classification often known as opinion mining.

Banerjee & Chowdhury (2021)were involved in developing a method to study the relationship between reviews and textual and non-textual parameters in user-based analysis. They have analyzed two different datasets from Zomato and Yelp which have geographical differences and diverse user reviews. The authors have applied feature engineering and supervised and ensemble machine learning algorithms such as Linear regression, Logistic regression, XGBoost, and Gradient Boosting algo to construct a predictive model.

Here, in these above papers, the authors have worked on different technologies like clustering and classification, data analysis, filtering, and many more. For the location recommendation, they have used a hierarchical clustering model. In this paper, we are using an affinity propagation algorithm to overcome the limitation of low accuracy with non-spherical clusters.

Proposed Methodology

This proposed system aims to provide users with a more personalized location by utilizing the Exploratory Data Analysis technique and Affinity Propagation algorithm. The system will take into consideration various factors such as user preferences, weather, and climate conditions to provide accurate and relevant recommendations. The Affinity propagation algorithm is used to discover the ideal area based on chosen choices for climate conditions, crime rate, amenities, budget, and proximity to the place and EDA is used for data visualization.

Affinity Propagation (AP) algorithm is a clustering algorithm that uses a message-passing approach to identify exemplars or prototypes that represent clusters. The algorithm is based on the concept of “similarity” and “responsibility” between data points, which are represented by matrices. Here is the equation for the AP algorithm. Similarity Matrix S (u ,v) represents the similarity or preference of point u to be an exemplar or prototype for point v . It is calculated based on the similarity between pairs of data points. The equation is presented in Eq. (1).

(1)
S(u, v) =  − d(u, v)

where d (u,v) is the Euclidean distance between point u and v. The negative sign is used to convert the distance measure to a similarity measure. Responsibility matrix R(u ,v) represents the accumulated responsibility that points u assigns to point to be an exemplar or prototype.

(2)
R(u, v) = S(u, v) − max [a(u, k) + S(u, k)]for allk! = v

where a(u ,v ) is the availability matrix that represents the accumulated availability that points v assigns to point u to be an exemplar or prototype.

(3)
$$a(u,v) = \min\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {0,R(v,u) + sum\lbrack\max(0,R(k,v))\rbrack} \\ {for\ allk! = uandk! = v} \\ \end{array} \right\rbrack$$

Availability matrix A(u ,v ) - It represents the accumulated availability that points v assigns to point /4 to be an exemplar.

(4)
$$\begin{array}{l} {A(u,v) = \min} \\ {\lbrack 0,R(u,v) + sum\lbrack\max(0,R(k,v))\rbrack\, for\ allk! = u\rbrack} \\ \end{array}$$

The AP algorithm iteratively updates the responsibility eq (1) and availability eq (2) matrices until convergence is reached. The exemplars are identified based on the diagonal values of the responsibility matrix. We are using the Affinity propagation algorithm over the k-means clustering in this paper. In this, each data point communicates with every other data point by telling them how desirable each target is to the sender comparable to the other proportional point. So, it can overcome the major drawback of when two circular clusters centered at the same mean have different radii and fails if the clusters are not circular. The Affinity clustering algorithm works by constructing the similarity matrix and responsibility matrix. And the developed system considers user context-aware and interactive recommendations. Eqs. (3) and (4) are representing the availability matrix in different cases.

For example, the time of day, weather conditions, or the user’s current location, and users can rate locations or provide additional information about their preferences. These can improve the accuracy of the recommendations and make the recommendation process more engaging and user-friendly. And these are the following various steps involved in developing the proposed system.

Figure 1 depicts the various stages involved in the development of a proposed system. It involves matrix construction as an intermediate step. In that, similarity matrix Eq. (1) is used to find the similarity between the data points.

Step 1: Collection of Datasets from Kaggle

The first step is to obtain data sets from Kaggle, which is an online platform for data scientists and machine learning practitioners to access and share datasets. Various datasets like air quality index, temperature fluctuations, apartment prices, hotels, and restaurants are collected as a sample preference for user.

Step 2: Using Pandas and matplodib library to clean data and visualize data.

Once the datasets have been collected, they need to be cleaned and prepared for analysis. This step involves removing any duplicates, correcting errors, and consistently formatting the data. After cleaning the data, it is important to explore it visually to gain insights and identify any patterns or trends. Boxplots are a useful visualization tool that displays the distribution of a dataset’s values, including the median, quartiles, and outliers.

Step 3: Matrix Construction

The matrix includes rows for each neighborhood or locality and columns for various features such as crime rate, school quality cost of living, etc. Each cell in the matrix would contain a value for the corresponding neighborhood and feature.

Step 4: Employ affinity propagation clustering algorithm to duster the locations.

Next step is to use the Affinity propagation clustering algorithm that automatically determines the number of clusters and their centroids based on the data’s similarities by using scikit-learn library.

Step 5: Get geolocational data points.

The next step is to obtain geolocational data points and coordinates for the localities in the dataset. This is typically done using the Foursquare API, which is a location data platform that provides access to a database of points of interest and user-generated content.

Step 6: Display the resultant locations on the geolocational map using the Folium tool.

Finally, we can use Folium, a Python library for creating interactive maps to display the clustered locations on a geolocational map. This step allows us to visualize the different clusters and explore the relationships between them.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the proposed locality recom- mendation system that utilizes exploratory data analysis and affinity propagation clustering algorithm has shown promising results in identifying similar locations based on their characteristics and attributes. By using data collected from various sources and applying data cleaning techniques, the system was able to effectively cluster the locations and provide accurate recommendations based on user preferences.

Currently, there are various locality recom- mendation systems available that use different algorithms and techniques. However, most of them rely on collaborative filtering or content- based filtering to recommend localities to users. These systems have limitations in terms of accuracy, scalability, and sparsity of data. Also, they do not consider the user’s location, which is an important factor in recommending localities. The proposed system aims to overcome the limitations of existing locality recommendation systems by using exploratory data analysis and an affinity propagation clustering algorithm.

The use of geolocational data and mapping tools helped in visualizing the results and making them easily understandable for the users. Overall, the system has the potential to provide personalized and relevant recommendations for users looking for locations with similar characteristics by improving their overall experience and satisfaction. Further research and development can be done to improve the accuracy & scalability of the system and to incorporate additional features and data sources.

Real-Time Pothole Detection Using Deep Learning

Sanchay Chakraborty, Dakshita Prashar and S. Sathya Priya34

Department of Computer Science and Engineering Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science Chennai, India

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-43

Abstract

The detection and prevention of road accidents are a more complex and tough issue in India due to the use of subpar construction materials in the creation of road drainage systems. Owing to the aforementioned issues, roads deteriorate quickly and develop potholes, which result in accidents. The proposed work is to enhance safety by early real-time precise detection of potholes as it proves to be essential especially for emergency services like ambulances, firefighters and general public as well, especially in India where roads run for thousands of kilometres across the country. Road accidents claimed 1,53,972 lives and injured 3,84,448 people in the country in 2021, According to reports of 4,12,432 accidents, road accidents claimed 1,53,972 lives and injured 3,84,448 people in the country in 2021. Unfortunately, the age range most severely affected by road accidents is 18 to 45 years old, accounting for nearly 67 percent of all accidental deaths. According to studies, potholes and poor road conditions cause 60% of all road accidents in India. Without the necessary marking, many potholes are regularly neglected, and waterlogging prohibits the detection of any of these holes. In order to prevent accidents and fatalities brought on by badly maintained roads, harsh weather, late-night driving, and human error, road safety typically becomes a top concern at this time. The effectiveness of roads and the prevention of serious traffic accidents are both impacted by road maintenance surveillance. The proposed work would help to prevent loss of life and property by using You Only Look Once (YOLOv4), MIDAS, and adding an audio module to warn against potholes deeper than a particular depth.

Keywords: Deep Learning, MIDAS, Object detection, Pothole, Road safety

Introduction

According to studies, 60% of traffic accidents are caused by structural problems and bad conditions of the roads. Today, roads are the primary form of transportation, and people rely heavily on them for daily travel. Due to heavy reliance on them as well as climatic changes, roads alter and deteriorate with time. This results in the formation of potholes and curved roadways, which are unsafe and cause life-threatening accidents. It is challenging to spot them on the road, particularly in a nation like India where there are thousands of kilometers of roadways. Since these potholes can’t always be located and examined by bare sight, automated detection of them is required. It is extremely important for a safe ride because even minor jerks or the invisibility of these potholes can prove to be extremely dangerous and fatal, especially for emergency services like firefighters and ambulances that operate at high speeds 24 hours a day, even in darkened areas and harsh weather conditions like fog and rain. Some current models identify potholes using different approaches, but they are not shown to be very efficient. As a result, a work is proposed that integrates an audio module, YOLOv4, and MIDAS for finding pothole deeper than a particular depth by making a buzzing sound as the car approaches them and notifying the driver and vehicle.

The suggested study can be used for both manual and self-driving vehicles, and the model is anticipated to demonstrate greater precision and accuracy for improved safety. YoloV4’s high accuracy makes it a great choice for finding potholes: Because of its smart architecture and improved training process. YOLOv4 is built on a more sophisticated architecture than YOLOv3 and SSD Mobilenet V2, it has a larger backbone network and used CSPDarknet53 which is better than traditional residual connections. Several convolutional layers and residual layers make up CSPDarknet53. It has optimizing techniques such as squeeze-and- excitation (SE) and spatial pyramid modules, by recalibrating the feature maps with channel-wise attention, SE blocks are employed to enhance the network’s feature representation. SPP modules handle objects of several scales by integrating and extracting features from various scales.

The CSPDarknet53 architecture boosts the YOLOv4 model’s performance by expanding the network’s capacity and lowering its computational expense, which makes it better compared to YoloV3 and Mobilenet V2.YoloV4 is relatively easy to train compared to other object identification algorithms, which is important for customizing the system to recognize specific types of potholes in different circumstances.YoloV4 provides more choices for customizing the algorithm to specific applications, including the capacity to alter the anchor box sizes and the amount of training iterations.YoloV4 offers support for new features including dynamic convolution and mesh activation that improve accuracy and performance. In conclusion, YoloV4 outperforms MobileNet SSD and YoloV3 in terms of pothole identification thanks to improvements in accuracy, microscopic item detection, speed, customization possibilities, and support for new features.

Literature Survey

Prakash & Sriharipriya (2022) trained and compared the YOLOX-nano model to several YOLO models, such as the YOLOv3, YOLOv4, and YOLOvS models. The test demonstrates that the YOLOX-nano model is more precise than any other model. The YOLOX dataset was formatted based on the COCO 2017 dataset. The pre-processed data collection, which has been assigned a specific folder, serves as the YOLOX model’s training input. The model was designed to find a single class of potholes. The model’s average precision was 85.6%, which was slower than other models’ inference rates but 24.06% higher than the YOLOvSm model’s value.

The works by Asad et al. (2022) state YOLOv4 and Tiny-YOLOv4 are the best-fit pothole detection models as it uses AI kit (OAK-D) on a single-board computer (Raspberry Pi) as an edge platform for pothole detection. The custom weights are converted into the OpenVino IR format to perform real-time detection on OAK-D and Raspberry Pi as host computers. However, the proposed method is not cost-effective.

According to the study of (Anandhalli et al., 2022), sequential CNN and YOLO are compared, with CNN requiring less training time than YOLO (anchor-Based) while preserving pothole detection performance. Object detection in CNN was carried out by Object Classification and Object Localization. This method failed to encode the position and object orientation.

According to Egaji et al. (2021), a sufficient amount of samples from roads and automobiles will be needed to conduct further analysis and develop more effective models that work effectively in a variety of circumstances.

The approach used by Abhiram et al. (2021) is a vibration-based technology that detects the hole and hump mechanically, as well as the severity of each. The paper is devoid of technical specifications and detailed methodology explanations. Furthermore, the work has insufficient experimental validation because it only navigates a four-kilometer road. The work lacks novelty and resembles Google Maps. At a 95% confidence level, the average accuracy for the five machine learning models, SVM, Naive Bayes, KNN, Logistic Regression, and Random Forest Tree. The manual recording of pothole events uses GPS and UNIX timestamp data. Due to poor object orientation and detection, training input from manual dataset collection is less reliable.

The work by Peng et al. (2022) emphasizes pattern representation and suggests three sets of numerical features for expressing road conditions. Three deep learning techniques—Deep Feedforward Network, Convolutional Neural Network, and Recurrent Neural Network— are also considered to solve the classification problem. RNN was discovered to be the finest. The Adam optimizer was used, and 10 internal nodes of the LSTM cell were selected. However, it is outside the purview of this research and has not been investigated to evaluate the performances of different RNN cells on the dataset presented.

The suggested technology, which combines infrared imagery and convolutional neural networks, can compete with the pothole detection techniques already in use (Anandhalli et al., 2022). Three distinct ratios are used for the training and validation dataset: 60:40, 80:20, and 90:10. The approach that is recommended by Aparna et al. (2022), uses a CNN-based ResNet model. This is the first time that pothole identification has been done using infrared imaging. But as the use of thermal imaging for pothole identification is a new concept, there is no pre-existing work in this direction to be compared.

Proposed System

For the desired beneficial consequences, the acquired data is converted and put through several processes. The work’s entire process is depicted in Fig. 2 in its entirety. From several sources, a dataset of 700 road pictures is gathered for both with and without potholes. The images were split between training and testing sets with an 80-20 split. To ensure data completeness, data preparation is done by converting pixel values to the range [0, 1] and handling missing data with a median filter. To maintain the spatial dimensions, the feature extraction is accomplished using 19 convolutional layers with 3x3 filters and 5 max-pooling layers with 2x2 filters. LeakyReLU activation functions are then applied with a 0.1 negative slope and additional padding. A binary cross-entropy loss function with an IoU threshold of 0.5 was used to train the YOLOv4 model. To broaden the training set, data augmentation methods are used including random flipping and rotation.

MIDAS (Monocular Depth Estimation via Adaptive Structural Loss) approach is utilized to measure the distance of potholes from the camera. Using the pinhole camera concept, the depth map created by MIDAS was transformed into actual distances. The technology was able to provide precise information about the location and severity of potholes thanks to distance estimation. For MIDAS normalization of pixel values is done to the range [0,1] and enlarge the input image to 256 x 256 pixels. The depth map is then obtained by running the normalized image through the MIDAS model. The pinhole camera model translates depth map to actual distances. It assumes that light moves in straight lines and that images are created by directing light rays from a scene’s 3D point onto a 2D picture plane. Use the following equation to get the separation between a point in the scene and the camera: distance = (focal length * object height) / image height, while object height is the height of the object in the scene. It calculates the object’s coordinates by using the pothole’s coordinates as its bounding box, as detected by YOLOv4. Where focal length is the distance between the camera and the picture plane, object height is the height of the object in the scene, and image height is the height of the image in pixels. It calculates the object’s coordinates by using the pothole’s coordinates as its bounding box, as detected by YOLOv4.

Results and Discussion

Experiments were conducted wherein a test set of 700 photos, YoloV4 has an average precision and recall of 0.85 and 0.91 respectively. The Fl score of 0.88 demonstrated a good level of pothole detection accuracy. Out of the 700 test photos, 95% were accurately identified as potholes or non-potholes. The YoloV4 model successfully detected potholes of various sizes, shapes, and lighting situations, showcasing its potential for use in practical settings. Future research might concentrate on enhancing the model’s robustness and accuracy in difficult conditions.

The YoloV4 model’s visual depiction demonstrates its higher accuracy, precision, and mAP compared to YoloV3 and SSD MobileNet V2.Yolov4 has advanced augmentation techniques like mix up data augmentation and cutmix data augmentation that are not present in YoloV3 and SSD MobileNet V2, which helps to increase the diversity and amount of training data and improves the accuracy of the model.

According to the visual representation, YoloV4 performs better than YoloV3 and SSD MobileNet V2 across all evaluation measures, with higher values and more reliable outcomes. Advanced loss functions that are not included in YOLOv3 or SSD MobileNetV2 are used by YOLOv4, such as the focused loss function and the DIoU (Distance-IoU) loss function. These loss functions aid in addressing the problem of class imbalance and boosts the model’s accuracy in challenging situations, including spotting tiny potholes. YOLOv4 can be easily linked with distance estimation algorithms, such as MIDAS, to determine the distance of potholes from the car. This is crucial for warning drivers ahead of time that there will be potholes so they can prevent damaging their cars.

Conclusion

Techniques for identifying potholes based on artificial intelligence could improve road maintenance, notably in India. Emergency services must take every precaution to avoid obstructions that could endanger their lives. This work is expanded to determine the place where the potholes are located after classifying a photo as a pothole. A driver can be warned by an alarm system to avoid uneven roads and avoid accidents by using factors like the depth and severity of the potholes that are discovered.The model showed very good accuracy and pothole identification in real time. The system’s usability and security were further improved by the incorporation of a sound alert system and distance measurement using MIDAS. The web application makes the model’s user interface accessible and makes it easier for people to apply it in practical situations. In future research, the pothole detecting system developed in this study might be improved even more by including GPS and other sensors to gather more data. Using GPS, the system would be able to more precisely locate potholes and provide drivers with more detailed information about the route ahead, including the condition of the road and traffic patterns.

Contact Less Virtually Controlling System Using Computer Vision Techniques

Yakkala Lahari, Genipi Yaswanth and D. Chitradevi35

Department of Computer Science Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

E-mail: yakka1a1ahari1181@gmail.com; yaswanth2808@gmail.com;

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-44

Abstract

The paper suggests a contact-free virtual controlling system that uses hand movements and fingertips to detect mouse clicks (Scrolling functions, Left-click, Right-click, Brightness control, Volume control, drag operations) rather than using a physical mouse or wireless (Bluetooth) mouse. This proposed system has a built-in camera or web camera which will detect the face of authorized persons, only those persons can access the virtual mouse. The physical mouse and wireless mouse are great inventions of HCI technology. Currently, technology is rapidly changing so this paper introduces a mouse that replaces the physical and Bluetooth mouses. The Bluetooth mouse needs a dongle that should be connected to a laptop or system and a battery is needed for power. By capturing hand movements, we can detect using computer vision, the proposed method can get over the limits by means of a webcam or integrated camera. It also decreases the contagious virus COVID-19 spread as there is no human interaction with the devices/computers.

Keywords: Face Recognition, Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), Hand gesture recognition, Hand tip detection, Virtual mouse.

Introduction

A mouse is an important device used to perform all the operations in system/laptop. The screen shows the operations that are requested. There are various kinds of mouses such as mechanical mouse, optical mouse, and wireless mouse (Shriram et al., 2021). The movement of the rubber ball, which is the only component of the mechanical mouse and may rotate in any direction, controls the pointer movement. A mechanical mouse also be called as ball mouse. The rubber ball is located underside of mouse, the sensors inside it will detect the movement and send the signals to cursor displays on the screen. As the technology is changing the optical mouse replaced the mechanical mouse as it is more weighted and more costly (Venkateshwar et al., 2021). The optical mouse consists of an LED sensor and a small camera that will take thousands of pictures and detects the movement of the pointer. An optical mouse has a light, but a mechanical mouse has a rubber ball. The laser mouse was suggested after some time had elapsed to get over the optical mouse’s drawbacks. The development of technology has led to introducing wireless mouse for overcoming the limitations of mechanical, optical, laser mouses and for helping the persons having problem to operate the physical mouse (Katona et al., 2021). When there is no space to utilize a mouse in the actual world, the proposed contact free virtual controlling system can be employed to solve the problems (Nandhini et al., 2014). The computer vision-based, contact- free virtual controlling mouse system uses the SSD algorithm to detect hand gestures. The proposed system employs a transformational technique to translate the fingertip’s coordinates a full-screen computer monitor is used for mouse control after moving the camera there (Lugaresi et al., 2019). The proposed model outcome demonstrates good accuracy and excellent performance in using a CPU instead of a GPU for real-world applications.

Related Work

Shriram discussed about a system that uses computer vision and deep learning to prevent the spread of COVID-19. The mouse is important to perform operations in system/laptop. The mouse uses Human Computer Interaction (HCI) technology to complete its work properly. It also decreases the contagious virus COVID-19 spread as there is no human interaction with the devices/ computers (Shriram et al., 2021). Devanshu Singh described Virtual Mouse using Open CV. It recommends that you rebuild your hardware. The idea is to show that can we use digital technology and a webcam for monitoring mouse movements (clicks and scrolls) and make all conventional mouse devices. This paper shows how to build a mouse operating system (Singh et al., 2021). Venkateshwar described the HCI’s use of a virtual mouse by identifying hand gestures. Since, the advancement of computer technology, HCI technology has developed continuously. Having additional devices in the mouse complicates the hardware. Recommended mouse systems are outside this limit (Venkateswar et al., 2021). The authors of “Virtual Mouse Control Using Colored Fingertips and Hand Gesture Recognition” (Reddy et al., 2020) described this technique. Using image- based fingertip recognition and hand motion tracking in real-time videos, a contact-free virtual mouse has been built for human and computer interaction. The control of a virtual mouse using hand motion recognition and fingertips detection is described in this work (Pranav et al., 2020). Manthan Bhatkar, Ofrin Lopes, Prof. Monali Shetty, and Christina Gtv. Daniel described about using an object tracking system as a virtual mouse. All devices today use touchscreen technology for their systems, and not all applications can use them. A virtual mouse that helps you interact using gestures and specialized interactive modules such as object tracking is a possible substitute for conventional screens (Reddy et al., 2020).

Materials and Methods

In Fig. 1, the proposed work’s entire development is shown. There are six steps in the procedure they are as follows:

A. Workflow

  1. Step 1 Download and install the requirements in the system. Import the modules and libraries.
  2. Step 2 The algorithm usage should be known completely.
  3. Step 3 Testing contact-free virtually controlling system is very hard as the available datasets are limited. The faces for the access are added in dataset. The tests are performed under different conditions and distances using webcam/built-in camera for face recognition and hand movements (Vinay et al., 2016).
  4. Step 4 There are 0-20 co-ordinates or landmarks which makes hand tip detection easy and improves the accuracy in detecting hand gestures. The proposed model of the hand will contain 21 joint coordinates which mainly focus on fingertips (Shriram et al., 2021).
  5. Step 5 Firstly, the hand detection model is implemented and trained for detecting and tracking hand movements. In the next step, face biometrics is added as security for the virtual mouse.
  6. Step 6 The proposed model can perform various mouse functions. It is used to control system as a physical mouse but performs functions virtually.

B. Select a framework for hand tracking

It is an opensource and cross-platform. It is mainly utilized for hand motion detection and tracking (Singh et al., 2021). The framework analyses and build the graphs of system by developer and for the sake of application develops the systems. It includes a few Machine-Learning (ML) pre-trained solutions, including face and object detection, pose estimation, hand and object recognition, and more.

C. Capture frames using webcam

The virtual contact-free controlling system captures every frame of the video until the video is completed by using webcam in system/ computer or a built-in camera. To identify hand movements from frame to frame, BGR color is transformed to RGB. The face and hands movements are tracked by webcam and the mouse operation will be performed according to the movement (Christina et al., 2020; Katona et al., 2021). The hand movements are detected and according to that the mouse operations are performed.

D. Detect the hand gestures, hand tips, and face recognition.

The faces are detected by generating a rectangular box around face and it also shows the name of person. The hand movements are detected and according to that the mouse operations are performed. The computer detects the movements of fingertips and performs functions (Reddy et al., 2020). A single-shot detector model is utilized to detect and identify hands and fingers in actual time. A landmark model of the hand is composed of the locations of 21 joints or knuckles in the hand region. The algorithm can determine the location of the face, which can be utilized to direct the motion of the virtual mouse. In order to accomplish this, the algorithm would first need to be trained to identify the user’s face before being used to authenticate the user before granting them access to the virtual mouse.

Algorithm for SSD

Step 1: The foundation of SSD is a feature map based tiny convolutional filtering that predicts a particular set of default bounding boxes, there are category scores and box offsets (Venkateshwar et al., 2021).

Step 2: The explicit group predictions by aspect ratio and create predictions made at various scales using feature maps of various sizes to achieve excellent detection accuracy (Venkateshwar et al., 2021).

Step 3: Losses in localization (loc) and confidence (conf) are weighted sums that make up the function of the total objective loss:

Results

The web camera of a laptop or computer is used to capture images for the planned contact-free virtual controlling system. The webcam begins recording footage as soon as the computer vision library is used to identify the object in the video footage. A rectangular frame is generated when a hand is detected and the finger that should carry out a specific mouse function is identified and the area moves the mouse cursor through the window. To determine which finger is raised, this step uses the Id of the associated finger and the matching Id’s of the top finger:

4.1 To perform left click operation

When the thumb and index finger are both up and there is less than 30 pixels between them, the system is designed to click the left click operation when the two fingers are together. The system is designed to click the left click operation as illustrated in Fig. 2., whenever the thumb finger’s tip Id=0 and the index finger’s tip Id=1 are both up and there is less than 30px.

4.2 To use right click function

As shown in Fig. 3, the system is designed to use the right-click button on the mouse when the middle finger has a tip Id of 2 and the index finger has a tip Id of 1, both of which line up, and there are fewer than 40 pixels total.

4.3 To execute a scroll-up action:

If the middle finger has a tip Id of 2, and the index finger has tip Id of 1, and both fingers are up, the distance between them is higher than 40 pixels, and they move over the page.

4.4 To execute a scroll-down action:

The two fingers are relocated to the bottom of the screen if the space between them is greater than 40 pixels if the middle finger has tip Id=2 and the index finger has tip Id=1 are up. If the index finger is up and has tip Id = 1 or if both the index finger and middle finger have tip Id = 2 are up, as shown in Fig. 4, the mouse cursor can be made to move around the computer window.

The system is designed to conduct the double click using a package, as illustrated in Fig.5., if the middle finger has tip Id = 2 and the index finger has tip Id = 1 are both up and there is no space between the two fingers. If the distance between the index finger’s tip (Id = 1) and the thumb’s tip (Id = 0) is less than 30px and both fingers are bent at an angle where all other fingers are up. As shown in Fig. 6., the computer is designed to perform sound operations using packages when the space between the other fingers is less than 10px. If all the fingers are closed and there is no distance between any two fingers, the computer is made to perform the drag and drop operations using packages, as shown in Fig.7.

Discussion

In the recent papers, as compared to the existing systems which have accuracy of 82%, 73%, 71%, 65%, 58% respectively (Pranav et al., 2020). The proposed system also contains extra features compared to existing systems like face recognition for authorized persons. Before, virtual mouse systems used You Only Look Once (YOLO) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) algorithms, but the newly proposed system is based on the Single Shot Detector (SSD) technique to increase performance and accuracy. The accuracy of facial recognition for authenticated users will increase with the creation of a custom dataset. The quality and quantity of training samples, the input images, the model parameters, and the accuracy threshold all affect how accurate an object detection model.

Conclusion

The contact-free virtual controlling system is an idea for personalized multifunctional navigation/ interaction tools that break down physical barriers. The system is realistic enough that it does not significantly affect the interaction. Ease of use is improved accessibility, customization, features, and security. To lessen the growth of coronavirus and the conventional physical mouse, the proposed technology can be utilized virtually without palm motion. The right-click function in this model has a little loss of accuracy, and selecting text by clicking and dragging has problems. A virtual keyboard function can also be added to the suggested method so that it can be used in addition to a mouse function. This is yet another potential future application for HCI.

Underwater Benthos Detection in Marine Benthic Zone Using Single Shot MultiBox Detector

A. Milan Hussain, Vikram Varma and D. Chitradevi36

Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

E-mail: hussainmilan1@gmail.com, vikram14202@gmail.com

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-45

Abstract

The marine benthic zone refers to the bottom of a body of water, such as an ocean or lake, and includes all the organisms and physical features that are found there. Due to the maritime economy’s rapid growth, the demand for marine resources has increased dramatically in recent years. At present, target detection technology has several uses and future potential in ocean construction and benthic observation. However, the underwater environment is diverse and variable benthic organisms, existing systems may struggle to accurately detect and classify benthic species. This can lead to missed detections, false positives, and misclassifications, which can affect system’s accuracy. This paper addresses these issues for detecting and classifying benthic organisms in underwater images using the algorithm for single-shot multi box detection. The algorithm uses a single deep neural network to predict bounding boxes and class probabilities for objects in an image. The model has succeeded to get an accuracy 87.5% in detecting marine benthic organisms.

Keywords: Deep Learning, Convolutional Neural Networks, Segmentation, Fully Connected Layers, Pooling Layers.

Introduction

In recent years, advances in technology have provided new opportunities for underwater benthos detection, such as acoustic and optical sensors, autonomous underwater vehicles, and machine learning algorithms. These technologies offer the potential for more efficient, accurate, and non-destructive methods for studying benthic organisms. The benthic zone, which is the bottom layer of an aquatic ecosystem, is a vital component of marine and freshwater environments (Yang et al., 2020). The benthic community comprises a diverse range of organisms, including plants, invertebrates, and microorganisms, thatplay critical roles in nutrient cycling, sediment stabilization, and the overall health of the ecosystem (Kumari et al., 2019). Hence, identifying and keeping track of benthic organisms is essential for determining the ecological health of aquatic ecosystems (Huang et.al, 2019). Yet, conventional benthic survey techniques like bottom trawling and visual inspection can be time-consuming, expensive, and harmful to the benthic ecosystem. This work explores a technique for employing Single Shot Multibox Detector to detect underwater benthic organisms in the marine benthic zone (Bochkovskiy et al., 2020). The proposed method involves using annotated underwater images of benthic organisms to train the model (Zhang et al., 2021). The model is then used to detect and classify benthic organisms. Nowadays, nonphysical model image enhancement and physical model- based picture restoration are the two main categories of underwater image improvement and restoration techniques (Zhang et al., 2020). This paper comprises 4 main phases. Phase 1 involves the acquisition of underwater images of the benthic environment. In phase 2, the images are pre-processed. Image preprocessing is an essential phase in underwater benthos detection as it helps to improve the standard and suitability of the dataset for analysis (Zhang et al., 2020). In phase 3, The SSD model is trained to recognize objects using the annotated images (Bochkovskiy et al., 2020). The training process involves adjusting the model’s weights and parameters to optimize its performance. Phase 4 involves the process of detection of benthos organisms. Once the model is trained, it can be used to detect and classify benthic organisms like Sea Urchins, Starfish, Crabs, and Corals.

Related Works

Models with Deep learning are more effective in detecting the capacity to work with a larger amount of data concurrently and the ability to extract information from photos in challenging circumstances. Tian Zhou et al. described “Automated Small Targets Underwater Detection using Forward-Looking Sonar Images.” One of the fundamental imaging tools used to explore underwater targets is forward-looking sonar. This article proposes a clustering, segmentation, and feature discrimination-based autonomous underwater target identification technique. The experimental findings demonstrate that the suggested low detection inaccuracy and good real-time performance with low false alarm likelihood are characteristics of the technique, which is comparable to current mainstream deep learning algorithms (Zhou et al., 2022). Yeh et al. (2022) in “Lightweight Deep Neural Network for Concurrent Learning of Color Conversion and Underwater Item Identification” described that it has been shown that there is great potential for underwater image processing in the research of underwater ecosystems. A deep model must be supplied in order to successfully learn color conversion and object detection for underwater photographs. The experimental outcomes showed with our implementation on the Raspberry Pi platform (Yeh et al., 2022). Jia Liu et.al explained in — “Swin Transformer- Based Two-Stage Underwater Object Detection Network” that Ocean exploration relies heavily on underwater object detection, and research into effective underwater object recognition algorithms is crucial for use in real-world applications due to the increasing number of underwater object image data. In order to resolve these problems, a Faster R-CNN-based. The proposed algorithm is enhanced to 80.54% when compared to other algorithms since it is based on improved Faster- RCNN using the URPC2018 dataset. (Liu et al., 2022). Athira. P et.al (2021) described “Deep neural networks-based Underwater object recognition model based on the YOLOv3 architecture” a deep learning model that uses YOLOv3 architecture, the darknet framework, and automatic underwater object detection. Also, this study investigates the potential for tailoring YOLOv3-based aquatic object detection algorithms using the dataset (Athira et al., 2021). Huang et al. (2019) described — “Convolutional Neural Network-Based Object Detection in the Water” and suggested a multi-scale convolution neural network-based underwater multi-target identification technique (MSC-CNN). The evaluation parameters used include accuracy and test time, and the recognition performance of several underwater picture recognition techniques is examined by comparison with leading algorithms. The results of underwater image experiments demonstrate the benefits of this strategy for many evaluation measures (Huang et al., 2019).

Materials and Methods

The proposed method for underwater benthos detection using SSD is a promising approach that can automate the discovery and investigation of benthic ecosystems in marine environments. The project aims to create a system for detecting species in the benthic zone, the lowest region of the ocean floor which is often difficult to study due to limited visibility. The detection of underwater benthos in marine benthic zones can be achieved using the Single Shot Multi-box Detector algorithm, which is a popular object recognition algorithm. The following steps can be followed for underwater benthos detection using the SSD algorithm:

Workflow:

  1. Step 1 Download and install the requirements in the system. Import the modules and libraries.
  2. Step 2 The second step determines the study area and depth range. We choose Marine Benthic zone as our area of interest that we want to study and determine the depth range that we will be exploring.
  3. Step 3 Collect underwater image dataset. Ensure that the data set at a high enough resolution and frame rate for accurate detection.
  4. Step 4 The data is Pre-processed and cleaned by removing any unwanted frames.
  5. Step 5 Training the SSD algorithm using a dataset of annotated images of the benthos species that we are going to detect.
  6. Step 6 Applying the trained SSD algorithm to the pre-processed image data to detect and localize the benthos species.
  7. Step 7 The results are post-processed to remove false positives and track the movement of detected benthos species.
  8. Step 8 Optimization and Tuning step involves optimizing and tuning the hyperparameters, such as learning rate, batch size, optimizer, etc., until the desired accuracy is achieved.

Underwater benthos detection using Single Shot Detector (SSD) is a module designed for automated detection and recognition of benthic organisms in underwater images. Data collection is the first step in the module where input images of underwater benthos are collected and the unnecessary images are removed. Data Preprocessing and Annotation is the second step where the images with bounding boxes around each benthic object and labeling with their respective species. We used the CLAHE enhancement method in this blog to improve image quality in a real-time system. CLAHE method helps in improving visibility and it preserves local details. The next step is to select an appropriate machine-learning algorithm for Underwater Benthos Detection. The proposed method uses SSD algorithm for underwater benthos detection. The algorithm uses a single deep neural network to predict bounding boxes and class probabilities for objects in an image. The Single Shot Detector uses a multi-box to identify several items in a single shot. It is a high-accuracy object-detecting technique is substantially faster. The SSD model is a trained annotated dataset that has been pre-processed using CLAHE method. The SSD model takes an input image and outputs a set of predicted bounding boxes and their corresponding class probabilities. The performance of the SSD model is evaluated using standard metrics such as precision, recall, and F1 score. This helps to assess the accuracy of the model in detecting benthos in marine benthic zones.

Algorithm for SSD:

  1. Step 1 : The foundation of SSD is a feature map based tiny convolutional filtering that predicts a particular set of default bounding boxes, there are category scores and box offsets.
  2. Step 2 : The explicit group predictions by aspect ratio and create predictions made at various scales using feature maps of various sizes in order to achieve excellent detection accuracy.

  3. Step 3 : Losses in localization (loc) and confidence (conf) are weighted sums that make up the function of the total Objective loss:


    $$L(x,c,l,g) = \frac{1}{N}(L_{conf}(x,c) + \alpha L_{loc}(x,l,g))$$

  4. Step 4 We go backwards to the default bounding box’s offsets parameters in a manner similar to Faster R-CNN.

  5. Step 5 center (cx, cy), as well as for its width (w), and

    height (h).


    $$\begin{array}{l} {L_{loc}(x,l,g) = \sum\limits_{i \in Pos}^{N}\sum\limits_{m \in \{ cx,cy,w,h\}}x_{ij}^{k}smooth_{\text{L}1}(l_{i}^{m} - {\hat{g}}_{j}^{m})} \\ \begin{array}{ll} {{\hat{g}}_{j}^{cx} = (g_{j}^{cx} - d_{i}^{cx})/d_{i}^{w}} & {{\hat{g}}_{j}^{cy} = (g_{j}^{cy} - d_{i}^{cy})/d_{i}^{h}} \\ {{\hat{g}}_{j}^{w} = \log(\frac{g_{j}^{w}}{d_{i}^{w}})} & {{\hat{g}}_{j}^{h} = \log(\frac{g_{j}^{h}}{d_{i}^{h}})} \\ \end{array} \\ {L_{conf}(x,c) = - \sum\limits_{i \in Pos}^{N}x_{ij}^{p}\log({\hat{c}}_{i}^{p}) - \sum\limits_{i \in Neg}\log({\hat{c}}_{i}^{0})} \\ {where\,\,{\hat{c}}_{i}^{p} = \frac{\exp(c_{i}^{p})}{\sum_{p}\exp(c_{i}^{p})}} \\ \end{array}$$

Performance Metrics

Precision = (Number of True Positives)/ (Number of True Positives + Number of False Positives).

The ratio of actual (relevant) objects to genuine positives is known as recall.

Recall = (Number of True Positives)/ (Number of True Positives + Number of False Negatives).

There is a value range of 0 to 1, with 1 denoting the maximum accuracy.

Fl score = (Precision x Recall)/ (Precision + Recall)/2.

Discussions

The results of these studies imply that SSD has the potential to be a useful method for finding underwater benthos. In comparison to conventional sample techniques, SSD can save time and resources by automating the identification and counting of benthic species. Moreover, SSD can deliver data that is more precise and consistent than manual sampling techniques, which are subject to bias and human error. The use of SSD algorithm for underwater benthos detection shows promise and is an area of active research. SSD and other computer vision techniques are anticipated to play a more and bigger role in understanding and monitoring the health and ecology of aquatic ecosystems as technology and algorithms continue to advance. The accuracy of an object detection model depends on a number of factors, including the input photos, model parameters, and accuracy threshold (Kumari et al., 2019). A ratio can be used as a threshold to determine whether a certain transaction is a true positive or a false positive using the Intersection over Union (IoU) method (Dixit et al., 2019). The IoU ratio quantifies the degree to which the bounding box of a projected item overlaps the bounding box containing the ground reference data. The proportion of real positives to all forecasted positive outcomes is known as precision.

Conclusion

In conclusion, Underwater Benthos Detection in the benthic zone is a significant area of research with numerous applications in marine biology, ecology, and conservation. Techniques like the SSD algorithm are used in this process. Researchers can better understand the distribution, abundance of benthic creatures by precisely detecting and localizing them. The utilization of marine resources sustainably can be supported by this knowledge as well as management and conservation activities. Yet, finding underwater benthos is a difficult undertaking that calls for specific tools and knowledge of picture processing and analysis. As a result, furthering our understanding of the benthic zone and its inhabitants will depend on ongoing research and development in this area.
