Digital Human Creator Using Facial Expression and Voice

Medagam Siva Vamsidhar Reddy, Tanikanti Venkat Kiran, D. Chitradevi37

Department of Computer Science Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

E-mail: m.s.vamsidhar678@gmail.com, Tanikantikiran@gmail.com

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-46

Abstract

The Digital Character Creator is a state-of-the-art system that allows users to generate and animate virtual characters using facial expressions and voice commands. Manually creating a digital character takes more time and human effort. The software can reliably recognize and understand these inputs by employing powerful machine learning techniques, resulting in distinct characters with a spectrum of emotions and personalities. The system is intended to be simple and easy to use, with a number of tools and interfaces that allow users to create original characters from scratch or build on pre-existing templates. With real-time manipulation capabilities, Overall, the Digital Character Creator is a powerful and innovative tool that has the potential to transform the way characters are generated and animated. Its advanced features and accessibility make it an essential resource for artists and animators seeking to bring their creative visions to life. the Digital Character Creator is ideal for use in creative industries such as film and gaming.

Keywords: Digital Character Creator, Facial expressions, Voice commands, Animation, Machine learning

Introduction

Deep learning plays a significant role in the advancement of computer vision by improving the speed and accuracy of assigned tasks. It is opening opportunities for improvement and enhancement of processes and initiating human- driven tasks in an automated manner. Digital character creation has become a significant area of research in computer graphics and animation. The creation of digital characters that can express emotions and exhibit personality traits has many applications in fields such as film, video games, virtual reality, and social media. One of the most challenging aspects of digital character creation is animating the characters’ facial expressions and voices (Hongcheng Wang and Ahuja, 2003). Facial expression and voice recognition technology have been used to create digital characters that can mimic human emotions and speech patterns (Hong et al., July 2002). These technologies use machine learning algorithms to recognize and analyze facial expressions and audio input. The output is then used to generate corresponding facial animations and speech output (Andre Teixeira Lopes et al., 2017). One of the commonly used approaches for facial animation is facial animation parameter generation. This involves mapping facial movements to a set of animation parameters that can be used to control the animation of a virtual character’s face (Zoric, 2003). Motion capture data is used to generate realistic and natural- looking facial expressions and movements. Automated rigging and facial animation systems are also being developed (Testa et al., 2021). These systems incorporate machine learning algorithms that can generate facial animations in real time from speech or other input. The systems enable the creation of virtual characters with automated facial animation capabilities, making it easier for artists to create believable and natural-looking facial expressions and lip-syncing (Sadoughi and Busso, 2021, Kim et al., 2021). Digital character creation using facial expression and voice technology has the potential to revolutionize many industries. It has many applications in healthcare, education, communication, and entertainment. As these technologies continue to evolve, we can expect to see the emergence of more realistic and human-like virtual characters. Another approach is real-time facial animation, which allows virtual characters to display facial expressions in real time as the user interacts with them (Spiros Ioannou et al., 2005). This is accomplished through the use of motion capture data or by developing machine learning models that can generate facial animations in real- time from speech or other input (Vougioukas et al., 2020). Several systems have been developed that combine facial expression and voice recognition to create more realistic and expressive virtual characters. These systems typically incorporate machine learning algorithms that analyze speech and facial expressions to generate corresponding facial animations and lip-syncing (Fu Jie Huang and Tsuhan Chen, 1998). Developing digital character creation systems that incorporate facial expression and voice recognition can be a complex and challenging task to the above literature. Accuracy of the digital character, facial expression, and voice recognition will be increased by using tools. Face animation may be utilized to produce more realistic and engaging educational and training simulations, such as medical simulations or public speaking simulations. design more natural and intuitive assistive technology interfaces.

Related Work

Despite the success of traditional shallow features and generic image descriptors, recent development in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has demonstrated ed-significant success of automatically learned features (Hill et al., 1988). Other studies have explored the use of motion capture data to create realistic facial animations. Several systems have been developed that allow for the creation of virtual characters with automated rigging and facial animation capabilities. These systems incorporate machine learning algorithms to generate realistic and natural-looking facial expressions and lip-syncing (Huang and Chen, 1998). Other studies have explored the use of facial expressions and voice recognition to create more realistic and expressive virtual characters. Speech-Driven Automatic Facial Expression Synthesis, M. Ozkan, and A. M. Tekalp proposed an approach to voice- controlled facial animation for virtual characters. The system uses machine learning algorithms to analyze speech input and generate corresponding facial animations (Bozkurt et al., 2008). Deep Facial Expression Recognition (DFER) is a type of machine learning technique that focuses on automatically recognizing emotions expressed by a person’s face in real time. DFER involves using deep neural networks, which are a type of artificial intelligence model, to analyze facial images and extract features that are indicative of specific emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger, or surprise (Li and Deng, 2002). Facial expression recognition from images is the task of identifying the emotional state of a person from an image of their face. It has applications in various fields such as psychology, human- computer interaction, and security (Wang et al., 2019). Automatic analysis of facial expressions refers to the process of using machine learning algorithms and computer vision techniques to automatically recognize and interpret facial expressions in images or videos. This technology has applications in various fields such as psychology, human-computer interaction, and security (Pantic and Rothkrantz, 2000).

Methodology

Our proposed method for creating digital characters using facial expressions and voice consists of the following steps:

Step 1: Go to the Reallusion website download and install the I clone 8 and Character Creator 4, headshot plugin, and live link plugin. (We need iPhone to capture facial data with help of live mocap it will be available in App Store.)

Step 2: Collect a dataset of facial expressions and voice samples from real actors. This data contains a wide range of emotions and expressions that the character will need to

Step 3: The obtained data must be processed to reduce noise and match the facial expression and speech samples. To extract features from processed data, we employ plugins that operate with deep learning approaches such as convolutional neural networks.

Step 4: Integrate the trained model with the digital character to enable it to express emotions and communicate with the users through facial expressions and voice.

Step 5: Evaluate the performance of the system using metrics such as animation quality, computational efficiency, and user satisfaction.

Step 6: Refine the system based on the evaluation results and repeat the evaluation process until satisfactory results are achieved.

iClone 8

iClone 8 is a powerful 3D animation software that allows users to create and animate virtual characters, environments, and objects. It offers a variety of tools and features to create high-quality animations, including motion capture, facial animation, physics simulation, and more. Character Creator 4 is a companion software to iClone 8 that specializes in character creation. It provides a suite of tools and features to create and customize 3D characters, including facial and body morphs, clothing and accessories, and textures. Live Motion Plugin is a plugin for iClone 8 that provides motion capture capabilities. It allows users to capture live motion data and apply it to their 3D characters in real time, creating realistic animations with minimal effort

Discussion

Face animation parameterization methods involve mapping facial movements to a set of animation parameters that can be used to control virtual character facial animations. This approach has proven to achieve the most advanced results in terms of animation quality and computational efficiency. However, this requires a large dataset of facial expressions and can be difficult to implement in real-time systems. The real-time face animation approach allows virtual characters to display facial expressions in real-time as the user interacts with them. These systems have been shown to generate realistic facial animations from voice input and have potential applications in areas such as entertainment and education. Systems that combine facial expressions and speech recognition are capable of creating more realistic and expressive virtual characters. These systems use machine learning algorithms to recognize and analyze voice input, and animate faces and lip-sync accordingly. They have been proven to produce realistic facial animations and lip-sync from voice or video input.

Conclusion

The article describes the technical aspects of the Digital Character Generator, including the algorithms and techniques used to interpret facial expressions and voice commands. It also provides examples on how to create and animate virtual characters using this technology. This article argues that digital character generators using expressions and voices represent a new frontier in character animation, providing a powerful and creative tool for artists and creators. It has the potential to revolutionize the way characters are created and animated, providing a more intuitive, accessible, and flexible approach to character animation. The document suggests that the technology is an essential resource for anyone looking to create engaging and dynamic virtual characters. These characters can be used in using facial animation, allowing filmmakers to create more lifelike and emotionally engaging characters.

Enhancing the Security of Electronic Health Records Using Consortium Blockchain

G. Suman, C. H. Maruthi and S. Revathy

Department of Computer Science Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

E-mail ID: sumangadde54@gmail.com, maruthich432@gmail.com, srevathy@hindustanuniv.ac.in

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-47

Abstract

Security of electronic records (EHRs) is of foremost significance in the medical services industry, given the delicate idea of patient information. The existing restrictions on the use of private and public blockchains in healthcare include issues of scalability, data transmission latency restricting interactions between the different systems. By providing a tamper-proof, decentralized, and permission environment for storing and sharing patient data, consortium blockchain can improve the security of electronic health records (EHRs) by overcoming the drawbacks of private and public blockchains. The consortium blockchain is the combination of private and public blockchain, where it converges the advantages of both the blockchain. The proposed model restricts data sharing and transmission among patients and doctors by the validation of their roles using smart contracts. It increases transparency and security as the health records are managed by both the patients and doctors.

Keywords: Consortium blockchain, EHR, Security, Smart contracts

Introduction

Electronic health records (EHRs) contain private and sensitive patient data, their security is of the utmost importance to the healthcare sector. The term “blockchain” refers to a distributed ledger that keeps permanent records of all networked transactions. Protecting a patient’s health record from adversary attackers is crucial. The ability to store patients’ health records in a decentralized ledger is made possible by the blockchain, which enables medical professionals to gain a better understanding of the patient’s medical history.

Consortium blockchain’s potential to improve EHR security is provided. The difficulties of implementing blockchain in healthcare, the modules of a consortium blockchain system for EHRs, and related works in the field are discussed. Additionally, the advantages of using consortium blockchain include reduced expenses, enhanced data privacy, improved patient outcomes, and more efficient data sharing. There are drawbacks to using blockchain, including issues with scalability, data transmission latency, interactions between various systems, and concerns about data security and confidentiality.

Consensus blockchain provides a private and secure environment for storing sensitive health data, enhancing data privacy. Patient care is improved and costs associated with duplicate tests and procedures are decreased when healthcare providers share data effectively. Costs can be cut, errors can be reduced, and middlemen can be eliminated by automating processes. the implementation of consortium blockchain and its potential benefits, which have the potential to significantly enhance the security and efficiency of electronic health records.

Stages involved in the processing of health records using blockchain are:

  1. Patient registration and identity management Patients can register and create an identity on the blockchain network using this module, which stores personal information like name, date of birth, contact information, and medical history.
  2. Electronic health record creation: The secure and tamper-proof creation and storage of electronic health records (EHRs) on the blockchain network, ensuring that authorized healthcare providers have access to accurate, complete patient health data.
  3. Access control and authentication: In order to guarantee the confidentiality and integrity of health data, this module is used to authenticate users and control access to health records
  4. Data sharing and interoperability: ensures interoperability between various blockchain networks by sharing health data among various healthcare providers and systems.
  5. Data analytics and reporting: To support clinical decision-making, research, and quality improvement, analyze health data and produce reports.
  6. Smart contracts: A smart contract is a transaction protocol or computer program designed to automatically execute, control, or record events and actions as specified in a contract or agreement.

Challenges in the Security of Health Records in Blockchain

The key challenges in securing health records using consortium blockchains are

  1. Interoperability: Standardization and compatibility between various blockchain networks are required to ensure seamless data exchange in order to overcome the difficulty of interoperability when securing health records using a consortium blockchain
  2. Scalability: Due to the requirement of a robust infrastructure that is able to support the growth of the blockchain and handle a high volume of transactions, securing health records
  3. Security: attacks such as 51% attacks, double-spending attacks, and other forms of malicious activity. Robust security measures such as strong authentication, access controls, and encryption must be implemented to prevent unauthorized access to health data

Consortium blockchain technology

Compared to a public blockchain & private blockchain network, a consortium blockchain is more secure, scalable, and effective. Like mixed and private blockchains, it has access restrictions.

The structure of the paper is as follows: Section 2, various use cases of blockchain technology are discussed, and in Section 3, the related work on security enhancement of blockchain technology in electronic health records is covered. Section 4 illustrates the existing system of EHR detection. The proposed work on blockchain technology based on security enhancement of electronic health records using consortium blockchain is presented in Section, and the conclusion is presented in Section 5.

Use Case of Blockchain Technology

Secure sharing of data: Secure data sharing between various healthcare providers can be made possible by blockchain-based EHR systems, allowing for improved collaboration and care coordination.

Data control by the patient: Blockchain-based EHR systems give patients more control over their health data because they can grant or deny access to their data as needed.

Enhanced data precision: Blockchain-based EHR frameworks can guarantee information precision by carrying out information approval and confirmation components, which can diminish mistakes and irregularities in well-being information.

Clinical research and trials: EHRs based on the blockchain can make it easier to share health data for clinical trials and research by protecting privacy and confidentiality.

Related work

Blockchain technology has been used in education, agribusiness, and healthcare, according to the literature review (Almery et al., 2019). Identified the potential of blockchain in enhancing the transparency and security of educational data through a systematic review of blockchain- based applications in education (Rocha et al., 2021). Proposed a blockchain-based electronic health record system that aims to enhance the trustworthiness of healthcare data and improve patient outcomes. The authors of Mahmoud et al. (2019) conducted a systematic review of blockchain technology in healthcare and identified the potential of blockchain in enhancing data privacy, security, and interoperability of healthcare data. Reegu et al. (2021) conducted a systematic review of blockchain applications in agribusiness and highlighted the potential of blockchain in enhancing supply chain management and traceability of agricultural products. Makridakis and Christodoulou (2019) highlighted the potential of blockchain in enhancing trust, transparency, and security in a variety of domains. Alex et al. (2022) highlighted the need for effective security and privacy mechanisms to ensure the trustworthiness of blockchain-based systems and discussed the security and privacy challenges in blockchain applications.

According to the review of the available literature, blockchain technology can enhance education, agribusiness, and healthcare’s transparency, security, and trustworthiness. However, in order to ensure the successful implementation of blockchain-based systems, scalability, interoperability, and regulatory compliance must also be addressed.

Existing Model for Patient Data Manage- ment Illustrate in Fig. 1

The traditional method of keeping track of medical records is difficult and requires a lot of space to store all of a patient’s test results. The data in previously used systems is unstructured, making data exchange challenging. Therefore, we intend to implement the provided model for managing health records in blockchain using Medicare in order to resolve the aforementioned issues. The medical industry is being transformed by blockchain-based EHR.

To build trust in the medical industry, it addresses the majority of the issues that arise today. It not only provides a fast and empowering system but also a dependable platform for the exchange of patient data. Utilizing an electronic health record (EHR) can significantly reduce the amount of time and effort required to manage patient data and produce results that are both effective and efficient.

Proposed Security Enhancement of Elec- tronic Health Records Using Consortium Block Chain

The doctors and patients should register the patient management system with a unique identifying address. After registering a patient can find a doctor and book an appointment. The doctor can request access to the patient’s electronic health record after registering with the system. The doctor can look at the patient’s records if the patient agrees to share their EHR information and the same applies to patients to view doctor information. Once the transaction request is validated, the block will be added to chain.

The working of proposed consortium blockchain technology has been illustrated in Fig. 2.

  1. Establishing a blockchain consortium network is created by a number of healthcare providers and stakeholders involved in the management of electronic health records.
  2. Patient identification and registration on the blockchain network, patients’ identities are protected through encryption, digital signatures, and two- factor authentication.
  3. Electronic health records creation when creating and storing electronic health records on the blockchain network, data integrity and confidentiality are guaranteed by access controls and encryption.
  4. Access control and authentication clients are verified with advanced marks and two- factor validation to forestall unapproved admittance to wellbeing records, which are controlled by both the patients and doctors.
  5. Data sharing and interoperability by sharing health data among various healthcare providers and systems, standardization, and compatibility measures guarantee interoperability between various blockchain networks.

Conclusion

The private blockchain has more restrictions as only the owners of able to manage the data- sharing privileges. The public blockchain is vulnerable to threats as all can participate in the network. To a tamper-proof, decentralized, and permission environment for storing and sharing patient data, consortium blockchain is the best solution as it improves the security of electronic health records (EHRs) with fewer restrictions and more security. The proposed EHR management using consortium blockchain leverage the existing restrictions and vulnerabilities of private and public blockchains by converging the advantages of both blockchains. It increases transparency and security as the health records are effectively managed by both the patients and doctors. In the future, the work will be extended by integrating the blockchain with machine learning to identify anomalies in the healthcare network.

Deep Learning Model for Segmentation of Brain Tumor in MRI Images

Kamani Praveena, Mopati Gowtham Reddy and S. Sathya Priya38

Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

E-mail: praveena.kamani@gmail.com, mopatigowthamreddy@gmail.com

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-48

Abstract

Segmenting brain tumors manually from the numerous magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images generated in cancer diagnosis labs is a challenging and intensive undertaking. Segmenting a brain tumor is a necessary step in the processing of a medical image. Early diagnosis of the brain tumor improves the chances for successful treatment and improves the survival rates. The proposed method is divided into three categories: MRI image preprocessing, data augmentation, and segmentation. The models like UNet, AlexNet, and LeNet don’t include data augmentation, so the accuracy of the model is reduced. So in the proposed system, the three data augmentation techniques Cropping, Rotation, and Shifting are included to the CNN and ResNet models to improve the accuracy. An adaptive filter is used during the image pre-processing stage to get rid of the noise in the MRI picture. In order to visualize the presence of tumor in brain, image segmentation is utilized. Also utilized a deep learning model to categorize different sorts of pictures. Hence, the segmentation of brain images for tumor identification becomes necessary. CNN and ResNet models were used to create picture segmentation in an effort to solve current issues, and utilizing data augmentation, the model’s accuracy was improved. The proposed CNN method is compared with the ResNet model.

Keywords: Deep Learning, Convolutional Neural Networks, Segmentation, Fully Connected Layers, Pooling Layers, and Activation Function

Introduction

To train and optimize complicated models, deep learning needs a lot of data and processing capacity. Additionally, it necessitates careful adjustment of the hyperparameters and critical thought on the moral implications of using the models. Deep learning is still an active area of research and development as a result, with lots of room for growth and use. An aberrant cell or tissue growth in the brain can cause the formation of a brain tumor. Currently, neither the particular causes of brain tumors nor their symptoms are known. Hence brain tumors may be present in persons who are unaware of how serious their condition is. To preserve the patient’s life, early tumor detection and removal are essential. For early detection, the MRI is a crucial tool. However, analyzing an MRI image requires expertise, time, and effort. Furthermore, manually detecting tumors is extremely difficult, and depending on the level of knowledge, the results can vary from clinical expert to clinical expert. In many clinical applications, MM is an essential step, as it impacts the overall outcome of the examination. Precise segmentation of anatomical regions is necessary for various processing steps, including surgical planning, image-guided interventions, lesion delineation, and measuring and visualizing different brain regions, among others that rely on it. Due to the wide range of image processing applications, numerous segmentation algorithms have been created, each with varying degrees of complexity and precision. A brain tumor is one of the most deadly conditions that individuals today might have.

Typically, tumors are visible all across the brain. Less cancers in the brain may make it more challenging to identify them by image processing methods or manually segmenting images, which may have an impact on how the body operates. Finding dangerous tumors in diverse body parts and treating them in a timely manner are difficult tasks. The signs of these tumors didn’t appear for a very long time before they posed a major threat to human life. Personality changes, memory loss, hearing or speech difficulties, frequent headaches, vision loss, and memory loss can all be brought on by brain disorders. Semantic segmentation, object detection, and image categorization are just a few of the computer vision problems that deep learning techniques have shown promise in solving. Brain tumors have been divided using a variety of deep learning-based algorithms, with positive results. The primary goal of this approach is to distinguish malignancies from healthy brain tissue. Here, deep learning-based MRI image segmentation of brain cancers saves millions of lives through early diagnosis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MM) can improve patient survival by finding brain malignancies earlier. Brain tumor predictions made using the CNN model on MRI scans can help patients receive therapies much more quickly and accurately. Existing systems like Unet, LeNet, AlexNet, and ZfNet, which take a lot of time to analyze images, do not incorporate data decompression.

The results are accurate since data enrichment enhances the image quality. Not only is the classification of tumor types the primary driver but also the identification of brain cancers. Also, it supports clinical practice and offers helpful information for planning a diagnosis and a course of therapy. Materials and Methods

The proposed method in fig1 is CNN based MRI segmentation to segment brain tumors from MRI images, using the CNN model. Pre- processing, CNN segmentation are key phases of the suggested methodology. In the proposed system Fig1, images of the brain are collected. Data preprocessing is performed to remove noisy data from the image. The images are then trained and validated. The model is trained on CNN. 2D image data augmentation is applied. Therefore, the accuracy of image processing is improved. This is how brain tumors are segmented from brain tissue.

In the proposed system, Medical images are collected followed by sorting the images based on the number of masks present and what each mask represents. The next step is to visualize the data through graphical depiction and by using the technique called Data Augmentation, the size of dataset is fictitiously expanded through various transformations like Rotation and Shifting.

  1. Data Collection: Collection of data sets from Kaggle that contain all of the images. Sorting the images based on the number of masks present and what each mask represents. In an MRI scan, the automated system would be able to identify and pinpoint the precise position of the tumor.
  2. Data visualization: The graphical depiction of data and information is referred to as data visualization. It is a way to communicate complex data in a way that is easy to understand and interpret. Data visualization can take many forms, including charts, graphs, maps, and infographics. Some common examples of data visualization include line charts, bar charts, scatter plots, heat maps, and bubble charts.

  3. Data Augmentation: By creating new samples through various transformations, data augmentation is a method used in machine learning and deep learning to fictitiously expand the size of a training dataset. It is often used in computer vision applications, such as image recognition, where the number of available training examples is limited.

    Random rotations: Rotating the image by a random angle to create a new example.

    Shifting: Moving the image pixels in one direction.

  4. Training the model: The model is trained on the preprocessed data using a suitable optimization algorithm. The training process involves training, validation, and testing sets and using the data augmentation technique to improve the model’s performance.

CNNs are made up of several layers, each of which serves a specific purpose in the learning process. In summary, CNNs extract features with convolutional layers, introduce nonlinearity with ReLU layers, reduce feature map size with pooling layers, prevent overfitting with dropout layers, and make the final classification decision with fully connected layers. CNNs can learn complex patterns in image and video data and get cutting- edge performance on a variety of recognition tasks by combining these layers in a deep learning architecture.

Conclusion

The categorization of brain tumors was separated into four categories Glioma, Meningioma, no tumor, and Pituitary tumors. The most current data augmentation techniques for segmenting brain tumors from an MRI are analyzed and the data augmentation tactics utilized in these approaches are explored. According to the findings, adding additional data improves the prediction potential of the model. Lastly, similar approaches may be easily applied to both single-modal and multi- modal scans, generally by generating bogus instances specifically for each visual modality. The suggested technique’s performance was evaluated on the Kaggle dataset utilizing the Keras and Tensorflow Python tools with testing and training data. Cropping, Rotation, and Shifting are also included as Data Augmentation techniques for the CNN and ResNet models, and the two models were compared to existing models that performed better. Utilizing MR images, the proposed method correctly diagnosed the tumors 91% of the time. Further Augmentation techniques, including flipping and shearing, might be used in the future to increase the accuracy of the suggested system.

Embedding Intelligence on Edge Computing for the Classification of IoT Data Using Machine Learning with Deep Autoencoder

S. Sujiritha and Linda Joseph

Department of Computer Science, Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India

E-mail: sujiritha.s11@gmail.com, linda24in@gmail.com

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-49

Abstract

There is a demand for a centralized system or cloud storage due to the massive amount of data produced by numerous IoT devices. But there is a possibility of network traffic or data packet loss. In order to prevent this, Edge Computing is introduced. Keeping the edge device close to the source helps perform computation much easier. By embedding intelligence on the edge, less data will be sent to the cloud, allowing it to keep only the data that is necessary. Since edge computing has limitations on computational capacity, the proposed framework, Machine learning with Deep Autoencoder is a lightweight approach. This approach divides the data into normal and problem data, with only the problem data being sent to the cloud via edge gateway. Using the Deep Autoencoder, the problem data is compressed at the edge and reconstructed at the cloud end. Thus, the reconstructed data can be visualized to analyze the abnormalities seen from the sensor to take appropriate action.

Keywords: Internet of Things (IoT), Edge Computing, Machine Learning (ML), Deep Autoencoder

Introduction

Edge computing can be referred to as a computational process of sensor data toward various data sources, close to the edge of the network and away from centralized nodes. It may be defined as a distributed IT network architecture that allows mobile computing to produce data locally Shen et al., (2021). Rather than relying on centralized cloud data centers, edge computing distributes processing power to safeguard real-time processing without loss of data while maintaining storage space bandwidth and on the network. Without edge computing, IoT today is functional across a wide spectrum of use cases (Ashouri et al., 2019).

Edge computing, however, may become a key enabler as more and more things become connected and as we investigate use cases with progressively stricter latency, bandwidth, and security requirements (Ananda Mohon Ghosh & Katarina Grolinger, 2021; Junlong Li et al., 2022) . But there are still questions and difficulties that will determine how much of an impact edge computing will have on IoT in the future (Liu et al., 2021). These include technical difficulties with assuring the edge infrastructure’s physical security (Hastbacka et al., 2022), as this infrastructure is likely to be used to store data outside of the extremely safe setting of dedicated data centers. Another technical challenge that many platforms are attempting to address is how to solve interoperability problems and make device management and control simpler.

While edge computing can enable real-time processing of data, many IoT edge devices, like sensors, do not have enough computational power to carry out any deep learning algorithms locally which may be complex (Wisultschew et al., 2022). As a result, these devices may rely on cloud or centralized systems which are used for storage and computational processing. Nevertheless, there are also efforts to develop more lightweight machine learning models that can be implemented directly on edge devices, such as sensors, without relying on cloud or centralized systems. These models, known as edge AI models, are designed to be more computationally efficient and require less memory and processing power than traditional deep learning models. This can help enable real- time processing and analysis of data directly on the edge devices, without transmitting data to a central system. Combining both edge and cloud computing has the likely to overcome the latency and support complex data analytics tasks. Considering Edge-Cloud, maximum features to be reduced can be a challenging problem. However, transferring all the data to the cloud is not feasible for computation as well as for storage (Ghosh & Grolinger, 2021; Li et al., 2020)and requires edge devices to act and perform computation (Liu et al., 2021). In this paper, only the necessary IoT sensor data is transferred to the cloud leaving the others.

Machine learning can be a powerful tool for classifying IoT data, as it enables the automatic identification and classification of patterns and trends within the data. This can help to unlock insights and drive better decision-making in a variety of domains, such as manufacturing, healthcare, and smart cities. Applications of ML for classifying IoT data include predictive maintenance in manufacturing, anomaly detection in healthcare, and traffic flow prediction in smart cities. By using ML to classify IoT data, organizations can gain new insights, optimize operations, and improve decision-making.

Section 5 presents the evaluation of the paper. Section 6 shows the result. Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper.

Related Work

This section presents the combination of IoT- Edge-Cloud for different applications using algorithms of various sorts. Edge computing is playing a major role in the present day by connecting IoT and the cloud for purposes like storage, computation, alarm, prediction, gaining insights, etc.

Ghosh & Grolinger,(2021) investigated integration of edge and cloud computing by means of decreasing network traffic and latencies for IoT based data using Autoencoder. Sliding window is applied for data reduction (Fekri et al., 2020; Essien & Giannetti, 2020)and network traffic reduction Ghosh & Grolinger,(2021). On the other hand, Ferrari et al., (2020) examined the personalization of Human Activity Recognition models and carried out sliding windows and the generation of input features. Li et al., (2022)used fog computing to provide privacy protection for the data getting from smart grid via SCADA while transferring from IoT to cloud.

Essien & Giannetti (2020)proposed ConvLSTMAE which is a multi-step machine speed prediction for time series data. The presented framework of both Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) combined which extracts features for representation and sequential learning respectively. Finally, the encoder and decoder for dimensionality reduction which ultimately reduced the computational demands and the time taken for training.

Pelle et al., (2021)introduced the public serverless E-C platform which uses the AWS Greengrass making it easier for computation on edge. On the other hand, Wisultschew et al., (2022)shift the computing from cloud to the edge of IoT. Deep Neural Networks (DNN) work well with high-volume data in terms of accuracy. This paper uses different edge architectures for object classification and compares them to make a perfect solution for IoT applications.

Lahasan & Samma (2022)attain a lightweight model, an effective two-layer optimizer that develops a lightweight Deep AE model by carrying out instantaneous selection for the input features, the number of hidden neurons and the number of training instances. The dataset is normalized where all the features are scaled to [0,1] using a min-max scaler (Fekri et al., 2020; Lahasan & Samma, 2022).

Cheng et al. (2021) used a framework, Transformation Invariant AutoEncoder (TIAE), that accomplishes constant and better performance for unsupervised outlier detection by learning high-level semantic features. For each epoch, it incorporates self-paced learning for training the dataset. Queiroz et al. (2022) use fuzzy recommendation system which identifies data analysis needed at a certain layer of cloud-edge-IoT.

Proposed Framework

This section represents Machine learning with Deep Autoencoder. The proposed framework for IoT devices to identify the abnormal behaviors from the sensor using the proposed algorithm at the edge device and making a Visualization of the problem data to analyze the issues.

Data Preprocessing

Normalization: Data standardization is accomplished using the pre-processing method of normalization. Having various data sources that fall within the same range. It can be problematic for the network to train if the data is not normalized prior to training, which will significantly slow down learning. The min-max scaling can be used for normalizing the data. The formula for a min-max of [0, 1] is given as:


$$x^{\prime} = \frac{x - \min(x)}{\max(x) - \min(x)}$$

Where x represents the actual value, max( x ) and min( x ) are the maximum and minimum of the feature values and represents the standardized value.

Parallel processing: In the context of autoencoders, n_jobs could potentially be used for data preparation or other parts of the training process that do not involve the neural network itself. For example, n_jobs could be used to parallelize loading the data and pre-processing steps before feeding the data into the autoencoder for training. This can be useful for large datasets where loading and pre-processing the data can be time-consuming.

Deep Autoencoder

This algorithm shown in Fig. 1, will help with compressing the huge data being transferred from edge to cloud with the encoder-decoder concept. Encoder at the edge side and decoder at the cloud side. At the cloud side, the compressed data is reproduced to its original state.

Feature selection: To overcome the limitation of overfitting from happening, Embedded methods like regularization L1 and L2 is carried out for feature selection which by Selecting the best features help the model to perform well.

a) LI Regularization - L1 helps to overcome overfitting as well as improves the efficiency of the model. L1 regularizer can also be used for feature selection since it sets the weights of unrelated features to zero.


$$\left. f = \frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{L = 1}^{N}{(\hat{y} - y)}^{2} + \lambda\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N} \middle| \theta_{i} \right|$$

Where N is the number of features. λ represents the regularization parameter and θ is a sum of vectors. y and y’ are the actual and predicted value.

ML Classifier

The encoded data is classified into normal and problem data which is separated using Logistic Regression (LR) model since the data comes closer to linearly separable after encoding. Logistic regression can identify a linear decision boundary that separates the data into different classes. However, when the data is not linearly separable, logistic regression may not be able to find a good decision boundary and may lead to poor classification performance. SVMs work by finding the hyperplane that best separates the data into different classes, where a hyperplane is a decision boundary that maximizes the margin between the classes. Thus, it can be compared with original data being classified using Support Vector Machine (SVM) as its accuracy is comparatively similar to the classification of encoded data. The separated problem data is easily transferred to the cloud.

Implementation on Edge Device

Data normalization is a common pre-processing step in machine learning, which involves scaling and shifting the values of a dataset so that they fall within a specific range. The goal is to ensure that different features in the dataset are on a similar scale, which can increase the efficiency of the model, and make it easier to interpret the results. Autoencoders ( Kurihana et al., 2022; Ohashi et al., 2021; Chinnasamy et al., 2023) are a type of neural network that can be used for unsupervised learning tasks, such as data compression, feature extraction, and anomaly detection. They consist of two main parts: an encoder which can be used to map the input to a lower-dimensional latent space, and a decoder which rebuilds the original data from the latent space representation.

This algorithm will help with compressing the huge data being transferred from edge to cloud with the encoder-decoder concept. To overcome the limitation of overfitting from happening, Pre-processing step shown in Fig. 2 like regularization is carried out for feature selection which by Selecting the best features helps the model to perform well. Parallel processing reduces the time taken to train the model. Classification of normal and problem data can be done by logistic regression and support vector machine. Each can be used for the classification of encoded data and the original data. The problem data thus gets transferred to the cloud for visualization.

Mean Squared Error, and is a mainly used metric for evaluating the performance of regression models. It calculates the average squared difference between the predicted and original values of the target variable. The formula for calculating MSE is as follows:

(4)
$$MSE = \frac{1}{n}\underset{n}{\overset{i = 1}{\sum^{}}}{(y_{i} - {\hat{y}}_{i})}^{2}$$

Where n is the total number of data points, yi is the actual value of the target variable for the i-th data point and ŷi is the predicted value of the target variable for the i-th data point.

Experimental Result

The experimental result provided by the implementation of ML with Deep Autoencoder is presented in this section. This part includes the different metrics which is used for checking the performance of the proposed model. These include: Accuracy, precision, Fl score, and recall shown in Table III. Precision and recall are two important metrics for evaluating the performance of a binary classification model, which classifies examples into one of two classes, typically labeled as positive or negative.

Precision calculates the ratio of true positive predictions amongst all positive predictions made by the model. It is calculated as:

(5)
$$Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$$

Recall calculates the ratio of true positive predictions amongst all actual positive examples in the dataset. It is calculated as:

(6)
$$Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$

The Fl score is a frequently used metric for evaluating the performance of a binary classification model, which is the mean of precision and recall. It can be calculated as follows:


$$F1\ Score = \frac{(2 \ast Precision \ast Recall)}{(Precision + Recall)}$$

Where TP represents the true positive, FP and FN are the false positive and false negative respectively.

From Table 3, we can conclude that ML with Deep Autoencoder is only suitable for large datasets unlike small datasets like Smartwatch data. The performance and accuracy of the model are not up to the mark when dealing with a small dataset. In general, a high Fl score indicates that the suggested model is performing well in terms of both precision and recall. 7 Conclusion

By sending sensor data to any centralized system or to the cloud from IoT devices for processing and storing. Increased latencies and strain on communication networks and computations involved in cloud would result due to the expansion of linked devices. This paper investigates the combination of edge as well as cloud computing for IoT to decrease data loss and the computation at cloud side by minimizing the input features and selecting the appropriate data which is needed for monitoring and identifying issues utilizing the suggested approach. With the use of ML and Deep Autoencoder, computation can be executed efficiently and inexpensively on the edge. In the end, the suggested algorithm helps data from IoT devices get transmitted to the cloud without any need for further computation and data cleaning of the IoT data. At the cloud’s end, the minimized data get reproduced and used it to make visualization to identify issues and gain insights leaving cloud with less computation and space storage.

Future work will involve working with real-time world data and adding features to the proposed framework like alert messages getting from the cloud via an Android application or mail.

Teens, Screens, and Mental Health- A Study on Digital Wellbeing

Elizabeth Leah George39

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-50

Abstract

Social media is a new trend of socializing, communicating, and maintaining friendships among the young and old. Major amount of time is spent interacting through a screen, the conversations in the digital space through texting, Instagram posts, and Facebook comments, Twitter tweets make it difficult to understand unexplained emotional changes. This minor research study examines the different ways in which social media impacts social comparisons among individuals of different age groups, and how this influence affects their overall physical and mental well-being. The study specifically focuses on the digital paradigm shift of social comparisons brought about by social media use. The study explores the frequency of social media usage, cyberbullying, sleep patterns, FOMO, and self-identity using questionnaires as primary data. A classification of mental health-related tweets with accuracy parameters can relate to health data analysis. Data visualization to understand the most influential parameter of digital well-being is relevant to social media.

Keywords: Social media, Mental health, Sentiment Analysis, Naive Bayes, K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic regression, Data Visualization

Introduction

Social media is a forum that captures real time moods of users in different forms of communication. In a study #status of Mind by the royal society for public health mental disorders have been taken as a serious public health problem. Many of the individuals with depression go undetected. Various theories and research studies have found profound influence on social relationships that can help young people manage the challenges of adolescence, reduce face-face communication, freely express ideas online, and anonymity in internet communication for identity formation. The digital platform allows people from all different age groups to connect with one another globally creating an impact on both the physical and emotional health of a person.

An individual’s mental health varies depending on their age group, gender, line of work, and social environment. Similar to how a person’s mental health is influenced by their dietary habits, way of life, sleeping patterns, and extracurricular activities.Individuals ranging in age from 14 to over 45 access social media. Depending on their ages, it has different consequences on their mental and physical health. This research paper aims to analyze how social media usage affects an individual’s mental health regardless of age.

Related Papers

The reviews by Hilal Bashir (2017) explore the correlation between adolescents’ mental health and their use of social media. It delves into identifying the specific social media platforms the findings of the survey, adolescents who spent more than 2 hours per day using social media tended to have lower levels of mental well-being compared to those who used it for less than 2 hours. that exert a considerable impact on mental well- being with a focus on social relationships and mental health, social media and anxiety, stress, depression, loneliness, etc of any age group. The Studies by Stones (2019) have mentioned mental issues in youngsters such as Cyber-bullying, body image concerns, irregular sleep cycles, and self- abuse due to social media, and provided valuable resolutions for each problem such as reducing screen time, portraying yourself without makeup and filters, blocking/reporting abusive and offensive content, etc. Latest studies by Mireya Marquez (2022) portrayed a comparison between Millennials (1981-1995), and Generation-Z (1996-2012) with a self-respond survey using Bergen social media addiction scale, Beck depression inventory (BDI), the generalized anxiety disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7), Rosenberg self-esteem scale (RSES) to check how long an individual is using social media, which platform is used majorly by them and to check their present mental state and in the past if they were under any medication due to social media. After conducting the survey, they came up with the conclusion that generation-Z faces more depression, anxiety, and loss of self-esteem compared to the millennial generation. A similar survey conducted by Anjali Singh (2020), the mental health effects of social media were examined among 100 adolescents aged between 16 to 18 years old which includes stress, depression, anxiety, etc. The scale which they used for collecting data was proposed by Lovibond (1995). Lovibond Then they used several statistical tests to examine. According to

Methodology

The information gathered here is divided into two categories: primary data and secondary data. Actual questionnaires conducted using Google Forms were used to gather primary data and Twitter web scraping was used to gather the secondary data. 275 responses were cleaned from the core data and 1000 plus data was retrieved from the web using several keywords. The objective is to establish that the conclusions drawn from primary data regarding the influence of social media on mental health are equivalent to those obtained from secondary data through comparison and demonstration.

Various studies, such as Abbasi (2008), Chau (2012), and Ceron (2014), where machine learning has been widely used in text-based contextual classification and object recognition, resulting in successful applications in fields such as sentiment and affect analysis. Cambria (2013) and Feldman (2013) are examples of research that have demonstrated on the effectiveness of machine learning in sentiment and affect analysis. Nonverbal behavior analysis (Subasic, 2000) is used as a key to automatically understanding social interactions. The cues can then be used as machine-detectable evidence for automated analysis and understanding of social behavior. The performance of the machine learning approaches can be improvised with a rule-based classification approach (Hutto, 2014; Neviarouskaya, 2010; Wu, 2006).Datasets: Collection of Primary dataPrimary data was collected through a survey that was spread online across different age groups where the intended age ranged from 14 to 18, 18 to 30, 30 to 45, and 45+. They were questioned about their screen time uses, frequently used platforms, and their physical and mental well-being. After the survey was completed 275 responses were gathered. The outcome of the survey’s key questions are as follows: 141(51.3%) of the total replies are from women and 134(48.7%) are from men. The highest response rate 213(77.5%) came from respondents who were 18 to 30 years old while the lowest 18(6.5%) came from respondents who were 30 to 45 years old. The usage pattern of social users have their time spent on social media as 2-3hrs (41.8%), 3-5 hrs (25.1%), and more than five hours (19.6%). According to our survey, 207(75.3%) respondents chose Instagram as their most used app, which is consistent with the fact that it is one of the most widely used social networking applications thanks to its appealing features. WhatsApp is the second most popular app 206(74.9%) that practically everyone uses. A few more frequently utilized apps include Facebook, Linkedln, and YouTube. The survey revealed that social media has an impact on both their physical and mental health with stress on pain in the head, eyes, neck, and body, interrupted sleep etc are few examples of how social media negatively affects people’s physical health. Similar repercussions on mental health include anxiety, depression, stress, and development of an inferiority complex, etc.

Collection of Secondary data:

Web scraping to extract secondary data from Twitter using the keywords #mentalhealth, #mentalhealthandwellbeing, #healthandwellbeing, and #MHSM. Data was collected from over 1000 tweets using the hashtags #mentalhealth, #mentalhealthandwellbeing, #healthandwellbeing, #MHSM. A total of 1531 tweets were collected as secondary data. Tweets are randomly sampled, 80-20 training tests are distributed across the dataset, and all classifiers are trained and scored. Sentiment analysis, also known as opinion mining with computational linguistics, enables us to determine the sentiment of provided data, whether it is positive, negative, or neutral as shown in Fig. 2. Machine learning algorithms make predictions, discover hidden patterns, and improve performance. We employed a range of machine learning techniques, including the Naive Bayes classifier, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), to analyze our data sets.

Results and Discussions

The experiments and results discussed are the outcomes of the methodology. The pre- processing of the collected data is mentioned with classification scores, sample influence measures, and recommendations for sentiments. The keywords from Twitter taken are based on mental health keywords such as #mentalhealth, #mentalhealthandwellbeing, #healthand wellbeing, #MHSM. For the above keywords, a sentiment analysis is done to find the polarity of the keyword. The same dataset is analyzed through Gephi to find the influential nodes based on three categories (Text-Location), (User-Text), and (User-Location) as in Fig. 3.

The communities formed are chosen and the modularity is calculated as in Fig. 4. The sentiment analysis approach used for the posts involved a classification strategy to determine whether a tweet was related to mental health or not. Using SVM classification, the multi-class classification approach achieved an 81% accuracy rate in identifying mental health conditions. The results of all four classifiers remained high, resulting in an overall weighted average of high precision, recall, and Fl score, as shown in the table below. It was observed that the overall accuracy of the classifiers varied based on the content of the tweets collected. The model provided better accuracy with higher tweet content. The mean Reciprocal rank (MRR) measure was used to weigh the probability distribution for each prediction and account for the ranked order of true calculations compared to actual predictions. MRR consistently outperformed accuracy for all classifiers.

Conclusion

Digital well-being is an utmost important health influence based on mental and emotional satisfaction. It spans the way social networking tools impact social measures to lead a healthy and positive life. This minor research is a small initiative taken to understand mental well- being and physical health among different age groups using a questionnaire method. The study reveals comments Positive approach for users as an excellent platform for self- exploration, an advertising platform to pursue their career and encourage others, and a platform for news, information, spiritual and educational content, blogs, videos, and other forms of communication. Negative remarks of a confused mind with negative comments and posts deal with crimes, gender discrimination, and harassment of people. Social media takes up too much time and attention, often disrupting sleep patterns, causing memory loss, impairing academic performance, and leading users to begin comparing their lives to those of others. It appears that being always online is something that young people love “Fear of Missing — Out (FoMO).” Adolescence is also plagued by mental health issues, including depression, anxiety, etc.

The minor research carried out in social media was modeled on the basis of a collection of posts based on mental health keywords to create a dataset, the tweets analyzed had set parameters and user tags that formed small communities where the machine learning algorithms showed accuracy in classification to detect various mental disorders.

AI-Enabled Human and Machine Activity Monitoring in IIOT Systems

S. Sridevi and S. T. Deepa

Associate Professor, SSS Shasun Jain College for Women, Chennai

E-mail: sridevi@shasuncollege.edu.in, stdeepa@shasuncollege.edu.in

DOI: 10.1201/9781003430452-51

Abstract

For the past few decades, getting insights from industrial systems are explored a lot, for timely decision-making, right from the era of switches, pneumatic gauges, PID controls, PLC/DCS to current IIoT automation, where over a trillion dollars are spent in research & manufacturing globally. Cyber physical systems along with recent advances in AI, ML, Cloud, Edge, virtual computing power, high volume streaming services and real-time big data analytics have enhanced information collection, exchange, analysis, decision making & control to much higher levels. Similarly, human activity monitoring plays a key role in elderly care, disease detection, assisted living & remote consulting. The prevalent human monitoring sensors like PIR, GPS & HD cameras are expensive and have limitations like compatibility with existing systems. The proposed model HMAMnet is built over device-free localization, hybrid capsule CNN combined with Model predictive controls (MPC) methods for input( s) optimization. Standard protocols like OPC enables open device connectivity and data exchange. The model process enriched activity data from popular IOT datasets, with random Smote & PCA methods, and with appropriate choice hyperparameters, this not only makes the model robust with enhanced accuracy but also insights to control input parameters to get the desired output pattern. Industrial advantages of these solutions include increased uptime, productivity, quality, and revenue while reducing the cost of ownership, maintenance, energy, and waste. This module supplements the digital twin simulation process, with trends of environmental behavior patterns. Thus, the idea enhances the intelligence of activity monitoring systems, to auto-sense, process, decide & act, over the possible scenarios, in industrial and social domains.

Keywords: Human Machine activity monitoring, IIOT, MPC, CapsuleNet, Predictive control, CNN

Introduction

The invent of Internet of Things (IoT) (Rose et al., 2015) around 1999, has opened a plethora of applications in connected devices in consumer, automotive, business, industrial & domestic spaces Beecham Research (2014). IoTs widespread adoption simplified processes and opened new avenues there were not feasible earlier. In healthcare, it helps from remote consulting to elderly care by remote monitoring their vitals and activities, disease detection to assisted living & Medication adherence. IACS processes were well established over the last few decades. While the first 3 industrial revolutions are based on steam, electricity, and robot automation & electronics, industry 4.0 (Moller, 2016) is widely based on IOTs, sensors, and machine learning to create smart products, smart production, and smart services (The fourth ICT-based industrial revolution, 2015).

The inherent distributed but connected nature of IOT, along with the digital technologies backbone, proposes a simpler alternative to industrial control systems and resolved the data sharing & visibility issues across enterprises. While still the performance, availability, and security are the threats for its widespread adoption, this chapter proposes a framework for IIOT components to intelligently monitor & control machine activities schematically. Below section describes the characteristics of IIOT & the principles governing its operations (Boyes et al., 2018).

IIOT Governing Principles & Characteristics

IIOT Governing principles typically include: 1. IIOT to offer Perpetual & continuous connectivity with the environment to Monitor, Maintain, and Monetize (the 3 M’s); 2. IoT resolves large Analog data conversion problems. The big data derived from physical world, people, devices, environment & things in real-time is massive. it is mostly sensor acquired and digitized via A/D converters; 3. IOT data is Real-time and the data from thousands of sensors and actuators pump through the PLC/DCS and we need robust Real-time DB and infrastructure to store & process its historic trends; 4. Business, Engineering, and scientific insights can be derived from IIOT data in real-time, motion, rest, or archival stages; 5. IOT outputs present a real Time to insight at acquisition vs In-depth historic data analysis needs and take control actions; 6. IIOT improves edge data visibility throughout an enterprise, along with its traditional goals of handling data volume with velocity, value, and variety; 7. The shift towards Operational technology ( OT), with high-performance computing, virtualization, improved latency, bandwidth, security, duplication, reliability, etc. to distributed devices, shall eventually collapse different layers of data flow from distributed IOTs to IT-cloud, which saves space, energy, and deployment time.

IIOT Device Characteristics

The functionality, criticality & management of the IOT devices typically defines its characteristic like: a) Criticality defines how important the device is to the ecosystem, and its replacements and usually manufactured with high standards & security compliance; b) Functions like data collection and algorithms used to analyze/transfer data, etc.; c) Interfaces that are used to configure the device and control its operations; d) Relationship with the environment /devices like a temperature sensor sending insights to increase fan speed, close shutter, etc.

Architecture

The proposed 4 stage IIOT architecture depicts all the components of data acquisition, collection, dissemination, analysis, cloud storage & visualization as in Fig. 1.

Primarily the physical systems, environments, machines, devices, people who generate data in real-time like a valve controlling the water level of a tank, a burning kiln and cooler system that can generate thousands of parameters in a cement plant, an accelerating electric vehicle controlled by various sensors over its battery, weight, temperature, etc. The sensors and actuators (motion tracking systems) in stage-1 are the devices that track motion, position, measures mass, temperature, pressure, etc., and convert them to digital signals. It could measure discrete or continuous data feeds. The concentrators in stage-2 are the PLC (Programmable logic controllers), DCS (Distributed control systems), and visualization systems like SCADA (Supervisory control & data acquisition system), connected manufacturing systems & controllers

Stage-3 Edge IT systems transfer the data transferred from distributed systems to higher IT environments like cloud, virtualization, etc. IoT edge computing resolves the latency problems linked with the cloud, as data is processed in proximity to its point of origin. For example, devices in large distributed mobile communication towers can be synced with IOT edge model. Remote IT and enterprise IT systems on cloud processing these plant floor data and disseminating the insights to different stakeholders forms stage 4. Purdue (Williams, 1992) is another popular model which is built on separating the enterprise with different zones like manufacturing, demilitarized, and safety zones for better data security and control.

Connectivity & Data Exchange

Below aspects are critical in devising the connectivity between different layers: a. Mechanism with the devices is connected like wired, wireless, and physical modes; b. The nature of data transfer like Real-Time, offline, or asynchronous; c. Date exchange initiation like, by the device, by receiver or both.; d. Security mechanisms like authentication, identification (mutual or one-way), authorization (by user role), encryption (full or partial); e. Protocols at discovery, infrastructure, data transfer and security layers. Above models provide infrastructure for better Connectivity, Compute, and Control needs of manufacturing and enterprise entities (Bradicich, 2017)

Protocols for IIOT Data Exchange

A software Process is defined as “Program in execution.” When 2 different programs are running in a system, they typically communicate with each other with a set of protocols. The data between these 2 distinct processes are exchanged through “Object Linking and Embedding (OLE)” method. The same concept is extended to do data exchange from a plant control system and an IT monitoring tool with protocols like OPC (OLE for Process control) which was framed during 1996 by OPC foundation and still it is prevalent in industries.

The other popular Inter-process communication (IPC) methods in use since late 80’s are like, Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) (Kostek, 1996), Shared memory where a common memory space is used by both processes, named pipe connections, etc., as supported by the operating system. These are capable of connecting to the process running in another system in network as well like remote named pipes, NetDDE, etc. Thus, protocols like OPC lays the standards that the tools that intend to read/write data to & from proprietary PLC/DCS like ABB, Siemens, Allen-Bradley, etc., through set of communication handshakes and acknowledgment in asynchronous callbacks.

This is typically a COM/DCOM based client-server architecture, where a client system requests the server component running in PLC/DCS with inputs like the field parameter to read/write, its value, and timestamp and get data asynchronously. For example, to decrease the load on a grinding mill having higher vibration, the parameters from mill sound level, measurements, temperature, and grinding pressure sensor are to be read through OPC as input process variables and the input feed to the mill is to be reduced by writing back to the conveyer belt (RPM) speed parameter to maintain the feed set-point parameter of the mill.

The frequently used industrial protocols are: Modbus, EtherNet/IP, PROFIBUS, DeviceNet, IEEE 802.11, TCP ISA100.11a, HART etc (Gutierrez et al., 2018). Due to incompatible nature of these legacy protocols, data interoperability and exchange were always a challenge. Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC UA) is adopted more as it is based on TCP/IP, SOAP & higher security, as compared to older COM/DCOM methods (Ferrari et al., 2018). It can be used in TCP/IP layer or with cross-platform SOAP/https with 128 / 256 bits encryptions as in Fig. 3.

AUML Machine Monitoring & Control

While previous sections highlighted the data extraction and control methods with plant system, Ann models helps to build intelligent control systems over collected data for needed machine activity monitoring and control tasks.

As in Fig. 4, the typical enterprise use cases of plant floor integration are like the client systems, Say an ERP or MES managed by an enterprise IT team requires plant data processing. These systems could use OPC UA protocol and connect to an OPC server running on a PLC/DCS and read and process data. Similarly, plant optimization software that needs to control plant machinery can write on an actuator through OPC protocol.

Machine Monitoring & Control Systems

With the above HMI interfaces plant equipment’s monitored & controlled for operations. Figure 5 describes the various variables (CV, MV, SP, etc.) which are used to control the level of a water tank (CV) to the intended Setpoint (SP) by measuring the error from Setpoint and taking control action on changing the inlet water flow valve position (input manipulated variable (MV).

While the above is a typical control system’s usual use cases in any continuous process industry, today’s world requires to have intelligent control mechanisms which monitor & learn the process dynamics of the environment it operates, tunes itself, and takes control actions to achieve desired results. This chapter proposes such an intelligent monitoring and control prototype, from data collation, learning (ANN), Predictive Control models (MPC), and act-generated insights on time. The AI/ML component in Fig. 4 above, could be expanded to the below proposed monitoring and control flow as in Fig. 6.

HMAMnet Model

The algorithm of the proposed Human & Machine Activity Monitoring network (HMAMnet) is depicted as in Fig. 6. As in the notation list of Fig. 6., SP (Setpoint) is the value in which the plant system to be maintained like the water level of the tank in Fig. 5, to be maintained at 75 feet for a given period. Manipulated variables (MV) is the inlet water valve used to regulate the water flow to the tank & maintain the level (CV)

  1. Let the nonlinear process data [collated by IOT Edge] being modeled be denoted by the difference equation: Ô (t + 1) = O(t- No + 1), I(t), I(t - Ni + 1))

    Where Ô is the output prediction, typically a target variable of the plant (CV). No & Ni are the Past outputs & inputs.

  2. Formulate deep learning neural model: f(x) ∂o (w2 ∂o (W1x + al) + a2) = Ô(t + 1),

    Where ∂o & ∂o — sigmoidal activation functions; W1 & W2: optimized weights matrices & al, a2: bias vectors of output & hidden layers; x = [O(t),..., O(t – No + 1), I(t), ..., I(t - Ni + 1)]T;

  3. The neural network or a capsule convolutional neural network (CNN) model provides predictions like time series value or classification probabilities like an abnormality. The MPC model (model predictive control) which suggested input changes (MV) needed to maintain target setpoint are trained offline.
  4. The process data validated from IIOT/Edge are validated with PCA (Principal Component Analysis) or SVD (Singular Value Decomposition) to include only the influential inputs having a higher impact on predicted output and Weights are serialized to find forthcoming values of Ô.

  5. As above non-linear modeling is impacted by differences in replicating real plant processes, the stabilizer module is introduced to process noise and unknown disturbances in data.

    If model errors are represented as e(t) and if model without process uncertainties is: Ô, then the stable model is denoted as: O(t)= Ô (t) + ê (t)

  6. The above disturbance is restricted to the list of allowable policies defined by the Piecewise Affine function (PWA) of previous disturbances (Bemporad et al., 2004). The nonlinear MPC aims to minimize the cost function to attain the needed set point range the target systems are to be controlled. The HMAMnet output (future MV changes) is validated by a fuzzy optimizer and fed to process and the deviance of CV from setpoint determines the need for online tuning of the model again. The model asymptotically converges faster and closer to the process being modeled.

Thus, the intelligent AI/ML based monitoring and controls as in the proposed HMAMnet model above or at simplified versions to suit use cases are really helpful to avoid human interventions and ensure continuous monitoring of the process parameters by creating a stable environment for the systems to operate. The attributes of HMAMnet are listed in the below table

Table 1 I-IMAMnet characteristics
Parameters Methods used
Process dynamics Non-linear
System Identification ANN / Capsule CNN providing probability/pose of observation
Uncertainties Type Invariant additive disturbances with multiplicative uncertainties
Uncertainty propagation Unbounded disturbance through neural stabilizer model
Control input parameterization Affine parameterization of control policy
Input constraints PCA/SVD
Prediction Constraints Output constrained tubes
Receding-horizon implementation Output feedback
Optimization algorithm Modified GPC cost function

Below Figs. 7 and 8 illustrate the input variance in process variables with disturbances and how the proposed ML model has lesser variance and stable maintenance of controlled output variables over time as compared to manual operations.

IIOT Activity Monitoring Apps, Benefits & Challenges

IIoT has a transformative impact on productivity & operational efficiency across domains from manufacturing to supply chain, significantly with below use cases, benefits, and constraints.

Following are typical applications of industrial IoT: 1. Process monitoring, 2. Temperature / Pressure monitoring, 3. Water quality monitoring, 4. Flow monitoring, 5. Remote asset monitoring, 6. Steam trap monitoring, 7. Machine health monitoring etc.

IIOT Monitoring Benefits

Offloading AI & Analytics capability and load to distributed devices. For example, when a predictive model is deployed on a quality control camera the IoT Edge triggers an alert when there is an issue and processes it locally or sends to the cloud for further analysis. Other benefits include 1. Reduced Downtime, 2. Reduced waste (Man, Machine & Material) 3. Improved System Security & Quality, 4. Proactive Maintenance 5. Valuable Performance Insights 6. Seamless visibility of plant floor data across enterprise; 7. Decreased Cost of Ownership,

IIOT Challenges

Industrial IoT monitoring and control solutions are essential, but most industrial systems have proprietary monitoring solutions in silo. Constructing a unified custom monitoring solution is not practical for large industrial establishments. Customization of widely used industrial interfaces to localization needs is also a deterrent factor; Other challenges are listed below:

 1. Deployment and operation of a remote monitoring system across larger regions or countries is not feasible. 2. Interfacing equipment’s to a third-party monitoring solution makes the process more complex leading to uncertainty. 3. Capabilities from different suppliers with niche or additional features, makes the system more expensive. 4. Existing connectivity network infrastructure of older plants may not aid in the provision of a custom IoT monitoring solution. 5. Creating a custom mix of capabilities from solutions of different vendors can lead to a complex system. 6. To augment the capabilities of built-in systems, often additional instrumentation and sensors are to be added, and data collection capabilities are to be enhanced enterprise-wide.

Conclusion

This chapter introduces the evolution of IIOT from legacy control systems, data acquisition, and aggregation layers along with its Edge distribution to cloud/enterprise-wide network. Various industrial connectivity protocols with elaboration on Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC UA) standards and its client-server communication on TCP/IP & SOAP layers are discussed. OPC UA can also assign manufacturing resources, and embedded systems, to needed areas and extended computing nodes through the address space & pre-built models. Its main advantage is enabling a platform for unified information access to different systems Chen et al. (IEEE)Machine activity monitoring through IIOT forms key areas of Cyber-physical systems and it can be enhanced to service-oriented models (Rojas and Garcia, 2020). Typical Machine Activity monitoring use cases along with the proposed HMAMnet intelligent prediction model prototype are discussed, which fits over the 4 stage IIOT stack to augment needed value. Such custom AI/ML solutions (William and Ferraro, 2022) which could be built over the wealth of inexpensive cloud data collated from IIOT Edge & underlying PLC/DCS systems gives the cost-effective and faster intelligence control advantage over legacy systems.
